articles.title: "Empiezas a comprar camisetas, y luego te salen muchos más anuncios": Zuckerberg descubre la moda a través del algoritmo de Instagram
articles.text:
Si nos ponemos a mirar fotos antiguas de Mark Zuckerberg, el cambio en su estilo es abismal. Lleva el pelo más largo, tiene un aspecto más masculino y su armario ha pasado de los vaqueros y sudaderas grises a camisas de cuello mao, camisetas de diseñador, cadenas y marcas de lujo. El CEO de Meta ha hablado sobre moda y estilo con Vanessa Freidman, la directora de moda del New York Times.
Una nueva afición. Zuckerberg empezó a experimentar con prendas atrevidas durante la pandemia. Solía ponerse bermudas con diseños más atrevidos que nadie podía ver en las largas videollamadas, pero después empezó a mostrarse así en público. El MMA también influyó en su forma de vestir y Zuckerberg empezó a apostar por conjuntos más holgados, inspirados en la ropa que suelen llevar los luchadores. En 2024 se produjo un punto de inflexión cuando mostró su nuevo estilo en una sesión de fotos que le regaló su mujer, Priscilla Chan.
Lo que comenzó como una elección práctica durante el confinamiento se fue convirtiendo en una afición consolidada. Aunque ha habido rumores de que todo formaba parte de una estrategia de marketing con un estilista detrás, en realidad el propio Zuckerberg dedica tiempo a buscar ropa, descubrir marcas y probar distintas combinaciones.
Compras algorítmicas. ¿Dónde se compra la ropa Zuckerberg? Lo lógico sería pensar que acude a tiendas exclusivas de lujo, pero según Priscilla Chan "Creo que nunca ha estado en una tienda". En su lugar, Zuckerberg hace muchas compras a través de Instagram y deja que sea el algoritmo el que le recomiende nuevas prendas: "Empiezas a comprar camisetas, y luego te salen muchos más anuncios de camisetas, y entonces piensas: 'Vale, la verdad es que estas camisetas son mejores que las que compré ayer’". Al preguntarle si cree que estas compras algorítmicas enganchan a los usuarios, responde que no.
Pero comprar por Instagram no siempre le sale bien. Una vez compró una prenda y usó su correo electrónico, su tarjeta de crédito y su dirección particular. La tienda pensó que era alguien haciéndose pasar por él y canceló la compra temiendo que fuese un fraude.
La relación con Meta y las gafas inteligentes. El interés de Zuckerberg por la moda y el diseño coincide con la apuesta de Meta por las gafas inteligentes. El objetivo, más que venderlas como un simple wearable tecnológico, es que sean un accesorio vinculado a celebrities, marcas y tendencias de moda. La nueva imagen de su CEO funciona como una demostración personal de esta estrategia.
Recientemente Meta anunció nuevos modelos de gafas con distintas monturas, incluyendo sus primeras gafas sin cámara, una clara respuesta a las polémicas protagonizadas, como la grabación sin consentimiento. Aquí es donde está el verdadero reto, en conseguir que las Ray-Ban Meta dejen de ser percibidas como un accesorio de vigilancia.
El nuevo Zuck. Como decíamos, el punto de inflexión del estilo de Zuckerberg se produjo en 2024, cuando dijo adiós a su estilo discreto y básico para empezar a proyectar una imagen más masculina y atlética. Sin embargo, aunque el cambio sea más que evidente, no significa que haya transformado cómo lo percibe el público. En una encuesta de Pew Research Center publicada en febrero de 2025, dos tercios de los estadounidenses tenían una opinión desfavorable de él, una puntuación peor incluso que la de Elon Musk.

Wednesday, September 30th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
Thermaltake Introduces the Stage 500 TG ARGB Mid Tower Chassis
Thermaltake, a leading PC DIY brand for premium hardware solutions, introduces the Stage 500 TG ARGB Mid Tower Chassis, designed to bring PC hardware and personal collections together in one showcase. Available in Black and Snow editions, the Stage 500 TG ARGB features a one-piece curved tempered glass panel, a dedicated display stage, a wooden base, and an integrated bottom light strip, creating a distinctive presentation that blends modern PC hardware with personalized aesthetics.
Curved Tempered Glass Creates Panoramic Views
The Stage 500 TG ARGB features a one-piece curved tempered glass panel that extends across the front and side, providing an uninterrupted panoramic view of the hardware and display area inside. The curved design minimizes visual separation and puts every detail of the build on display.Dedicated Display Stage for Personal Expression
The front display stage provides a dedicated area for showcasing collectibles, figures, and decorative pieces alongside the hardware. This added space allows users to bring their own elements into the build, creating a setup that feels more personal and distinctive.
Wooden Base with a Distinctive Look
A wooden accent integrated into the base brings warmth and elegance to the Stage 500 TG ARGB. Paired with the curved tempered glass and modern chassis design, the wooden element adds a distinctive visual contrast to the overall showcase.
Pre-Installed Infinity ARGB PWM Fans
The Stage 500 TG ARGB features three 120 mm Infinity ARGB Reverse PWM fans positioned on the right side for intake, along with a 120 mm Infinity ARGB PWM fan at the rear for exhaust. This pre-installed fan setup helps establish efficient airflow while bringing distinctive ARGB lighting to the overall build.Flexible Hardware and Cooling Support
Designed to accommodate a range of hardware configurations, the Stage 500 TG ARGB is compatible with Mini-ITX, microATX, and ATX motherboards, including back-connect microATX and ATX motherboards for cleaner cable management. The Stage 500 TG ARGB is also compatible with the separately sold 6.0" LCD Screen Kit, offering another way to enhance the visual experience. articles.title: NASA squeezed Treasury, vibe coded, and broke the mold in bid to save Swift
articles.text:
Katalyst engineers attach Link to a baseplate inside the Space Environment Simulator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, on April 28, 2026. Katalyst performed environmental testing on Link inside a NASA test chamber because it was the only one sure to be available on short notice.
Credit:
NASA/Sophia Roberts
Katalyst engineers attach Link to a baseplate inside the Space Environment Simulator at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland, on April 28, 2026. Katalyst performed environmental testing on Link inside a NASA test chamber because it was the only one sure to be available on short notice.
Credit:
NASA/Sophia Roberts
An attempt to save NASA’s $500 million Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory from dropping out of orbit fell short, but the behind-the-scenes machinations required just to make a rescue possible deserve recognition, government and commercial space officials said in a recounting of the mission.
The rescue mission was developed by Katalyst Space Technologies, working under a $30 million contract awarded by NASA last September. NASA gave Katalyst nine months to build and launch a satellite to capture Swift flying some 200 miles above the Earth and boost it into a higher orbit.
Katalyst’s rescue spacecraft, known as Link, successfully launched July 3 and completed some of its initial checkouts before a malfunction caused it to spin out of control a few weeks later. NASA announced in August that Link would not be able to reach Swift as intended, and the rescue mission was aborted.
Still, designing and building a satellite, finding a rocket to launch it, and getting it to work in the harsh environment of space was a remarkable achievement. It would usually take several years to design, build, and test a satellite of Link’s size and complexity from scratch. Link weighed nearly a half-ton at launch, with electric thrusters, robotic arms, and large deployable solar arrays.
In the end, though, the Link satellite did not reach the Swift Observatory. The failure was bad news for scientists who rely on data from Swift, which has unique capabilities combining sensitivity to gamma rays, X-rays, and visible light with the agility to quickly turn toward astronomical targets. This has made Swift the go-to observatory for detecting gamma-ray bursts, the most powerful explosions in the Universe.
But Swift was going to fall out of orbit anyway. The spacecraft launched in 2004 and has far outlived its original design life. Swift does not have its own propulsion system, so it is unable to raise its orbit without help, leaving its fate at the mercy of aerodynamic drag in low-Earth orbit. Increased solar activity in recent years led to an increase in drag at Swift’s altitude, hastening its demise.
Racing against the clock
NASA and Katalyst officials are reviewing lessons learned from the mission to better prepare for the next time they need to rapidly call up a satellite rescue mission. First and foremost: Don’t wait until the last minute, said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s astrophysics division, in a meeting last week of the National Academies’ Committee on Astronomy and Astrophysics.
“The way that the timeline worked out, we didn’t have the ability to open up the doors fully to proposed solutions. We went with the teams we had on [contract] already. That is not a regret of the team we ended up with. It’s just I think I prefer the more open solutions.”
NASA commissioned 30-day studies from three teams—Katalyst, Starfish Space, and a joint proposal from Cambrian Works and Astroscale—in August 2025 to show how they planned to rescue Swift from destruction. The teams eligible for the studies were limited to partners NASA already had on contract for technology development. Under federal acquisition rules, it would have taken months or longer to start a brand new procurement and bring on a new provider.
The studies led to NASA’s selection in September 2025 of Katalyst to try to rescue Swift. Officials knew the odds were stacked against them.
Katalyst quickly put out orders to suppliers for all the parts required to assemble the Link spacecraft. In some cases, Katalyst found its suppliers couldn’t deliver in time, so it decided to build parts itself. Engineers also had to decide what to test on the spacecraft before handing it over to the launch provider, Northrop Grumman.
NASA’s strategy was to tell Katalyst what to do, but not how to do it.
“On paper, it was five requirements,” said Kieran Wilson, principal investigator for the Link mission at Katalyst. “In practice, it boiled down to do no harm and boost Swift. It was not specified how that was going to happen. That allowed us, in turn, to put engineering judgment ahead of exhaustive process, which allowed us to move much more quickly.”
The Link spacecraft attached to Northrop Grumman’s Pegasus XL launch vehicle.
Credit:
NASA/Ron Beard
The Link spacecraft attached to Northrop Grumman’s Pegasus XL launch vehicle.
Credit:
NASA/Ron Beard
Working inside a factory near Denver, Katalyst completed the Link spacecraft design at the end of last year and had the satellite ready for final prelaunch testing in April.
“We didn’t have a systems engineering organization,” Wilson said. “We didn’t have the traditional structure that you would see for most places that are trying to do something like this—a very complicated mission.”
The successful launch in July was followed by several weeks of in-orbit checkouts. Remarkably, it looked like the Swift rescue mission might actually succeed in reaching its objective, but a series of malfunctions in late July left the spacecraft spinning.
It’s always a valve
“We experienced a failure of a reaction wheel switch on our power system,” Wilson said. “This was something that we developed in-house. The reaction wheels themselves were from Rocket Lab, which is third party. They’re great. We would fly them again, absolutely. But it was the control electronics for those, particularly the regenerative braking circuit. That experienced a fault, and the transistor on that essentially shorted, and that caused it to overheat and render that circuit inoperable.
The spacecraft used cold-gas Reaction Control System (RCS) thrusters in combination with reaction wheels to control the spacecraft’s pointing.
“We implemented a bunch of software changes on the spacecraft and operational changes in order to mitigate the cause of that issue, which was kind of breaking too hard, too fast, too often, and that worked for a few weeks, and then we ended up having a series of events that started with an unresponsive RCS valve, causing the spacecraft to spin up,” Wilson said.
Those events prevented Link from rendezvousing with Swift and completing the reboost, and Katalyst had to forego its final incentive payment from NASA.
This image of NASA’s Swift observatory was captured at a distance of 12 to 15 kilometers by Katalyst’s Link satellite.
Credit:
Katalyst Space Technologies
This image of NASA’s Swift observatory was captured at a distance of 12 to 15 kilometers by Katalyst’s Link satellite.
Credit:
Katalyst Space Technologies
Some of the Link spacecraft’s most complicated elements, like its robotic arms and plasma thrusters, worked as expected. For a time, ground teams at Katalyst thought they might be able to use the plasma thrusters to regain control of Link’s pointing as it zipped around the Earth at nearly 5 miles per second.
“We were able to do some pretty significant orbital maneuvers,” Wilson said. “We did do a whole bunch of interesting things from the GNC (Guidance, Navigation, and Control) side in order to try to keep going even after we had lost two wheels, and those are what enabled us to get within about 10 kilometers [of Swift].”
A little more development time would have given Katalyst a better chance of finding the faulty circuit and valve before launch. Engineers made “gut-wrenching” decisions in the months leading up to launch on which tests to perform and what tests they simply did not have time to do, Domagal-Goldman said.
Wilson acknowledged shortcomings on Katalyst’s side, too, such as “overly light” staffing on the company’s power systems team. The satellite industry supply chain couldn’t deliver critical components for Link’s electrical system, like power conversion and distribution units, on schedule to meet the deadline for rescuing Swift.
“We had to develop a lot of that ourselves, and that meant that the engineers we had were overly stretched in too many different directions,” Wilson said. “There’s a lot of complexity there, and we just did not have enough time or people to test that with the level of care that was necessary. We did do a lot of testing on it, and we didn’t see anything quite like this in testing.”
But more time isn’t always available. Satellite reentries are difficult to forecast, and changes in solar activity can change the density of air molecules in low Earth orbit, resulting in more or less drag on satellites flying there.
“I think next time we’d like to get ahead of it in advance of an unexpected change in the de-orbit date,” Domagal-Goldman said.
What went right
Despite the technical failures after launch, officials pointed to Katalyst’s achievements with the Link spacecraft as showing the way for future satellite servicing and quick-response space missions.
The first step was to get the government to help where it could, and get out of the way where it couldn’t. NASA fell victim to a government shutdown last October due to a funding impasse between the Trump administration and the Republican-controlled Congress. The timing meant the shutdown would create a burden, not relief, for Katalyst. It started five days after NASA awarded Katalyst the contract to rescue Swift, just as the space agency started making payments.
“They needed a huge influx of cash in order to go buy stuff,” said John Van Eepoel, Swift’s mission director at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “Otherwise, we never would have made it.”
NASA’s procurement team worked in a “fever pitch” to arrange the payments before the government closed its doors, Van Eepoel said.
“That was, I think, heroic and herculean movement with people knowing how to make the procurement system just shake the money free,” he said. “I think somebody was on the phone to Treasury because I was sweating that we weren’t going to make it, and I’d done everything that I could.”
The engineers responsible for operating the Swift spacecraft also came up big in the run-up to the rescue mission. The reboost attempt would be moot if the atmosphere dragged the Swift observatory toward reentry before Katalyst could launch Link in pursuit.
Jamie Kennea, who led Swift operations until earlier this year, said his team at Penn State University devised a way to reorient the observatory to give it a more streamlined aerodynamic profile, minimizing drag and extending its time in orbit. This gave Katalyst a few more months of schedule margin at the expense of suspending Swift’s scientific observations.
“That sounds simple on paper,” Kennea said. “In reality, getting there was extremely hard. We had to use every single tool at our disposal to achieve that goal. That would include rewriting and rewriting software. The use of agentic AI, even vibe coding, helped us out in a lot of cases where we couldn’t figure out how to do things. GPU compute was used extensively to achieve this. What we ended up achieving was essentially extending the lifespan of Swift by several months.”
Wilson said the Link mission came in “within about 5 percent of our predictions” at the time of Katalyst’s bid. “We were within $1.5 of our $30 million mission target, which includes launch, labor, contractors, what have you.”
This shows that a satellite rescue or reboost mission doesn’t have to take hundreds of millions of dollars and years to get to the launch pad, as several government-led demonstrations have done, Wilson said. One example was OSAM-1, a NASA mission that would have attempted to grab onto an aging Landsat Earth-imaging satellite and refuel it.
With the refueling test, NASA’s OSAM-1 demo mission had more scope than Katalyst’s Swift rescue mission, but the agency spent $1.5 billion on the project before canceling it in 2024. At the time of cancellation, NASA officials noted advancements in the commercial industry as one reason for pulling the plug on OSAM-1 and breaking the mold in how they view satellite servicing.
“The industry is at the point where it’s ready to take off,” Van Eepoel said. “And we’re seeing that work out in real time with other companies that are doing rendezvous missions right now: Starfish and Northrop Grumman. They have launched RSGS, and that’s on its way to GEO (Geosynchronous Orbit). So this is just the beginning.”
“Speaking for NASA on its own, this isn’t the last servicing mission that we’re going to try to pursue,” Van Eepoel said. “There are other astrophysics platforms that need help. We’re actively looking at those as we move into some type of a service model for missions.”
Artist’s illustration of Katalyst’s Link spacecraft (left) with NASA’s Swift observatory (right).
Credit:
NASA
Artist’s illustration of Katalyst’s Link spacecraft (left) with NASA’s Swift observatory (right).
Credit:
NASA
The results from the Swift rescue mission “represent a floor, not a ceiling,” for what’s possible with a low-cost satellite servicing mission, Wilson said. “We did some really, really cool stuff. We got really, really close. I’m absolutely gutted we weren’t able to get further.”
Meanwhile, after moving to within 10 kilometers of Swift to test its navigation system, the Link satellite reentered the atmosphere on September 25. Swift has temporarily resumed scientific observations before it falls into the atmosphere and burns up later this year.
The loss of Swift “creates a big hole” in NASA’s science portfolio, Domagal-Goldman said. “We are doing the proverbial running around and seeing what we’ve got on the shelves to see what is available for us to put back up in space to replace the Swift capabilities we’re about to lose.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

articles.title: Promoção relâmpago: Galaxy Buds 3 FE com ANC despenca 56% com cupom • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Promoção relâmpago: Galaxy Buds 3 FE com ANC despenca 56% com cupom
Galaxy Buds 3 FE têm bateria de longa duração e suportam a suíte Galaxy AI; fones de ouvido da Samsung saem 56% mais baratos no Pix com cupom no Mercado Livre
Os Galaxy Buds 3 FE estão saindo por R$ 485 no Pix com cupom SITE60 no Mercado Livre. Os fones de ouvido wireless da Samsung, que trazem ANC, bateria de longa duração e funções do Galaxy AI, atingem o menor preço já visto pelo Achados, com desconto de 56% sobre o original de R$ 1.099.
Mas seja rápido: o cupom está em modo de “contagem regressiva” e deve esgotar em breve.
Os Galaxy Buds 3 FE contam com o recurso de cancelamento ativo de ruído (ANC), que filtra sons externos e melhora a experiência ao ouvir música em qualquer lugar (sons importantes, como de trânsito, ainda passam por motivos de segurança). O Modo Ambiente capta conversas sem precisar remover os fones.
Os recursos de Inteligência Artificial da suíte Galaxy AI incluem o Modo Intérprete, que traduz conversas em tempo real; o usuário escuta a voz da outra pessoa em seu idioma, e o celular Galaxy pareado (recurso exclusivo) exibe as respostas traduzidas, sendo uma ótima função em viagens ao exterior.
O suporte ao Google Gemini habilita um dos melhores fones da Samsung a realizar consultas aos fones diretamente ou a outro dispositivo Galaxy pareado, incluindo smartwatches. É possível criar lembretes, iniciar atividades físicas ou receber respostas sobre diversas dúvidas.
Outros recursos dos Galaxy Buds 3 FE incluem o áudio 360, que oferece maior imersão, e um equalizador de áudio personalizável. O design ergonômico com hastes longas facilita os controles por gestos, ao oferecer uma maior área de contato.
As baterias dos fones, quando combinadas à do case de transporte, resistem a até 30 horas com o ANC desligado, e cerca de 6 horas com o recurso ligado, segundo a fabricante. Assim, você pode ouvir suas músicas e podcasts sem se preocupar com tomadas e powerbanks.
Os Galaxy Buds 3 FE (R$ 485 no Pix com cupom SITE60) possuem certificação IP54, que confere proteção moderada contra água, suor e poeira. Não perca essa oferta relâmpago e leve os fones da Samsung para casa no precinho.

articles.title: The release of 'Avengers: Secret Wars' sounds like it could be pushed out of 2027 — and I think it would be a huge blow for Marvel if it is
articles.text:
A new Marvel rumor suggests Avengers: Secret Wars could lose its December 2027 release date slot — and a filming delay could be the reason why
- Avengers: Secret Wars might not make its December 2027 release date
- Various leakers suggest filming on the Marvel movie won't begin in late 2026
- Any delays would have a knock-on effect for future MCU projects
Avengers: Secret Wars might not make its December 17, 2027 launch date amid claims that its shooting schedule has been delayed by two months.
According to multiple insiders, the cameras won't start to roll on 2027's only Marvel movie until next January. X/Twitter user Apocalyptic Horseman, who has a very reliable track record when it comes to breaking comic book movie-specific news, was the first industry insider to warn fans to brace themselves for a filming delay announcement. Other leakers with more spotty track records, including DanielRPK and Alex P, quickly jumped on the bandwagon to say they'd heard the same.
In a follow-up post, Apocalyptic Horseman expanded on what they'd heard to say that a release date delay was not inevitable.
However, according to the same leaker, filming wouldn't likely wrap until late April/early May next year, meaning post-production would have to be completed in a seven to eight month timeframe if Secret Wars is to make its current December 17, 2027 launch date. With reshoots on its forebear Avengers: Doomsday being prioritized ahead of its December 18, 2026 release, I get the feeling that Secret Wars' shooting schedule and launch date will be pushed back.
I've approached Marvel and Disney for comment on this rumor, and I'll update this article if I receive a response.
Why an Avengers: Secret Wars delay would be really bad news for Marvel
If the rumors are true, Secret Wars wouldn't be the first Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) movie or Disney+ show to suffer a production and/or release date delay. Indeed, myriad other projects from the comic book giant have endured similar problems, especially in recent years.
Ordinarily, production and/or launch delays wouldn't be a bad thing for Marvel. Sure, fans have been disappointed to learn about such issues. However, if it means that a production's cast and crew aren't being run into the ground, and forced to crunch, to get it over the line to meet a set release deadline, you won't hear me or many others complaining.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
That said, any delay to the sixth Avengers flick would be problematic for two major reasons.
For starters, pushing Secret Wars out of its late 2027 release slot would be a huge blow. Not only would Marvel miss out on being the biggest movie of next year's holiday season, but it would also only be the third time in the comic titan's history that it hasn't released a single movie in a calendar year — the other instances being 2009 and 2020.
There's also the inevitable knock-on effect that Secret Wars' release delay would have on future MCU films.
If the final Marvel Phase 6 movie is pushed into 2028, fans would be forced to wait around 18 months for the concluding chapter of the Marvel Multiverse Saga. That would have a significant impact on Ghost Rider, X-Men, and Black Panther 3, all of which are lined up to premiere in 2028.
So, does Marvel give Avengers: Secret Wars the breathing room it deserves to bring the Multiverse Saga to a close, and move the aforementioned trio into 2029, thereby delaying the start of MCU 2.0? Or, does it only allow fans to take stock of Secret Wars — and the last 20 years of MCU storytelling — for a few months before officially kickstarting Marvel Phase 7 in late 2028?
Admittedly, all of these 'what if?' scenarios are based on some online conjecture that Marvel and Disney have yet to officially comment on, so your guess is as good as mine. If Secret Wars has suffered production and release setbacks, though, I'm sure we'll get a proper announcement sometime soon.
In the meantime, find out everything we know so far about Avengers: Secret Wars. Then, get the full lowdown on Avengers: Doomsday ahead of its late 2026 debut.

articles.title: NetApp ties intelligent data infrastructure to production AI - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
CEO George Kurian outlines NetApp’s data strategy for production AI
Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming critical as enterprises move artificial intelligence from curated pilots into production. NetApp Inc. is positioning its Novus architecture for that transition.
Ninety-three percent of organizations pursuing production AI identify data as their leading challenge, according to NetApp Chief Executive Officer George Kurian (pictured). Addressing the associated safety risks will require action from model builders, security vendors and enterprise operators.
“When you want to make AI scale across your enterprise, you need to integrate it into the operational systems and the workflows and how work gets done,” Kurian said. “That creates … new requirements on the infrastructure, like governance, security, control and so on.”
Kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight at NetApp INSIGHT, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed production AI, data governance and NetApp’s infrastructure strategy. (* Disclosure below.)
Intelligent data infrastructure connects scale and governance
This week, NetApp introduced Novus, which combines its established data layer with an independently scalable metadata layer. It’s designed to deliver more than 100 terabytes per second and support zettabyte-scale capacity within one namespace.
“The combination of those allows you to meet the performance requirements of the most demanding enterprise,” Kurian said. “The metadata service becomes a place for data discovery, data cataloging, and data governance and control. Having a super scalable metadata service allows you to implement [the] guardrails we talked about earlier.”
Organizations can start small and expand to large AI factories on a consistent platform, according to Kurian. He framed intelligent data infrastructure as essential to creating trusted knowledge.
“I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he said. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”

articles.title: TP-Link opens global preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, but ban keeps it out of US market — US left off launch list as FCC freeze refuses to thaw
articles.text:
TP-Link opens global preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 router, but ban keeps it out of US market — US left off launch list as FCC freeze refuses to thaw
The Archer 8 Ultra is launching across Europe and Australia, but the U.S. has given TP-Link the cold shoulder
Today is a big day for TP-Link, as the company revealed that it has opened preorders for its first Wi-Fi 8 hardware. The previously announced Archer 8 Ultra router makes the company’s first entry into what will become a fully stocked portfolio covering Wi-Fi 8 standalone and mesh routers, access points, and client adapters. Interestingly, TP-Link makes it clear that preorders kicked off today in the United Kingdom, Germany, Australia, and other global markets. 
Given that the United States is a key consumer market for TP-Link, the fact that the country is left off the preorder list is telling, but not exactly a surprise to anyone who has been following the wireless industry over the past six months. TP-Link has sat on the sidelines as competitors including Netgear, Asus, and Amazon gained Conditional Approvals from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to sell their hardware in the U.S. Without the Conditional Approval, companies are effectively banned from selling new wireless hardware in the country that wasn't already approved by the FCC.
So, while earlier Wi-Fi 7 gear from TP-Link that received FCC certification can still be sold, any new Wi-Fi 7 or Wi-Fi 8 products are effectively blocked from the market. The company has made several critical moves to position itself as a U.S. company, including incorporating TP-Link Systems in California, but those moves have been challenged in legal filings.
At this point, there haven’t been any clear signs that the U.S. government will lift its freeze on TP-Link hardware, so until that time comes, the Archer 8 Ultra will remain unavailable stateside. And it’s a shame, because the Archer 8 Ultra, which utilizes a Broadcom Wi-Fi 8 chipset, will deliver up to 33 percent more real-world throughput compared to TP-Link’s Wi-Fi 7 hardware, and 24 percent more consistent throughput when operating in high-interference conditions.
The Archer 8 Ultra will feature two auto-sensing 10 Gbps WAN/LAN ports and four 2.5 Gbps LAN ports. TP-Link says that the router covers up to 3,600 square feet and will support up to 200 devices.
"Wi-Fi 8 sets a new foundation, and we’ve built beyond it,” said Jim Poder, Senior Vice President of R&D at TP-Link. “Archer 8 Ultra combines our Wi-Fi 8 StabilityEngine with intelligent antenna technology and AI-powered optimization to deliver what matters most: a smarter, more reliable network that’s easier to use.”
TP-Link’s Wi-Fi 8 family will expand in Q1 2027 with a Deco 8 Ultra mesh router, and a Roam 8 travel router in Q2 2027. Throughout the year, further additions will come in the form of new PCIe/USB wireless adapters, access points, and range extenders.

articles.title: Signal : vous pouvez enfin sauvegarder vos échanges en local depuis un iPhone
articles.text:
Avec la version 8.30 de son application iOS, Signal permet d'enregistrer une copie chiffrée de ses conversations dans le dossier de son choix. Contrairement aux sauvegardes hébergées par Signal, elle est stockée là où l'utilisateur le décide.
La fonction sera bientôt accessible à tous les utilisateurs d'iOS. Elle reprend le format des sauvegardes locales d'Android et de Signal Desktop, ce qui permet de restaurer ses discussions d'un système à l'autre.
Une clé unique, mais une protection qui diffère selon la méthode
Pour activer la sauvegarde locale, il faut se rendre au sein des paramètres de Signal, puis dans Sauvegardes, Sauvegardes locales, et choisir un dossier. Signal propose alors d'afficher la clé de récupération, un code de 64 caractères sans lequel la sauvegarde reste illisible : les fichiers sont chiffrés de bout en bout, donc impossibles à ouvrir sans elle. Pour effectuer une restauration, il suffit de réinstaller Signal, de choisir "Transférer ou restaurer le compte", puis la nouvelle option "Restaurer une sauvegarde locale". La fonction peut être désactivée à tout moment.
Sur Android, ces sauvegardes existaient déjà, mais chaque copie quotidienne regroupait tout dans une seule archive, ce qui prenait beaucoup de place. Le nouveau format range les médias dans un dossier à part et procède de façon incrémentielle : un fichier déjà copié n'est pas recopié, et un document reçu en plusieurs exemplaires n'est stocké qu'une fois. C'est pratique si le dossier est ensuite synchronisé vers un disque externe ou un NAS. La première sauvegarde, elle, copie tout depuis zéro, ce qui peut consommer plus d'espace ou de bande passante que le service hébergé.
La protection n'est en revanche pas identique. Pour les sauvegardes hébergées du forfait payant, Signal ajoute une seconde clé, renouvelée chaque jour et gardée dans un environnement d'exécution sécurisé (une zone isolée du serveur). Elle ne déchiffre rien sans la clé de récupération, mais l'ancienne est détruite à chaque changement, ce qui protège les sauvegardes passées. Les sauvegardes locales n'ont pas ce dispositif, car elles doivent fonctionner avec n'importe quel support de stockage. La clé de récupération ouvre donc toutes les sauvegardes locales, y compris les anciennes. Comme le service hébergé remplace son archive toutes les 24 heures et qu'un dossier local ne se nettoie pas tout seul, Signal suggère de supprimer régulièrement les anciennes copies, par exemple sur une clé USB. Soulignons enfin que les messages éphémères programmés pour disparaître dans les 24 heures sont exclus des sauvegardes.

articles.title: Apollo debuts AI app builder, intelligence layer and signal-based outreach system - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
Apollo debuts AI app builder, intelligence layer and signal-based outreach system
Sales software company Apollo today unveiled a set of artificial intelligence products designed to move more of a revenue team’s daily work onto one platform.
The launch goes after a problem Apollo describes as tool sprawl. Most sales organizations assembled their software one product at a time, often ending up with a different vendor for prospecting than for enrichment or outreach. According to the company, AI has made that arrangement harder to justify because a model can only work with the context it is given.
An Apollo survey of more than 300 go-to-market leaders and operators found end-to-end workflow automation ranked as the top priority for revenue teams. Most of the teams surveyed are still juggling two to five sales and marketing platforms.
Three products make up the release. Apollo Builder Studio takes a plain-English description and produces a working tool, whether that is a web page, a database or an automation. A second piece, the Apollo Intelligence Layer, works out what a team should do next. Outreach is handled by Apollo Messaging OS.
Builder Studio, the first of the three, writes real code that runs on Apollo’s own data and execution infrastructure, so staff without engineering support can deploy their own systems. Less technical operators are one audience, since the tools they want would otherwise sit in an engineering backlog. Experienced builders, the company said, should be able to put systems together faster.
Inside the Intelligence Layer, Apollo Intelligence Profile maintains a continuously updated view of every contact and account, with data drawn from multiple sources and enriched along the way. The layer’s other half is GTM Harness, a set of specialized agents and skills for jobs such as prospecting, research and email deliverability. Those agents combine the profile data with a customer’s own sales context, plus memory and governance controls, before recommending or taking an action.
Messaging OS watches for buying signals and uses AI to decide who gets contacted, when and on which channel. Putting sales and marketing on the same system is meant to stop the two teams from hitting the same buyer with separate, overlapping campaigns. Every send also feeds results back into the system.
None of it requires customers to move everything into Apollo’s interface. Teams can work inside Apollo or plug its data and agents into the software and AI tools they already use. For smaller businesses, Apollo is positioning the new products as a substitute for hiring a large revenue operations team or buying a pile of point solutions.
Chief Executive Matt Curl, who took over from co-founder Tim Zheng in February, introduced the products during his keynote at ApolloNEXT 2026 in San Francisco. Go-to-market has reached “a structural inflection point,” in his view, with AI changing how companies set up their entire revenue operation. “You no longer need a RevOps army and millions of dollars to build a successful engine,” Curl said.
Apollo, officially ZenLeads Inc., is a venture capital-backed startup that says 5 million people at more than 600,000 companies use its software. Fortune 500 companies account for more than 100 of its customer teams. Apollo’s funding history stops, publicly at least, with a $100 million Series D round that Bain Capital Ventures led in August 2023 at a $1.6 billion valuation. Including that round, the company has raised about $250 million.

articles.title: En China nacen cada vez menos bebés, pero hay un negocio que no para de crecer: hoteles de lujo para mujeres que acaban de dar a luz
articles.text:
En China nacen cada vez menos bebés, pero eso no significa que los partos y la atención a las mujeres que acaban de dar a luz ya no supongan un negocio. Al contrario. Si bien la tasa de natalidad del gigante asiático está de capa caída, hay una industria en auge que ha pisado el acelerador en los últimos años y ya mueve cientos de millones de euros: la atención posparto de lujo, que ha convertido la medicina tradicional china en un mercado cada vez más jugoso en el que llegan a pagarse decenas de miles de dólares (incluso más de 100.000) por un mes de cuidados especiales.
Hay un término que lo explica: zuò yuè zi.
¿Qué es zuo yue zi? Literalmente "sentarse el mes". Dicho así quizás suene un poco raro, pero capta bien su esencia: zuo yue zi (坐月子) es un ritual de cuidados posparto de la medicina tradicional china que centra el foco en las madres y aboga básicamente por el reposo y el aislamiento.
La idea es facilitar la recuperación de la mamá durante los días y semanas posteriores a que dé a luz, algo que aspira a conseguir con una serie de pautas de nutrición, descanso e higiene. Se dice que sus orígenes pueden remontarse más de 2.000 años atrás, a la dinastía Han, lo que no quita que siga ejerciendo influencia en la China del siglo XXI.
¿Y qué recomienda? Sobre todo, descanso. De ahí lo de “sentarse el mes”. El zuo yue zi sostiene que los partos son experiencias agotadoras para las mujeres, tanto física como mentalmente, así que aconseja que durante el puerperio (las semanas siguientes a dar a luz) las madres guarden reposo.
Nada de levantar pesos. Ni realizar tareas agotadoras o caminar largas distancias. "Algunas mujeres son tan estrictas que no abandonan la cama durante las primeras dos semanas después del parto", comenta a la BBC Kity Wu, quien al menos en 2017 trabajaba como neuróloga en Londres.
¿Sigue respetándose? Sí. Prueba que el zuo yue zi sigue arraigado en la sociedad china es que la propia Wu, neuróloga, cumplió con ese confinamiento posnatal. No es la única pauta de este ritual, que aboga por evitar las comidas y alimentos "fríos", reducir la exposición a las corrientes de aire y limitar los esfuerzos durante 30 o 42 días, dependiendo de cómo se desarrolle el parto. Antiguamente incluso se pedía a las madres que no se bañasen ni lavasen el pelo, hábitos que se consideraban nocivos para su salud.
¿Qué tiene que ver eso con el lujo? Muy sencillo: hay empresas que han visto en los cuidados posparto un auténtico filón. Su idea es aprovechar lo arraigada que está la filosofía el zuo yue zi en China para profesionalizar la atención a las madres, modernizarla e incluso (para quienes puedan permitírselo) darle una pátina de exclusividad.
¿Por qué pasar esas semanas de reposo posteriores al parto en casa, de la cama al sofá del salón, cuando puedes alojarte en la lujosa planta de un hotel Four Seasons? ¿Por qué dejar que te cuiden tu marido y tu suegra cuando puedes estar rodeada de enfermeras disponibles las 24 horas del día, monitores de yoga, expertos en lactancia y rehabilitación posparto y (por supuesto) pediatras para tu pequeño?
¿Tantos centros así hay? En 2018 operaban en China más de 3.000 centros especializados en atención posnatal y cuidados inspirados en el zuo yue zi. Y desde entonces el negocio no parece haberse resentido. Al contrario. No todos los centros de atención a madres se orientan al mercado del lujo, pero hay pistas que sugieren que están en plena expansión.
Hace unos días Luxuru Tribune compartía un dato revelador: si en 2018 el sector de la atención posparto movía en China 9.300 millones de yuanes (1.200 millones de euros), en 2022 alcanzaba ya los 22.300 (2.900). Si esa tendencia no se revierte, Frost & Sullivan ya pronostica que a finales de esta década se superarán los 100.000 millones de yuanes, con un crecimiento anual cercano al 24% a partir de 2024.
Es mucho dinero, ¿no? Quizás lo parezca, pero hay centros especializados en cuidados durante el puerperio que cobran auténticas fortunas: en 2018 South China Morning Post hablaba de uno a las afueras de Shanghái que aplicaba una tarifa de 10.900 dólares al mes. Y no era ni de lejos el más caro.
En otro la estancia con servicio “premium” salía por más de 50.000 euros al mes. La revista Vogue deja una referencia algo más actualizada: en 2024 aseguraba que una estancia de 28 días en un centro Saint Bella salía por entre 21.000 y 105.000 dólares, lo que no impedía que algunas usuarias extendiesen su alojamiento hasta los 40 o casi 80 días. Otra firma especializada en el lujo posparto es CareBay.
¿Qué ofrecen exactamente? En su web, Saint Bella garantiza una "atención profesional para la madre y el bebé", lo que incluye desde tratamientos y seguimiento tras el parto a planes personalizados de lactancia, masajes, baños, conferencias sobre maternidad, un menú de resort cinco estrellas, consultas con nutricionistas o talleres de pintura, entre un largo etcétera.
Luxury Tribune asegura que la compañía aumentó sus ingresos al menos un 30% el año pasado, superando la barrera de los 1.000 millones de yuanes, el equivalente a algo más de 130 millones de euros.
¿No hay más negocios? Sí. Las clínicas de lujo no son las únicas que explotan el negocio de los cuidados posparto. Otra figura importante, muy conectada además con la tradición china, son las pui yuet, niñeras especializadas en atender a bebés y mujeres que acaban de dar a luz. En 2023 contratar los servicios de una pui yuet con experiencia en Hong Kong costaba entre 8.100 y 34.100 dólares. Y eso por 30 días como interna. Su figura, igual que el zuo yue zi, gana popularidad en Occidente.
¿Pero no estaban naciendo menos bebés? Exacto. En 2025 la tasa de natalidad de China cayó a 5,63 nacimientos por cada 1.000 mujeres, un mínimo histórico que hunde aún más el suelo alcanzado en 2023. Para firmas como Saint Bella lo realmente importante sin embargo no es cuántos niños nacen, sino cómo y dónde nacen. El valor pesa mucho más que el volumen.
A medida que la sociedad china cambia, aumenta el número de mujeres que dan a luz con más de 30 años y se adentran en la maternidad con carreras profesionales asentadas, buenas cualificaciones y una economía reforzada tras años de ingresos. Al reducirse el número de hijos, las familias chinas están también más dispuestas a aumentar el dinero que invierten en sus cuidados. Todo eso se suma a otra tendencia de fondo: el auge del mercado del lujo nacional chino.

articles.title: The iPhone Duo is reportedly facing production challenges with low yields and quality concerns
articles.text:
Bottom line: After years of rumors and speculation, Apple's first foldable iPhone is expected to go on sale next month, but getting enough of them into customers' hands could prove the harder part. Foxconn, the contract manufacturer responsible for producing the device, is reportedly facing severe production constraints that could limit early output, raising the prospect of tight supply for what is now Apple's most expensive iPhone.
According to an insider quoted by Chinese outlet Jiemian News, final assembly yields for the iPhone Duo were only slightly above 60% as of September 17. It could take Foxconn another six months to a year to raise yields to more mature levels while maintaining Apple's exacting quality standards.
The insider added that Foxconn has been continuously adjusting equipment, assembly processes, and production settings as it tries to bring yields up to acceptable levels. Suppliers are also reportedly lobbying Apple to ease certain quality requirements to speed up production and meet expected demand.
What makes matters worse is that the problems extend well beyond Foxconn. According to the report, several suppliers are also experiencing production issues, with Samsung Display singled out as one of the worst affected. The company is reportedly struggling with low yields for its foldable OLED panels and hinges, largely due to last-minute design changes by Apple.
Another supply chain source claimed that Apple's total production target for the iPhone Duo in 2026 is between six and eight million units, much lower than the 20 to 30 million units an iPhone Pro or Pro Max typically ships over its full product cycle. A separate source reportedly said Apple's sales guidance for the iPhone Duo is in excess of five million units.
According to a separate report from MyDrivers, several suppliers have told Apple it might have to choose between yield and output, as the entire iPhone Duo manufacturing ecosystem is facing serious production issues. The report, however, did not reveal the identities of any of the suppliers urging Apple to lower its quality standards to meet output targets.
The sources explained that ramping up production under the current constraints might improve output, but at the cost of yield, with the number of defective units expected to skyrocket, especially if Apple is unwilling to compromise on quality. Higher output would therefore result in higher scrap costs, which may not be in Apple's best interest.
Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo earlier this month at its 'Surprise and Shine' event in Cupertino, California. The device starts at $1,999 for the base 256GB model, lower than the $2,500+ range some analysts had predicted, and similar to the $2,099 asking price of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

articles.title: New Jailbreak Unlocks Nearly Every PlayStation 5 Model
articles.text:
Wednesday, September 30th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
New Jailbreak Unlocks Nearly Every PlayStation 5 Model
If your PlayStation 5 hasn't received a system update recently, it might now be open to usable jailbreak. A newly released jailbreak called Relapse works on firmware versions from 7.00 through 13.60, covering both the standard PS5 and the PS5 Pro. In simple terms, nearly every console is now exploitable, except for those updated within the last week. This release comes at a convenient time for Marvel's Wolverine. The game requires firmware 13.40, while patch 1.001.005 needs 13.60. A console on 13.60 can remain exploitable while running the game and at least some updates, although the latest download from PSN might require firmware 14.00.
Few jailbreaks target a title this recent, which is why researchers and PC emulation developers are closely monitoring the game. According to its GitHub repository, Relapse uses a combination of a browser exploit, and a kernel exploit to gain full read-write control over the system's core memory. From there, it can load additional payloads like etaHEN through a loader that listens on port 9021. To get started, follow two steps: first, change the Primary DNS in the console's network settings to 45.56.67.85. Then, either run the project's serve.py script on a local machine or open the Relapse Exploit website from the PS5 itself.A jailbreak removes the restrictions Sony places on the system, allowing for homebrew, emulators, mods, and other unofficial software. The trade-off is firmware dependence. Updating can close the door on access, while staying on older software can prevent access to new games, patches, and PSN features. For now, owners who want to keep this option open should refrain from updating until they decide which is more important.

articles.title: Razorpay enables Apple Pay for online and in-store payments in India
articles.text:
Razorpay
View Brand Publisher
Razorpay enables Apple Pay for online and in-store payments in India
From Zepto to IndiGo, shoppers can now skip OTPs and pay with Face ID or Touch ID, marking a new chapter in India’s digital payment authentication.
Razorpay has enabled Apple Pay for online and in-store payments in India, allowing eligible shoppers to complete transactions using Face ID, Touch ID, or their device passcode instead of manually entering card details or waiting for an OTP. The payment option is now live with businesses including Zepto, ixigo, IndiGo, Tata 1mg and JioMart.
The move comes as digital payment authentication in India evolves beyond SMS-based one-time passwords. In September 2025, the Reserve Bank of India introduced a framework allowing payment players to use alternative authentication mechanisms for digital payments. The framework came into effect in April 2026.
With Apple Pay enabled on Razorpay, shoppers can select the payment option at checkout, review the transaction, and authenticate it on their Apple device. Cards stored in Apple Wallet can be used without manually entering card details or waiting for an OTP.
For instance, a shopper buying a pair of headphones on Zepto can select Apple Pay at checkout, choose a card already stored in Apple Wallet, and confirm the payment with Face ID, without typing in card details or waiting for an OTP. The same experience can be used at supported stores by bringing an iPhone or Apple Watch close to a compatible payment terminal and authenticating the purchase on the device.
Apple Pay uses tokenized card credentials, meaning the shopper’s actual card number is not shared with the business during the transaction. This provides an additional layer of protection against fraud and can help reduce the risk of chargebacks.
For businesses, the integration means eligible merchants using Razorpay can offer Apple Pay without building and maintaining a separate checkout flow, subject to enablement requirements. Razorpay securely routes transactions across Apple Pay, card networks, and issuing banks, and processes the domestic payment once it is authorized by the shopper.
“Paying should be the easiest part of buying something, not the hardest. People expect every experience on their mobile devices and at payment outlets to be quick and effortless, and online payments via checkout should be no different,” said Rahul Kothari, COO, Razorpay.
“Apple Pay removes much of that friction, and with Razorpay, businesses don't need to rebuild anything to offer it. It fits right into the checkout they already use, backed by the reliability and scale thousands of Indian businesses count on. For merchants, that means faster checkouts and more successful payments.”
Apple Pay is available across iPhone, Apple Watch, iPad, Mac and Apple Vision Pro. It can also be used on PCs through browsers including Chrome and Firefox.

articles.title: AWS embeds DuckDB in its PostgreSQL DBMS to speed queries of live and historical data - SiliconANGLE
articles.text:
AWS embeds DuckDB in its PostgreSQL DBMS to speed queries of live and historical data
Amazon Web Services Inc. is adding the ability to query the popular Apache Iceberg data lake directly from its Aurora PostgreSQL database management system, allowing applications to combine live transactions with historical records without copying data or creating extract/transform/load pipelines.
The capability embeds the DuckDB analytical engine inside Aurora PostgreSQL to support data stored in Iceberg and Apache Parquet formats. Customers can use existing PostgreSQL applications, tools and endpoints to query operational records alongside data in Amazon S3, including S3 Tables.
AWS acquired DuckLabs B.V., developer of the popular open-source database, last month.
AWS is positioning the feature as a way to simplify application development and reduce the engineering work needed to maintain data pipelines. Potential uses include real-time dashboards, transactions enriched with historical information and artificial intelligence agents that need access to both current and archived records.
Previously, combining recent transactions in Aurora with historical records in S3 commonly required reverse ETL pipelines. That resulted in duplicated data, additional infrastructure costs and continuing work to keep records synchronized.
“This challenge only grows as you increasingly embed AI agents into your applications, where it is impractical to predict and pre-replicate every dataset an agent might need,” Esra Kayabali, a principal solutions architect at AWS, wrote in an announcement.
DuckDB processes analytical scans within Aurora, avoiding additional network hops for query processing. A single query can access data lake records alongside live operational data, including uncommitted writes. AWS said integration as an example of how it is incorporating the DuckDB engine widely into its services.
The feature also supports external catalogs compatible with the Iceberg Representational State Transfer Catalog specification through federation with the data catalog in the AWS Glue serverless data integration service. Customers register an external catalog with Glue and create foreign tables that reference its data. Applications can then join Aurora records with Iceberg tables registered across multiple catalogs.
To limit the amount of data read, Aurora filters records and selects relevant columns during query execution. It also caches frequently accessed data. Developers can inspect metrics including rows scanned, bytes read from S3 and cache hits.
In a financial example, Kayabali demonstrated a query combining seven days of customer transactions in Aurora with five years of historical transactions stored in a Parquet file in S3. Aurora inferred the historical table’s schema from file metadata, eliminating manual column definitions.
For workloads needing single-digit-millisecond latency, customers can copy selected data lake records into native Aurora tables using standard SQL commands. Read queries can run on the cluster’s writer or a read replica, offloading analytical scans from operational workloads. Commands that materialize data run on the writer.
Customers enable the capability through the aurora_analytics extension and an AWS Identity and Access Management role granting access to S3 and Glue. It supports Aurora PostgreSQL versions 17 and 18, starting with versions 17.11 and 18.6, respectively.
AWS said the feature is available in all commercial AWS regions without an additional feature charge. Customers pay for the incremental Aurora computing resources their queries consume and S3 requests used to read files.

articles.title: 8BitDo Launches Gears of War: E-Day Retro Mechanical Keyboard and Gaming Mouse in Xbox Collaboration
articles.text:
Wednesday, September 30th 2026
	
									
	
	
	
8BitDo Launches Gears of War: E-Day Retro Mechanical Keyboard and Gaming Mouse in Xbox Collaboration
8BitDo has carved out a niche for itself with its Xbox game collaborations, with the recent Tomb Raider 30th Anniversary Collection controllers being just one example. Now, the peripheral maker has officially revealed that its latest collaboration will see the launch of a Gears of War: E-Day Retro Mechanical Keyboard and Retro R8 gaming mouse. The Retro 87 keyboard is available for pre-order for $119.99, and the Retro R8 Mouse is available for $59.99, but both are expected to start shipping on October 30. 
The Gears of War: E-Day Retro Mechanical keyboard is the brand's 87-key variant, which features a classic TKL layout with three additional buttons on the top edge next to the tactile connectivity and volume dials. The keyboard itself is made from an opaque black ABS, and it features an E-Day-themed design with translucent red keycaps—presumably polycarbonate, but material is specified—in an MDA-like profile, giving the keyboard something of a unique look, compared to plain Cherry or OEM profile keycaps. The keyboard has north-facing per-key RGB backlighting, and it is compatible with 8BitDo's Ultimate Software 2.0 for Windows.The Gears of War: E-Day version of the 8BitDo Retro 87 keyboard uses semi-custom Huano Cloud Gray linear switches and has hot-swap sockets compatible with typical 3- or 5-pin MX-style mechanical switches. It foregoes the gasket mounts that are becoming more commonplace in favor of a top mount with an aluminium switch plate. As with other Retro 87 Keyboard models, the Gears of War: E-Day version of the keyboard comes with two themed Super Buttons that connect to the keyboard with a 3.5 mm TRRS cable. The keyboard supports both Bluetooth and 2.4 GHz wireless connections, in addition to the USB Type-C wired connection, and 8BitDo estimates 280 hours of use over 2.4 GHz and 300 hours connected over Bluetooth, thanks to a 4,000 mAh battery.The 8BitDo Retro R8 wireless mouse is a wireless mouse with an included charging dock that doubles as an extension for the 2.4 GHz dongle. It has a retro-inspired truly symmetrical shape with two side buttons per side, making it apt for both left- and right-handed use, and it weighs in at 77 g. The mouse uses a PixArt PAW 3395 sensor and polls at up to 8 kHz in wired mode or 4 kHz over 2.4 GHz. It also has Bluetooth 5.3 LE for wider compatibility. 8BitDo claims battery life of 26-105 hours over 2.4 GHz, depending on the polling rate set.

articles.title: Por qué usuarios en Estados Unidos no podrán usar routers WiFi fabricados en el exterior
articles.text:
La Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones de Estados Unidos vetó los routers hechos en el exterior, pero le otorgó a Asus una aprobación condicional para seguir vendiendo estos dispositivos fabricados fuera del país, según confirmó el propio organismo. La excepción, firmada el 9 de septiembre de 2026, vence el 6 de marzo de 2028.
La medida libera a la marca taiwanesa de un veto que ya dejó afuera del mercado a su competidor TP-Link.
PUBLICIDAD
La aprobación cubre prácticamente todo el catálogo inalámbrico de Asus: la serie de routers RT, las líneas para jugadores ROG GT y ROG Strix GS, los equipos TUF Gaming, la línea empresarial ExpertWiFi, los sistemas de malla ZenWiFi y los módems portátiles 5G MiFi.
También incluye los repetidores y puntos de acceso de la marca, según el aviso oficial de la FCC.
La medida se apoya en una determinación de seguridad nacional que el gobierno activó en marzo de 2026, cuando el organismo sumó a los routers fabricados en el exterior a su llamada Lista Cubierta, la nómina de equipos considerados un riesgo para el país.
PUBLICIDAD
La FCC citó como antecedente las campañas de espionaje chino conocidas como Volt Typhoon, Flax Typhoon y Salt Typhoon.
Esas campañas, según el organismo, usaron routers domésticos comprometidos como puerta de entrada a redes críticas de Estados Unidos.
Desde entonces, cualquier fabricante que diseñe, ensamble o produzca sus equipos fuera de Estados Unidos necesita una aprobación condicional del Departamento de Guerra o del de Seguridad Nacional para seguir autorizando modelos nuevos. Para conseguirla debe presentar un plan detallado y con plazos concretos para instalar o ampliar su fabricación dentro del país.
El trámite también exige abrir la estructura societaria de la empresa y su cadena de proveedores.
Netgear fue la primera marca en lograr la excepción, en abril de 2026. Después se sumaron Eero, la filial de Amazon, Nokia, Starlink de SpaceX, Adtran, Calix, Zyxel y Askey, una subsidiaria de la propia Asus. Seis meses más tarde, TP-Link, la marca que más routers vende en el país, todavía no la consigue.
PUBLICIDAD
Por qué Asus consiguió la excepción
The Verge le preguntó a Asus si el plan de fabricación que presentó ante la FCC contempla trasladar producción a suelo estadounidense o si solo garantiza el abastecimiento del mercado local sin mudar fábricas. La empresa no respondió esa pregunta puntual durante más de doce días, según el medio.
Un vocero identificado como Jay Jay Guerrero confirmó al sitio que Asus “presentó el plan requerido ante la FCC” y que la compañía “trabaja con socios de fabricación certificados para respaldar su futuro portafolio”, pero evitó precisar en qué país ocurrirá esa producción.
La mayoría de los routers de Asus se fabrican hoy en Taiwán, con una porción en China continental, aunque la marca diversificó parte de su producción hacia Vietnam, Tailandia, Indonesia, México y República Checa en los últimos años.
PUBLICIDAD
La compañía también promociona su condición de “marca de equipos de red de confianza” y “proveedor de routers de confianza para consumidores” en sus comunicados. Según constató el medio, esas denominaciones no figuran en ningún registro del gobierno de Estados Unidos y solo aparecen en los propios materiales de Asus.
La FCC, por su parte, tampoco respondió a los pedidos de verificación del medio.
Qué ocurre con TP-Link
TP-Link domina las ventas de routers residenciales en Estados Unidos, pero no logró la misma excepción pese a haber trasladado la sede de su unidad local, TP-Link Systems, a Irvine, California. La empresa se reunió con funcionarios de la FCC en abril de 2026.
PUBLICIDAD
En ese encuentro, TP-Link prometió invertir cientos de millones de dólares para mudar parte de su fabricación de Vietnam a Estados Unidos, pero ese compromiso no alcanzó todavía para destrabar la aprobación.
La Electronic Frontier Foundation, una organización que defiende los derechos digitales de los usuarios de internet, cuestionó el criterio de la FCC. Según su análisis, las vulnerabilidades de seguridad también aparecen en dispositivos fabricados dentro de Estados Unidos.
PUBLICIDAD
PUBLICIDAD

articles.title: Cambridge A100 SE review: delightfully cheap wireless earbuds that hit all the right notes, but could be a just touch smoother in their delivery
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
Just in case you didn't have enough choice when it comes to true wireless in-ear headphones costing between £100 and £150, here’s the Cambridge A100 SE to make your decision trickier still. A thorough audition is the very least they deserve.
Reasons to buy
- +Spacious, informative and disciplined sound
- +Dynamic and punchy presentation
- +Impressive specification
Reasons to avoid
- -Not the most accomplished when it comes to rhythmic expression
- -Don’t look or feel in any way special
- -Touch controls could be more reliable
Why you can trust TechRadar
Cambridge A100 SE: Two-minute review
At a glance, not much separates the Cambridge A100 SE true wireless in-ear headphones from their older A100 stablemates — and that’s because not much does.
The most obvious difference on first acquaintance is the addition of a (very attractive) deep blue finish — and when you glance at the spec-sheet, it’s only the (admittedly not inconsiderable) addition of Dolby Audio functionality that justifies the ‘SE’ in the model name.
Which means that the A100 SE are, at the asking price, a lavishly specified pair of wireless earbuds for the the best budget earbuds market. Class A/B amplification, aptX Lossless and LDAC codec compatibility, 10mm dynamic drivers featuring a lot of recycled Neodymium, adaptive hybrid active noise cancellation, and very nearly 40 hours of battery life from the ‘buds and their charging case are high up on the list of highlights.
And in practice, the way the A100 SE perform is almost all ‘gain’ and very little ‘pain’. They are spacious and organised, control a soundstage well, offer plenty of detail, balance their frequency response and tonality pretty well, and include voice, touch and app as control options.
A price-comparable alternative such as the JBL Live Beam 4 can go even further where battery life is concerned, and have a more naturalistic way with rhythmic expression — the A100 SE are just slightly lumpy in this regard — but ultimately they’re ‘different’ rather than obviously ‘better’. Because at this sort of money, finding something obviously ‘better’ than the Cambridge A100 SE is going to prove tricky.
Cambridge A100 SE review: Price and release date
- Released on October 2, 2026
- $149 / £129 / AU$249
They're hot off the press at the time of writing, friend! We're publishing this review to meet their embargo. What you need to know is, the A100 SE earbuds arrived on October 2, 2026. So, they're new — albeit very much built upon their older siblings.
And that's a big plus. The original Cambridge Audio Melomania A100 arrived in June 2025 (Cambridge has since dropped the 'Audio' from its moniker and, it seems, the 'Melomania' from its buds) to a resounding five-star review.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
So while the price of these new earbuds is hardly huge, it does mean that the older set can now be found for around $99 / £79 — being superseded by newness can have this effect. So, there's plenty to consider…
Cambridge A100 SE review: Specs
| Type | True wireless in-ear | 
| Drivers | 10mm full range dynamic (Neodynium) | 
| Active noise cancellation | Yes | 
| Battery life | 39 hours (maximum) | 
| Weight | 4.7g (earbud); 38g (charging case) | 
| Frequency response | Not stated | 
| Connectivity | 5.4; LDAC, aptX Lossless codec compatibility | 
| Waterproofing | IPX5 | 
| Control | Touch; app | 
Cambridge A100 SE review: Features
- Class A/B amplification2
- Bluetooth 5.4 with aptX Lossless and LDAC compatibility3
- 39 hours battery life (maximum)
There’s no need to offer any kind of ‘at the asking price’ qualification here — the Cambridge A100 SE have a very worthwhile feature set, full stop.
The use of the same Class A/B amplification that’s at the heart of the company’s well-regarded CX and EX full-size integrated amplifiers delivers a hit of hardcore hi-fi credibility. Compatibility with cutting-edge aptX Lossless and LDAC Bluetooth codecs means the biggest wireless streams possible are available from source devices that are capable of delivering it. Snapdragon Sound (complete with dual-core 240MHz Qualcomm Kalimba DSP) should mean ultra-low latency, and dual-point connectivity means content from two connected devices can be switched between seamlessly. Sound itself is delivered by a pair of 10mm full-range dynamic drivers, and they make liberal use of recycled Neodymium in their composition.
Three QualComm cVc mics per earbud handle voice assistant interaction, telephony, and the adaptive hybrid noise-cancellation system. With ANC engaged, the earbud and the charging case offer more than 21 hours of playback time between them, and if you switch ANC off this figure rises to closer to 39 hours. And you can spend these many hours in pretty much any realistic environment, thanks to the earbuds’ IPX5 rating.
- Features score: 5 / 5
Cambridge A100 SE review: Sound quality
- Open, detailed and controlled sound
- Good sense of dynamic variation
- Not the most naturalistic where rhythms are concerned
Some true wireless in-ear headphones are more in-ear than others when it comes to the sound they make — the sensation of music being inside your head can be strong with some designs, and quite oppressive it is too. That’s not the case with the A100 SE; even without their ‘Dolby Audio’ mode being engaged they’re a notably open and airy listen, and when it’s switched in they become even more spacious. It’s not like listening to loudspeakers, of course, but it’s a lot less stifling than some alternatives.
It doesn’t do any harm in this respect that the Cambridge are quite adept when it comes to creating and controlling a soundstage. They have outright scale on their side, especially when it comes to the width of the stage, and they have absolute authority over the elements on it. There’s appreciable space between instruments, but a commonality and unity to the sound at the same time — the sensation of space doesn’t compromise the idea of ‘performance’.
A listen to a big FLAC file of LCD Soundsystem’s Daft Punk is Playing at My House allows the A100 SE to demonstrate a very even-handed way with frequency response and tonality. Leave the EQ settings out of the equation and the top-to-bottom presentation of the frequency range is smooth and undramatic in the best way — there’s no sense that the earbuds want to meaningfully favour any particular area of information over any other, and the same is true of the fairly neutral tone the Cambridge adopt. In ultimate terms they hint at spotlighting and gently heating the lowest frequencies, but overall they’re significantly less coloured than quite a few price-comparable rivals.
The A100 SE handle detail retrieval well, and are alert to even quite minor variations in timbre and texture — events deep in the mix or at the outer edges of the soundstage are not overlooked, and they’re given an appropriate amount of weighting in every circumstance. Details around the dynamics of harmonics are attended to well, and the more overt dynamics of attack and intensity are made absolutely apparent.
Really, it’s only where rhythmic expression is concerned that the Cambridge are anything less than really quite assertive. They’re reasonably adept when it comes to the attack and decay of bass sounds, and they certainly don’t drag at tempos — but they’re not as straight-edged as they might be, and consequently they handle rhythms in a relatively stiff, upright manner. ‘Lurch’ is too strong a word, but ‘lumpy’ isn’t — the A100 SE are, in absolute terms, just a little lumpy in this regard.
- Sound quality: 4.5 / 5
Cambridge A100 SE review: Design
- Choice of three finishes
- App and touch control
- Dolby Audio functionality
You’ve a straight choice if you’re designing a pair of true wireless in-ear headphones: either the pebble-like ‘twist to fit’ shape, or the dangly stem alternative popularised by Apple. For the A100 SE, Cambridge has gone down the second route.
The earbuds, and the slender charging case they travel in, are made to a perfectly acceptable standard, mostly from plastic that’s unremarkable both in look and feel. My review sample is a new dark blue finish, but more usual black or white alternatives are available.
The outer section of the top of each earbud features a capacitive touch surface, and here it’s possible to control playback, to handle telephony, to cycle through your ANC options, and to summon your source device’s native voice assistant (should it have one). They’re not as reliable as they might be in operation, but patience brings its rewards. Eventually.
You can also control the A100 SE using Cambridge’s ‘Melomania Connect’ control app. It’s a fair bit more reliable than the touch controls, and as well as being where you can engage (or disengage) the earbuds’ new Dolby Audio feature (which has the very welcome knack of bring a little more space to the sound, and a little less of the ‘directly into your head’ sensation some IEMs can suffer from) it allows you to remap the touch controls to get the sequence on taps, presses and holds you prefer.
It also features a seven-band EQ — there are six presets and the option to save a few custom settings of your own. It’s also where you can switch the ‘wear detect’ function on or off, engage ‘game’ mode, check for firmware updates and, perhaps most importantly of all in this instance, select your preferred ‘audible feedback’.
Not for the first time where a pair of Cambridge wireless headphones are concerned, the usual options of ‘off’, ‘tone’ and quite a quantity of different languages are available, along with a ‘Southwark’ option which turns out to be Matt Berry really Matt Berry-ing it up. It’s a frivolous, profoundly funny option that I am nowhere near tiring of — and TechRadar's Audio Editor agrees wholeheartedly.
- Design score: 4 / 5
Cambridge A100 SE review: value
- Great specification
- Some proper performance highlights
- Matt Berry!
This is a very competitive area of the true wireless headphones market, and Cambridge has done a lot to ensure the A100 SE can be seen to represent good value for money.
The type of amplification that’s on board, the extensive Bluetooth codec compatibility, the spacious, detailed and dynamic nature of their presentation all point to a product that’s well worth the asking price, with only the slightly hit-and-miss touch-control implementation and slightly lumpy rhythmic expression counting against them.
- Value: 4.5 / 5
Should I buy the Cambridge A100 SE?
| Attributes | Notes | Rating | 
|---|---|---|
| Features | Class A/B amplification, great call-handling, aptX and LDAC codec support | 5/5 | 
| Sound quality | Detailed and controlled with a good sense of dynamic variation, just not the most naturalistic rhythmically | 4.5/5 | 
| Design | Three finishes and highly functional, just a little unremarkable | 4/5 | 
| Value | A competitive area, but nevertheless there's great sound-per-pound value to be had here | 4.5/5 | 
Buy them if…
You like open sound
There’s a proper sensation of space to the way the A100 SE present music, especially where ‘Dolby Audio’ mode is engaged. 
You enjoy long listens
The Cambridge are relatively comfortable earbuds, and they have the battery stamina to let you listen right around the clock. 
You appreciate a point of difference
No other manufacturer has the ability to let you hear Matt Berry gleefully over-reading “waiting to pair!” and other classics of TWS audible feedback.
Don’t buy them if…
You’re easily frustrated
The touch controls are not absolute perfect in operation, and you’ll need to remain calm at times in order to get what you’re asking for. 
You’re rhythm-focused
The A100 SE are talented in many respects, but they don’t express rhythms with quite the confidence or the fluency of some rivals. 
You’re expecting a premium look and feel
This Cambridge product is keenly priced, so while the quality of construction is well up to standard there’s nothing luxurious about it. 
Cambridge A100 SE review: Also consider
The JBL Live Beam 4, while slightly more expensive, are probably the most impressive price-comparable rival to the A100 SE right now — and it seems fair to say that they’re slightly different, rather than obviously better or worse, than the Cambridge model.
They struggle to match the noise-cancellation the A100 SE offer, for instance, and don’t have quite as pronounced a spatial audio effect — but they hit back with a more convincing way of describing rhythms and straightforwardly impressive battery life of as much as 48 hours between charges.
Any other products of note? Yes, Apple's new AirPods 5 with Wireless Charging are right at this level and if you own an iPhone, they certainly look competitive on paper — just not for codec support (see "if you own an iPhone", above) or stamina. Our full review of Apple's newest buds is incoming, but food for thought at any rate.
How I tested the Cambridge A100 SE
- With Apple and Android devices
- With file types from MP3 to DSD3
- Indoors and outdoors
I used the Cambridge A100 SE at my desk, while out walking and on public transport. I connected them to an Apple MacBook Pro, an Apple iPhone 15 Pro and a FiiO M15S hi-res player.
This allowed me to access Qobuz and Tidal music streaming services, internet radio via Airable, and hi-res content stored on the DAP’s internal memory. I listened to lots of different genres of music and plenty of spoken-word content — and I did so, on and off, for two weeks.
- First reviewed in September 2026
- Read TechRadar's review guarantee
- Learn more specifically about how we test earbuds at TechRadar
Simon Lucas is a senior editorial professional with deep experience of print/digital publishing and the consumer electronics landscape. Based in Brighton, Simon worked at TechRadar's sister site What HiFi? for a number of years, as both a features editor and a digital editor, before embarking on a career in freelance consultancy, content creation, and journalism for some of the biggest brands and publications in the world.
With enormous expertise in all things home entertainment, Simon reviews everything from turntables to soundbars for TechRadar, and also likes to dip his toes into longform features and buying guides. His bylines include GQ, The Guardian, Hi-Fi+, Metro, The Observer, Pocket Lint, Shortlist, Stuff T3, Tom's Guide, Trusted Reviews, and more.
