articles.title: OpenAI convierte a ChatGPT en una plataforma para descubrir y usar aplicaciones dentro de los chats
articles.text:
OpenAI, la empresa liderada por Sam Altman, presentó durante su DevDay, un conjunto de funciones que convierten a ChatGPT en una plataforma para descubrir, instalar y usar aplicaciones, tanto para personas como para sus propios agentes de inteligencia artificial autónomos.
El anuncio combinó el lanzamiento de dots, sus nuevos asistentes autónomos, con una expansión de la arquitectura de extensiones (pequeños programas que se integran dentro de la conversación) que ya existía en ChatGPT. Juntas, apuntan a desafiar el modelo tradicional de tiendas de aplicaciones que dominan Apple y Google.
PUBLICIDAD
Según detalló la empresa en su evento, ChatGPT ya tiene 1.200 millones de usuarios semanales. A partir de ahora, el chatbot sugerirá aplicaciones dentro del flujo de una conversación cuando detecte que una herramienta externa puede resolver la tarea que pide el usuario, quien podrá conectarla y usarla sin salir de la interfaz.
La compañía presentó una función llamada Iniciar sesión con ChatGPT, que permite llevar la identidad y el cupo de uso de inteligencia artificial contratado a aplicaciones de terceros. En el lanzamiento participó un primer grupo de 16 socios, entre ellos Devin (de Cognition), Notion y Vercel.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo los agentes de IA que reemplazan a las aplicaciones
El corazón de la estrategia son los dots, agentes autónomos de inteligencia artificial que cuentan cada uno con su propia computadora y navegador en la nube. Pueden navegar la web, ejecutar tareas y conectarse con el ecosistema de más de 4.000 aplicaciones que ya trabaja con OpenAI.
A diferencia del modelo anterior, en el que el usuario debía descargar una aplicación distinta para cada tarea (armar un sitio web, coordinar una agenda de reuniones), ahora es el agente el que se encarga de reunir las herramientas necesarias y ejecutarlas por su cuenta.
Asimismo, los dots pueden actuar de forma proactiva: la empresa los describe como capaces de anticiparse a un problema o retomar una tarea que el usuario olvidó, siempre con su aprobación previa. Para eso, realizan lo que OpenAI llama “investigación proactiva” en modo de solo lectura sobre las aplicaciones conectadas.
PUBLICIDAD
En una demostración durante el evento, la empresa mostró cómo una aplicación propia de reuniones puede leer el calendario del usuario, tomar notas automáticas durante un encuentro y entregar un resumen de las tareas pendientes al finalizar.
Los dots funcionan con GPT-6 Astra, un modelo orientado a investigación, programación y tareas complejas de varios pasos, y disponen de una computadora propia en la nube, navegador y acceso a diferentes apps conectadas.
De qué forma se integra el mercado de software dentro del chat en ChatGPT
OpenAI anunció un mercado de aplicaciones empresariales con más de 30 socios de lanzamiento, entre ellos Adobe, Figma, Salesforce, HubSpot, ServiceNow, Palo Alto Networks y CrowdStrike. Los clientes elegibles podrán destinar parte de lo que ya pagan a OpenAI para contratar el software de esos socios.
PUBLICIDAD
La compañía también simplificó el proceso de revisión para que los desarrolladores puedan hacer un seguimiento del estado de sus extensiones, algo equivalente al sistema de revisión de aplicaciones que utiliza Apple en su tienda.
El movimiento le da a los creadores de aplicaciones una vía alternativa para llegar a usuarios sin depender de las tiendas de Apple y Google. Un desarrollador podría, por ejemplo, vender una suscripción directamente desde su sitio web y después conectarla a ChatGPT para que el agente del usuario la utilice.
Sin embargo, OpenAI no presentó en su evento anual ningún mecanismo de cobro o de reparto de ingresos comparable al que rige en las tiendas tradicionales de Apple y Google. La empresa se concentró en construir las piezas de descubrimiento, distribución e identidad del sistema, pero dejó sin definir cómo se cobrará por ese nuevo canal de software.

articles.title: Hébergement VPS : pour quels sites et à partir de quand y passer ?
articles.text:
Hébergement VPS : pour quels sites et à partir de quand y passer ?
Un hébergement VPS devient intéressant lorsque le mutualisé atteint ses limites : trafic plus important, ralentissements répétés ou besoins techniques spécifiques. Plus puissant et flexible, il demande aussi davantage de connaissances. Mais tous les sites n’en ont pas besoin. Voici les principaux signes qui permettent de savoir quand passer à cette solution.
Un hébergement VPS devient pertinent lorsqu’un site commence à manquer de ressources sur une offre mutualisée. Une boutique en ligne en croissance, une application web ou un WordPress très fréquenté peuvent notamment avoir besoin de davantage de puissance et de liberté de configuration.
Avec un hébergement mutualisé, plusieurs sites utilisent les ressources d’un même serveur. Le VPS repose également sur un serveur physique partagé, mais chaque environnement virtuel dispose de ressources qui lui sont attribuées. Il offre ainsi davantage de contrôle sur la configuration et le fonctionnement du serveur.
Cette liberté a cependant une contrepartie : l’administration demande plus de connaissances. Pour un petit site vitrine, le mutualisé reste donc généralement plus adapté.
VPS ou mutualisé : quelles différences ?
L’hébergement mutualisé constitue souvent le point de départ. Il convient aux blogs, sites vitrines et petits sites professionnels et demande peu de connaissances techniques.
Le VPS s’adresse plutôt aux projets qui commencent à avoir des besoins spécifiques.
|  | Mutualisé | VPS | 
|---|---|---|
| Ressources | Partagées | Allouées au VPS | 
| Contrôle | Limité | Important | 
| Configuration | Encadrée | Personnalisable | 
| Gestion | Simple | Plus technique | 
| Évolution | Limitée | Plus flexible | 
Le VPS n’est donc pas simplement un mutualisé plus puissant. Il apporte surtout un environnement plus indépendant, avec davantage de possibilités de configuration.
Quels sont les avantages d’un VPS ?
Le premier intérêt concerne les ressources disponibles. Un VPS permet de choisir une quantité de mémoire vive, de CPU et de stockage adaptée au projet.
Cette isolation peut également apporter davantage de stabilité. Sur un mutualisé, les ressources sont partagées entre plusieurs sites. Avec un VPS, l’environnement est mieux séparé des autres utilisateurs présents sur le serveur physique.
Par ailleurs, le VPS offre une plus grande liberté. Il devient possible d’installer certains logiciels, de modifier la configuration du serveur ou de déployer une application qui ne fonctionnerait pas sur une offre mutualisée classique.
Quand faut-il passer à un VPS ?
Il n’existe pas de seuil universel en nombre de visiteurs. Un site avec 10 000 visites mensuelles peut avoir davantage besoin d’un VPS qu’un autre qui en reçoit plusieurs fois plus, selon sa technologie et les ressources consommées.
Les limites du mutualisé se répètent
Si l’hébergeur signale régulièrement une consommation excessive de CPU ou de mémoire, c’est un premier indice. Une saturation ponctuelle ne justifie pas forcément une migration, mais des alertes répétées peuvent montrer que l’offre actuelle devient trop juste.
Avant de changer de serveur, il reste cependant utile d’optimiser le site. Une base de données trop lourde, des images mal compressées ou des extensions WordPress gourmandes peuvent provoquer des ralentissements.
Le trafic augmente
Une boutique en ligne ou un site média peut connaître des pics de fréquentation. Si les performances diminuent dès que le trafic augmente, un VPS peut apporter davantage de marge.
Cette évolution est particulièrement intéressante pour un site professionnel dont la disponibilité devient importante. Quelques secondes de chargement supplémentaires peuvent rapidement nuire à l’expérience des visiteurs.
Le site nécessite davantage de liberté
C’est parfois le meilleur signal. Si le projet demande une version particulière d’un logiciel, l’installation d’une application ou une configuration spécifique, le mutualisé peut devenir trop contraignant.
Le VPS permet alors d’adapter davantage l’environnement aux besoins du projet.
Quels sites peuvent avoir besoin d’un VPS ?
Le VPS convient surtout aux projets qui dépassent le cadre d’un simple site vitrine.
Les boutiques en ligne
Une boutique e-commerce doit gérer les produits, comptes clients, commandes, paiements et différentes extensions. Plus son activité augmente, plus les besoins en ressources peuvent progresser.
Un VPS peut donc constituer une étape intéressante lorsque le mutualisé commence à montrer ses limites.
Les applications web
Les applications sont particulièrement adaptées au VPS. Elles nécessitent parfois plusieurs services, une base de données spécifique ou des réglages qui ne sont pas accessibles sur un hébergement classique.
Dans ce cas, le contrôle offert par le serveur virtuel devient aussi important que la puissance disponible.
Les WordPress à fort trafic
Un petit blog n’a généralement aucune raison de passer sur un VPS. En revanche, un WordPress très fréquenté, avec de nombreuses extensions ou une base de données importante, peut finir par consommer davantage de ressources.
Le VPS peut alors apporter une marge supplémentaire, à condition que le site soit correctement optimisé.
Plusieurs sites professionnels
Pour un freelance ou une petite agence qui gère plusieurs sites, un VPS peut permettre de regrouper différents projets sur une même infrastructure.
Cette solution demande toutefois de surveiller la consommation de chaque site et de prévoir des sauvegardes adaptées.
Quelles offres VPS choisir ?
Les hébergeurs proposent aujourd’hui des VPS allant de petites configurations destinées aux projets modestes à des serveurs beaucoup plus puissants.
Hostinger : une offre accessible pour débuter
Hostinger propose plusieurs VPS KVM. Son offre KVM 1 est affichée à partir de 5,49 € par mois dans le cadre de la promotion indiquée, avec 1 vCPU, 4 Go de RAM, 50 Go de stockage NVMe et 4 To de bande passante.
Le KVM 2 propose 2 vCPU, 8 Go de RAM et 100 Go de stockage NVMe pour 7,99 € par mois dans le cadre de la promotion affichée. Une formule KVM 4 monte à 4 vCPU, 16 Go de RAM et 200 Go de stockage.
Hostinger mise également sur des outils destinés à simplifier l’administration du serveur. Cette approche peut faciliter une première transition depuis le mutualisé.
Il faut cependant regarder le tarif de renouvellement. Le prix promotionnel de départ ne correspond pas forcément au coût sur plusieurs années.
IONOS : davantage de ressources
IONOS propose de son côté plusieurs configurations VPS. Son VPS M+ est affiché à 3 € HT par mois pendant trois mois, puis à 9 € HT par mois. Il comprend 4 vCores, 4 Go de RAM et 120 Go de stockage NVMe.
Le VPS L+ propose 6 vCores, 8 Go de RAM et 240 Go de stockage NVMe. Son tarif promotionnel est de 5 € HT par mois pendant trois mois, avant de passer à 18 € HT par mois.
IONOS inclut également un trafic annoncé comme illimité et une connexion jusqu’à 1 Gbit/s. Là encore, le tarif normal doit être pris en compte pour comparer correctement les offres.
Un VPS demande-t-il des connaissances techniques ?
C’est le principal point à ne pas sous-estimer.
Avec un mutualisé, une grande partie de la maintenance est assurée par l’hébergeur. Sur un VPS, l’utilisateur dispose de davantage de contrôle, mais doit aussi gérer une partie de la sécurité et de l’administration.
Mises à jour, pare-feu, utilisateurs, sauvegardes ou surveillance du serveur peuvent nécessiter certaines connaissances. Les interfaces proposées par les hébergeurs simplifient plusieurs opérations, mais elles ne remplacent pas complètement l’administration technique.
Pour un site vitrine classique, cette charge n’est généralement pas nécessaire. Pour un développeur ou une entreprise ayant besoin d’un environnement personnalisé, elle peut au contraire être parfaitement justifiée.
Le VPS est-il vraiment nécessaire ?
Pas toujours. Un site qui fonctionne correctement sur un hébergement mutualisé n’a aucune raison de migrer simplement pour disposer d’une configuration plus puissante.
Le passage au VPS devient intéressant lorsque les limites sont concrètes : ralentissements réguliers, ressources insuffisantes, hausse importante du trafic ou besoin d’une configuration particulière.
Au final, le bon moment pour passer au VPS n’est pas lié à un nombre précis de visiteurs. Il dépend surtout des besoins réels du site. Le mutualisé reste adapté aux petits projets, tandis qu’un VPS devient pertinent pour les boutiques en croissance, les applications web, les WordPress très fréquentés ou les projets professionnels nécessitant davantage de contrôle.
Hostinger peut constituer une porte d’entrée accessible, tandis qu’IONOS propose des configurations plus généreuses à des tarifs d’appel attractifs. Dans les deux cas, le tarif de renouvellement et les ressources réellement nécessaires doivent être vérifiés avant de souscrire.

articles.title: Hacker Conversations: Rob Juncker, a Knock at the Door and a Moral Compass
articles.text:
Rob Juncker is chief product and technology officer at Mimecast. Is he a hacker? “Unequivocally yes,” he says. “And I think every security leader should be able to answer ‘yes’ to that question, for so many reasons.”
He started early, when his parents brought home an Apple IIc. He was 10. They wanted to use it for word processing; but within two days of it arriving he had the lid off, trying to figure out how it worked. He had a driving curiosity to understand it. This curiosity, which he describes more as a thirst for knowledge, started before the arrival of the Apple – but with hands-on access, it rapidly focused on technology.
Back then, especially for a 10-year-old, there were few books and little training available. But it was obvious that what made the Apple do things was software. So, he taught himself Basic programming by looking at the code on the screen and working out what words caused which actions.
“Pretty soon I found myself sitting there with the command prompt and starting to program in Basic. I think that was my first experience of the beauty of computers and electronics in general. Suddenly I was unlocking a world where I could write something and create it. It was like an artist being given a paintbrush for the first time and then realizing that you don’t need to stick within the confines of what’s on the paper in front of you – rather, you create your own canvas and what you can do with it.”
Then came modems. They were just 300 baud in those days but still magic to a new teenager with an Apple. His parents got one; but that wasn’t enough for him – especially after he discovered wardialers. To get the full benefit, he needed his own dedicated phone line for the modem, but his parents refused.
“So, I did what any hacker would do,” he explains – but remember that this was a hacker barely into his teens. “I called the phone company and ordered a phone line to be installed at my house. But the best part of this story,” he added, “is before the scheduled appointment, I was in the basement running laps around my house to get my body temperature high enough to tell my parents that I was sick and couldn’t go to school the next day. When the engineer arrived to do the installation, I was home alone with a forged letter from my dad.”
The forgery would not have been difficult. The family already had a computer being used as a word processor, and the engineer had nothing to verify the signature against. The letter explained that the family wanted a dedicated low-noise line for a modem – and it worked. The youngster expanded his hacking repertoire into successful social engineering – and all because he couldn’t afford the games he wanted and needed to find a different way to access them.
Think about this for a moment. He started when only ten years old. In the space of a year of access to an Apple IIc, he taught himself rudimentary hacking and the ability to code in Basic; and a few years later, he designed, delivered and succeeded with a complex example of social engineering. “I effectively did the first ‘deepfake’: a kid faking his father and ordering a phone line. I had no legal right to do this, but I succeeded in doing it.”
With the modem, he began more serious hacking. “I’ll admit it. I downloaded early samples of pirated software; and that eventually got me into trouble – which I’m completely free of now, by the way!”
By the time he was in his teens he had become more adventurous. He gave an example. “In the early days, SimCity asked you for the population of a city provided on a red sheet (red, so it couldn’t be photocopied) every time you played the game. I was working alongside another hacker to find a way to bypass such controls; so, we’d be working in code and especially assembly. To be honest, I wasn’t the one who solved the problem – it was another member of the group. But it’s an example of the sort of stuff I was trying to do.”
The trouble arrived with the proverbial knock on the door in his early teens.
“One day a certain US legal organization came to the house and the doorbell rang. My mother answered it, and I overheard the words, ‘We need to have a conversation with you all. We understand that there has potentially been some activity here relative to tapping into phone lines or trying to gain access to certain services.’ Well, that was true. I had been trying to. I hadn’t been successful, but I had been trying to.”
His mother replied, “No. That’s not possible.” And then he saw the lightbulb go on as it dawned on her. He heard, “Rob!” They sat down and had that conversation.
“Long story short, I lost my second phone line and had to rein back on my activities. I received a warning. And I’m grateful that I got a warning at that point, because had I continued along the path I was on, I think I would have ended up with more than just a warning. It was a turning point for me.”
The threat of jail time caused an immediate bit flip in his attitude. It was the moment he realized he should probably change what he was doing.
But that’s only half his story. When he later went to college, he wanted to continue learning about technology and computers, but he added economics. “If you mix Computer Science and Economics, you actually get the most boring geek on the face of the earth,” he mused.
On the one hand, he had been warned off using computer skills for negative purposes, while on the other hand, the new study of economics pointed toward an alternative use of computer skills. It made him realize he could have a legitimate and well-paid career in protecting computers rather than attacking them.
“What I learned through economics is you can make really good money in software and do great things with computing. I’ll go back to that artist analogy. I believe that hackers and their curiosity are no different than artists. The artist in the hacker doesn’t simply wish to paint a new picture; he wishes to create a new canvas on which to paint.”
He excelled at painting on his brand new ‘canvas of potential’, where computers could drive and push the boundaries through curiosity. “I think that’s something that I’ve brought to the industry; that maybe the way that we’re doing things isn’t necessarily the way we should be doing things, but rather just the way that we’ve always done them in the past. I love that quote from Grace Hopper: ‘The most dangerous phrase in the language is, ‘We’ve always done it this way’.”
It was the combination of legal threat and understanding the economics of business computing that led to a complete 180-degree about-turn from his early life. He fell in love with technology, taught himself to program in Basic and started hacking when he was 10. He studied computer science and economics at college – and the latter showed him negative hacking was not the only way to use his skills.
In his early twenties, a third factor emerged. Health issues made him question what he wanted in life. “As I went through those health problems, I asked myself, ‘What defines me; what is the legacy I want to leave in this world?’” The answer is simple to say, but hard to do: “I really want to leave the world a better place.”
Kick-started by health, a moral compass had appeared. He probably always had one (he thinks its subtle presence is what kept him just on the right side of prison when he was younger), but he only now became aware of it. It is the almost innate understanding that most of us possess: a natural understanding of right and wrong with a preference to do what is right. On his moral compass, morality became his true North Star.
“That North Star brought me to a place where I can use everything I’ve learned and the skills I’ve acquired to defend organizations – to make the world a little safer.” His knowledge of how to attack systems had given him an understanding of how to defend them; and that is where he has spent his professional career.
After senior R&D and engineering roles at VMware, LANDesk and Ivanti, he joined Code42 in 2017. He became Code42’s CTO in 2020, and moved to Mimecast when it acquired the company in July 2024.
Everything he began learning when he was 10 (software, technology and security) is now combined into his current position: chief product and technology officer at Mimecast.

articles.title: RFK Jr. thinks AI will free us from the "tyranny" of medical facts, expertise
articles.text:
At a Make America Healthy Again event Tuesday, anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy opened a “fireside chat” with Vice President JD Vance on the topic of artificial intelligence. While MAHA generally coalesces around things like healthy lifestyles and mistrust of drugmakers, Kennedy quickly turned to extolling the potential of artificial intelligence, surprising Vance, who said he was expecting to discuss “weight loss and acid, not AI.”
Kennedy boasted that the Trump administration is “making it easy for every American to use AI,” which he claimed would free us from the “medical tyranny” of doctors and health experts. He suggested Americans should start using AI to get second opinions about medical recommendations, saying AI is “better informed than any doctor in the country.” He also suggested that the technology would confirm his misinformation about vaccines and contrarian views on public health guidance.
“We’re never, ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us trust the experts, because every American will be able to check their own medical advice,” Kennedy said.
AI >>> Kennedy
Kennedy, who has no medical, scientific, or public health experience, then laid out specific examples in which he suggested AI would contradict health and medical experts and vindicate his own views:
“If somebody tells you masks work, trust the experts, AI may tell you otherwise. If somebody tells you social distancing works, trust the experts, AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection—oh, you need to take it to protect your grandmother—AI may say it actually doesn’t do that”
AI may contradict or “correct” experts, but does it actually? We checked—the answer was nope.
When we asked Google’s Gemini: “Do masks work to prevent spread of infectious diseases?”
The AI chatbot responded (including its emphasis): “Yes, masks work to reduce the spread of respiratory infectious diseases, operating primarily as physical barriers to outgoing and incoming infectious particles. Their real-world effectiveness depends heavily on mask quality, fit, and population-level adherence.”
ChatGPT offered a similar answer, responding: “Yes. Masks can reduce the spread of some infectious diseases, particularly respiratory infections transmitted through droplets and aerosols.”
Doctors and experts >>> AI
Chatbots provided similar affirmative answers to the question of whether social distancing works at preventing infectious diseases. “Yes, social distancing is an effective public health measure for reducing the transmission of infectious diseases, particularly respiratory pathogens,” Gemini responded.

articles.title: AMD's new Zen 6 Epyc Venice lineup starts at $700 and scales all the way to 256 cores for $14,900
articles.text:
First look: AMD is pricing its upcoming Epyc 9006 Venice server processors from $700 to $14,904, covering systems from small single-socket servers to dual-socket machines with 512 Zen 6 CPU cores. The lineup is built around two platforms with different priorities: SP7 for maximum memory bandwidth and capacity, and SP8 for systems that need more PCIe connectivity. The pricing list includes 31 processors ranging from the eight-core Epyc 9106 to the 256-core Epyc 9996.
AMD has not finalized the prices, but the list offers a clearer view of how it intends to position Venice in the data center.
The Epyc 9996 is the top model in the lineup. It has 256 cores and a list price of $14,904. Two installed in a dual-socket SP7 server would provide 512 Zen 6 cores, though the processors alone would cost $29,808 before memory, storage, networking and accelerators are added.
At that level, the price is not far from the previous-generation 192-core Epyc 9965, which launched at about $14,800. Venice changes the value calculation, however. The 256-core chip works out to about $58.21 per core. The 64-core Epyc 9556, priced at $8,008, costs about $125.12 per core. That makes the largest parts more attractive for customers trying to consolidate workloads or increase compute density in a limited number of servers.
SP7 is AMD's high-end Venice platform. It supports up to 16 memory channels and can use DDR5 RDIMMs or MRDIMMs at speeds up to DDR5-12800. It also provides up to 96 PCIe 6.0 lanes. The processors designed for the socket have thermal design power ratings from 400W to 600W.
The platform is meant for workloads that need a large pool of memory and high memory throughput, including virtualization, databases and analytics. It supports both one- and two-socket systems.
AMD is also offering high-frequency models for workloads that benefit more from clock speed than from very high core counts. The 64-core Epyc 9586F and the 96-core Epyc 9686F can boost to 5 GHz. The trade-off is price and power use. The 64-core 9586F is priced close to the 96-core Epyc 9656 even though it has fewer cores, and its TDP is 100W higher.
The lower-cost SP8 platform takes a different route. It has eight memory channels and does not support MRDIMMs, so it cannot match SP7's peak memory capacity or bandwidth. It does, however, offer 128 PCIe 6.0 lanes, compared with 96 on SP7.
That extra I/O could matter in servers built around GPUs, AI accelerators, high-speed networking cards or dense NVMe storage. SP8 parts are also rated from 130W to 400W, giving system builders more options for lower-power configurations.
The SP8 lineup begins with the $700 eight-core Epyc 9106 and tops out with the 128-core Epyc 9746 at $11,679. It also includes "P" models limited to single-socket systems. Those parts offer the same CPU performance as comparable standard versions at a lower price because they do not support two-socket configurations. AMD lists the 128-core Epyc 9736P at a price 6% lower than the regular Epyc 9736, while the 32-core Epyc 9356P is 26% cheaper than its non-P counterpart.
One of the more specialized chips is the 16-core Epyc 9176F. It has a 5 GHz boost clock and 192MB of L3 cache, or 12MB per core. That's four times the cache of the 16-core Epyc 9116. It also costs more than three times as much. The design appears aimed at customers that need strong per-core performance and large cache capacity while keeping core counts low, which can be important for software licensed by the core.
AMD expects SP7 Venice systems to arrive in the fourth quarter, with SP8 systems due in the first half of 2027. A Venice-X family using AMD's 3D V-Cache technology is expected later in 2027, with up to 96 cores and 1,152MB of cache.

articles.title: Noch vor den Prime Deal Days: Amazon reduziert neuen Fire TV Stick 4K direkt
articles.text:
Noch vor den Prime Deal Days: Amazon stellt neuen Fire TV Stick 4K vor und reduziert ihn direkt
Hinweis: Wir haben in diesem Artikel Provisions-Links verwendet und sie durch "*" gekennzeichnet. Erfolgt über diese Links eine Bestellung, erhält t3n.de eine Provision.
Bei Amazon gibt es viel zu kaufen. Manchmal ist die Auswahl aber auch etwas zu groß. Der Versandhändler verkaufte allein drei Fire TV Sticks mit dem Zusatz 4K: den 4K Select, den 4K Plus und den 4K Max. Die Unterschiede herauszuarbeiten und für sich das richtige Modell zu finden? Gar nicht so einfach. Deswegen stellt der Versandhändler sein Angebot für Streaming-Sticks neu auf. Es gibt nur noch den Fire TV Stick HD, den 4K Max und eine neu vorgestellte Variante.
Der Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K* ist ab sofort erhältlich. Er kostet regulär 74,99 Euro, ist aber direkt zum Start auf 34,99 Euro reduziert. Die Fernbedienung* allein ist für 15,99 Euro zu haben.
Fire TV Stick 4K mit neuem Betriebssystem
Für Kund:innen wird damit nicht nur das Portfolio übersichtlicher. Wer beim neuen Stick zuschlägt, soll auch von einigen Neuheiten profitieren. So ist der 4K-fähige Stick kompakter, nimmt hinterm Fernseher also weniger Platz ein. Zudem bietet er eine sogenannte „Diret Power“-Funktion. Der Anschluss per USB an den Fernseher soll für die Stromversorgung ausreichen. Ein zusätzliches Netzteil ist nicht nötig. „Dies minimiert Kabelsalat“, schreibt Amazon.
Wie es bei neuer Hardware üblich ist, soll die Rechenleistung steigen. Mit wie viel Tempozuwachs man rechnen kann, wird aus den Zahlen des Versandhändlers aber nicht ganz klar. Der 4K-Stick führe zwischen 20 und 40 Prozent schneller vom Einschalten bis zur Wiedergabe als „preislich vergleichbare“ Streaming-Dongles. Zudem schaltete sich das Amazon-Gadget schneller ein. Apps sollen mehr als 35 und die Wiedergabe etwa 20 Prozent schneller starten. Ob damit weiterhin die Konkurrenz oder eine Vorgängerversion gemeint ist, schlüsselt die Amazon-Meldung nicht auf.
Neu ist zudem das Betriebssystem. Wie beim Fire TV Stick HD installiert Amazon sein neues Vega OS, das von Nutzern in der Vergangenheit kritisiert wurde, weil nicht alle Streaming-Apps damit kompatibel waren. Amazon hat hier nach eigener Aussage nachgebessert und das Angebot um 2.000 neue Apps erweitert. Dazu zählen Xbox und Spotify. Die gängigen Anbieter wie Netflix oder Disney Plus waren vorschon kompatibel.
Fernbedienung mit neuem Design
Neben dem Fire TV Stick 4K wird eine neue Fernbedienung im Karton liegen. Durch das angepasste Design soll man sie schneller richtig herum halten können. Zudem hat Amazon die Tasten überarbeitet. Weil die Startseiten-Taste besonders häufig gedrückt würde, sei diese nun mit einer Metalloberfläche versehen. Alle anderen Tasten sind markant geformt oder tiefer ins Gehäuse eingelassen, damit sie sich leichter finden lassen.
Neu ist eine programmierbare Taste, über die sich eine App nach Wahl öffnen lässt. Wie vorher auch können Nutzer kompatible TV-Modelle, Soundbars oder Receiver über die Fernbedienung ansteuern. Wie viele neue Amazon-Geräte bietet auch der Fire TV Stick 4K Zugriff auf den KI-Dienst Alexa Plus, der Eingaben in natürlicher Sprache besser verstehen soll.

articles.title: Microsoft enables Windows settings backup by default for orgs
articles.text:
Microsoft announced that Windows settings backup and restore is now enabled by default on all Microsoft Entra-joined or Microsoft Entra hybrid-joined enterprise systems upgraded to Windows 11 26H2.
The Windows settings backup tool (formerly known as Windows Backup for Organizations) backs up and restores enterprise users' Windows settings after a device is reset, replaced, upgraded, or reimaged.
Microsoft unveiled it two years ago at the Ignite conference in November 2024 as an opt-in feature (disabled by default), and it reached public preview in May 2025 and general availability in August 2025.
As announced in July, Microsoft has enabled the Windows settings backup policy by default for eligible devices after the release of Windows 11, version 26H2 on September 29.
"If user devices ever enter recovery, you don't have to guess whether their Windows settings have a backup. With this feature on by default, users are more likely to have their settings and Microsoft Store app list available to restore after a device reset, replacement, or upgrade," Microsoft said in a Wednesday message center update.
"The new default applies only if admins haven't explicitly configured the policy. We honor any existing explicit enable or disable setting. Restore behavior is unchanged and remains admin-controlled."
The Windows backup default-on behavior also applies only to devices that run Windows 11 26H2 from countries or regions not regulated by the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA), aren't in sovereign or restricted cloud environments, and have the backup policy not configured.
Additionally, the tool's restore behavior will not be enabled by default, and users will still need explicit admin configuration to restore Windows devices.
On devices where the tool is enabled by default, IT administrators will still retain full control via mobile device management (MDM) solutions.
Admins can disable the backup policy through Microsoft Intune or Group Policy, as these will take precedence over the default.

articles.title: Samsung lance les Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra et S12+ : prix, autonomie, puissance… tout savoir sur les tablettes haut de gamme
TypeSafe AI Releases Jev: A Decision-Only Model That Returns Typed Probabilities Instead of Text
articles.text:
TypeSafe AI, a San Francisco lab founded by former OpenAI researcher Diogo Almeida, has released Jev, the first of what it calls System One Models. Jev does not generate text. It returns typed, probabilistic decisions that software can act on directly.
A caller sends a state, either a string or structured data, together with a set of typed questions. Jev evaluates them all in a single parallel pass and returns Choice, Score and Noul answers with a probability distribution and a confidence value, so calling code can act above a threshold and escalate below it. Input costs $0.042 per million tokens, output is free, the context window is 32,000 tokens, and TypeSafe quotes end to end latency of 70ms to 500ms. Training uses a method it calls Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions.
Vercel, which added Jev to AI Gateway on day two, said it reached nearly 13% of paid teams within 24 hours, twice the share of the GPT-5.6 family. Netlify followed, LangChain shipped a TypeSafeClassifier integration with model routing and an AutoMode middleware that screens tool calls before they run, and five independent Elixir clients appeared within days.
First day adoption of Jev on Vercel AI Gateway compared with other recent model launches. Credit: Vercel
Vercel engineer Pranit Sharma found a safety classifier ran five to 18 times faster than the LLM it replaced, while Bryo AI CTO Nikhil Mudholkar rated Gemini slightly more accurate on email classification but 10 to 20 times more expensive, and valued Jev as the only one handing back a real probability. Armin Ronacher, CTO of Earendil, told TechCrunch the design "delegates the hallucination problem a little bit to the user", who has to decide whether a 50% probability is worth acting on, and pointed to model routing as another good fit. An analysis of 12,759 launch tweets by OpenChamber put user reported speedups at a median of 7x against the 193.6x headline, cost savings at a median of 30x, and latency at a median of 76ms with an upper quartile of 270ms.
One developer on Reddit called the model "absolutely insane" for agent work at 200ms to 300ms latency, and an early access user on Hacker News called it "really neat" while cautioning that its out of distribution behaviour will differ from an LLM.
On Hacker News, one developer noted that Jev cannot emit an invalid type but can still emit a completely wrong valid value:
First, congrats to the team on launching something genuinely interesting and new.
Seems like a more accurate title would be "Jev: Trading general purpose generation for fast typed inference" or something like that.
This is interesting, but the speed comparison seems misleading? A generative model that can output code in a Turing-complete language can do anything a computer can do.
Jev can only generate structured output, right? This is probably super useful for classification/routing/scoring, but it's nothing like the code generating models we're all using today for code and automation.
Also "can't hallucinate" seems wrong? Sure, it can't emit an invalid type, but it can still emit a completely wrong valid value. You can enforce structured output from an LLM too, with an appropriate harness, etc.
Teams replacing LLM classifiers should start with the jev-1.13 jaggedness page, which documents unreliable counting, arithmetic and date comparison, plus accuracy loss on large noisy state, and advises keeping maths in code. Pin a version such as jev-1.13.0 rather than the moving jev-latest and jev-preview aliases, and use the System One adapter to run existing models against the same schema when benchmarking. The quickstart covers keys, SDKs and the playground.
TypeSafe AI is an AI lab based in San Francisco, founded by Diogo Almeida, Erik Gafni and Sasha Sheng. Almeida co-invented RLHF and worked on the research behind ChatGPT.

articles.title: The Pentagon taps Elon Musk and Palmer Luckey to help decide what the military should do next | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a “State of the Force” address on Wednesday to launch a new effort to study how war may be fought as tech advances rapidly. It’s being called Project Meridian.
Elon Musk, Anduril founder Palmer Luckey, and former House Speaker Newt Gingrich will co-lead the project. They’ll be joined by others from fields such as academia and policy, all working under the direction of Defense Department CTO Emil Michael. Their job is to “study the battlefields of the future” and the “weapons and technologies warfighters” may use on them, said Hegseth in a letter announcing the project.
The team (it is unclear how many people will be on it) will have 120 days to submit its findings and propose “actionable solutions to start developing, testing, and fielding” advanced technology meant to keep America a dominant military power, per Hegseth.
Hegseth also announced an Autonomous Warfare Command on Wednesday to speed up the development and deployment of autonomous systems and drones. One curious detail in the Pentagon’s announcement is that the study will come through a partner organization, but the announcement does not say what that organization is or who leads it.
After TechCrunch reached out to the Defense Department for comment, the department referred us to a press release, saying it had “nothing further to provide beyond the Secretary’s comments.”
Musk’s and Luckey’s involvement is hardly surprising. Musk, in particular, has reportedly renewed close ties with the administration and recently had lunch with the president — alongside other top AI leaders — to discuss the future of AI. The project seemingly marks his first official return to the administration’s fold since he left the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) last year.
Musk’s SpaceX launches satellites for the U.S. government and operates a satellite network that supports national defense and security missions. Luckey’s defense tech company, Anduril, meanwhile, creates autonomous military systems and drones and was recently awarded government contracts to produce long-range missiles and semi-autonomous fighter aircraft and to supply hardware and integration for the Army’s mobile intelligence system.
The Trump administration has made advanced military technology a priority, in both development and purchasing, and has looked to Silicon Valley-approved companies to help make this happen. Critics could argue that putting Musk and Luckey on Project Meridian directly aligns with their business interests, since they would be trying to find solutions their companies already sell.

articles.title: Turning Edge AI Data Into Real-Time Action
articles.text:
On-device AI can deliver faster insights, greater autonomy, and less cloud traffic — but only with the right infrastructure.
Key Takeaways:
More AI is moving out of centralized data centers and into devices that can interpret data and act on it in real time.
By handling more processing locally, these edge systems can sharply reduce latency, improve security and privacy, and address growing concerns about data center energy and water consumption. Some data is already processed locally in consumer, industrial, automotive, and medical applications, but that percentage is expected to grow significantly in the next few years as edge devices become more capable and smaller language models are introduced.
“Number one are your personal devices,” said Sathish Balasubramanian, head of product for EDA AI at Siemens EDA. “Those are small. For example, a watch that can track your ECG and so forth. If your heartbeat rhythm is off, you can set it up so that it calls your hospital directly. On the industrial side, for example, a control unit monitors pressure in a boiler, or a control unit monitors a particular assembly line in a given section of an automotive factory. At the very extreme edges, every time a robot is picking up something and doing something, the finger is an edge device.”
Vehicles contain multiple sensors and processors that process data locally. “I would say cars in general are not edge devices,” said Balasubramanian. “Edge devices are more like the lidar in the car. Lidar finds out all your obstacles and everything, then it needs to be processed on board the car. Every section of the car is an edge device, whether it’s radar, lidar, the camera, or what is sensing in the camera, which needs to make sense of what the camera is seeing. That whole system is an edge device.”
The medical space is also filled with intelligent edge devices. “For example, a robotic surgeon has arms and knows the position to make the cut, with the right pressure,” said Balasubramanian. “Then all the systems need to be monitored and connected so that if the patient’s heart rate goes up, or they are trying to wake up, the human needs to figure out what to do.”
Whatever the application, edge AI analytics focus on real-time performance and metrics that address how data is gathered, stored, and used, as well as what actions are taken based on that data. That information is then looped back to improve the process. In effect, edge AI analytics systems act as a bridge between different systems, and between people and hardware.
“By placing compute near data sources, edge AI infrastructure enables local inference across telecom nodes, industrial gateways, enterprise servers, and smart building controllers,” said William Chen, product marketing group director for design IP at Cadence. “These systems operate at the point of physical interaction, powering applications from automotive and industrial SoCs to wearables, smart cameras, and consumer endpoints.”
That connection between local intelligence and physical systems depends on a steady flow of usable data, collected close to the source, and filtered before it moves farther upstream.
Data comes from numerous devices and sensors. “From a data‑gathering perspective, edge systems primarily ingest information from two sources — sensors and human or agent interactions,” Chen explained. “Sensors span a wide range of modalities, including vision via cameras, light, environmental, industrial, and more. They generate data at very high volumes and speeds. Examples include multi‑camera video streams captured over millisecond‑scale intervals — or faster. To make this data tractable, raw sensor outputs must be processed locally to reduce bandwidth and latency requirements before being forwarded upstream, either to a local compute cluster or directly to a cloud‑based AI factory for higher‑level processing and reasoning.”
Setting up an edge AI analytics system
Several key considerations come into play when deploying an integrated edge AI analytics system.
“Organizations building edge AI systems will gain a durable advantage by tightly integrating compute, data movement, interfaces, and security models early,” Chen noted. “Once collected, all data must be transported efficiently for downstream or upstream processing steps such as reasoning, inference, and storage. These data paths span multiple hops and domains — from sensors to edge processors, between edge processors and adjunct accelerators or local memory, from edge devices to gateways, and ultimately from gateways to cloud infrastructure.”
Layers of software oversee all these elements, from digital twins to product lifecycle management.
“The key challenge is, how do you build a model for what the edge AI needs to do?” said Balasubramanian. “The second thing is, how do you connect the entire digital thread with what we see in the digital twin of the product to the digital twin in the factory? Then, how do you monitor everything, and how do you do the analytics? Finally, how do you act on it?”
Balasubramanian described three components to this flow:
Silicon lifecycle management (SLM) can provide additional device-level monitoring, while PLM serves as the data backbone of an edge analytics system.
“You can essentially trace back everything,” said Balasubramanian. “When I ordered this part, what maintenance was done on the part on this robot? When was the last firmware update done? Who came and accessed the data? Was anything different in this particular robot compared to everything else in the factory flow?”
Edge AI devices can use local processing to make decisions, or some combination of local, near-local, and cloud. But the ability to act locally is only useful if the surrounding infrastructure is configured to control where data moves, how models are deployed, and when humans remain part of the decision loop.
Systems administrators need to deploy edge devices effectively to benefit from analytics. “Companies want to have more edge-based analytics for the purpose of keeping their data on their own localized systems, so they would set up the infrastructure to enable that to happen,” said Matthew Bubis, director of product management at Imagination Technologies. “There would be a human in the loop to set that up, but once it’s set up, a company or an enterprise might have an automated system of managing that. For example, if you open your company laptop and you’re using an AI-based system, the IT department would have set up a way to manage really sensitive, secure data. They would put a wrapper on that to say, ‘We must process this on the edge and deploy to the edge systems only so that we’re keeping all our data closed.’ The data is automated, but that’s after a human has decided how the edge devices operate.”
The overall goal of edge AI analytics is to improve the organization’s operations. “AI is increasingly moving from the digital world into the physical world, where it can improve how systems operate, make decisions, and use resources more efficiently,” said Stephan Zizala, division president of edge systems at Infineon Technologies. “The next wave of innovation will not be defined by how much data we collect, but by how effectively we can turn that data into action. Across industries, organizations are looking for ways to improve operations through faster insights, greater efficiency, and more autonomous decision-making. Edge AI enables that shift by processing data close to where it is generated, whether from sensors in industrial equipment, smart homes, or robots. This allows systems to react in real time, reduces dependence on constant cloud connectivity, and helps keep sensitive information under local control.”
How those systems are connected depends on the operating environment, the sensitivity of the data, and the balance each organization wants to strike between autonomy, control, and cloud-based scale.
On one end, semiconductor fabs may keep their analytics systems air-gapped, so no data gets in or out. On the other end, a soda bottling facility may run entirely in the cloud for efficiency. Often, it’s a combination of both. “You will have a local model doing more of the regular work, but it is not working constantly all the time,” said Balasubramanian. “This is similar to how humans sleep and think through the day and get the brain to realign all the memories and skills. At some point, you will phone in to the cloud and update the models. Or if they come up with some corner cases, you need to be able to update the learning of the main model. For example, Tesla updates the software of the car.”
Edge analytics security considerations
Protecting proprietary IP is important, along with privacy, because applications such as wearables handle personal data.
“In parallel to sensor data, data generated through human or agent interaction includes inputs from AI assistants, via local inference models, as well as corrections, feedback, or direct inputs from end users,” said Cadence’s Chen. “These workflows drive a strong need for privacy‑controlled edge environments, where sensitive information is retained in secure local storage and only ‘must‑have’ and conditioned data, which has been filtered, encrypted, and policy‑controlled, is transmitted to the cloud.”
Security must be considered at every layer, or organizations risk impacting human worker safety in addition to financial loss through downtime or fraud.
The analytics layer needs specific attention. “For example, with the software that processes data and detects anomalies, triggers, and prioritizes alerts, the risks are related to decision integrity,” said Dana Neustadter, senior director of product management at Synopsys. “Analytics systems risk missing the real problems, failing to detect abnormalities, such as in a medical setting where signs of patient health deterioration are missed. It could also be fraud or equipment failures. In any of these settings, too many alerts can be created, similar to false positives, where there are repeated incorrect patient alerts. Other risks include the corruption of the analytics model itself, including hidden backdoors that allow specific untrusted users to be trusted.”
Edge analytics fleet management platforms and alert systems also face compromise. “For example, by allowing malicious updates, model deployment, or manipulation of a whole fleet of devices,” said Neustadter. “These types of platforms have a large — maybe one of the largest — attack surfaces, and are becoming high-value targets because edge AI deployments rely on them for device onboarding, AI model deployments and management, alerts, analytics, and policy management. There are also software supply-chain attacks, such as compromising models or updates of infrastructure even before deployment.”
Edge AI devices also bring specific security risks. “The biggest shift in edge AI security is that cyber attackers are moving from trying to steal information to trying to manipulate decisions,” Neustadter observed. “Edge devices are evolving to autonomous decision-makers, where a successful attack can influence not just the data collection, but real-world actions.”
Verifiable trust is needed across the entire lifecycle, from device authenticity and software integrity to data provenance, model integrity, and secure management, Neustadter explained. “AI model compromise includes adversarial attacks, poisoning, extraction, and unauthorized modifications.”
A recent NIST publication identified adversarial machine learning as a major emerging security concern. “For example, attackers intentionally manipulate inputs to cause AI systems to make incorrect decisions while appearing normal to humans,” said Neustadter. [1] “Model theft is another example because AI models themselves are valuable assets as companies invest significantly to differentiate in the market and secure business.
AI reliability/safety must also be considered, especially for medical devices, industrial automation, robotics, and autonomous devices. “An incorrect AI recommendation can create safety or operational consequences even if there is no malicious intent,” she noted. “Unlike traditional software, AI systems can make incorrect decisions even if no attacks have occurred.”
Those security and reliability requirements ultimately flow back into silicon choices, because edge processors must support local intelligence while meeting tight constraints on power, latency, connectivity, and trust.
Edge AI processing chips
A programmable logic controller (PLC), which generally consists of a microprocessor (MPU) with a CPU, memory, and interface ICs, acts as a bridge between the sensors and AI. The AI could be processed by a low-power MCU, NPU (neural), or VPU (vision).
“There will be an MCU, but also the PLC running industrial edge,” said Balasubramanian. “A virtual PLC is already security-proven, so you could have that in the edge as part of your system to run and monitor everything based on what you’re getting from the PLM (product lifecycle management) thread and what you’re getting from real-time data.”
GPUs also have a role to play. “Traditionally, AI was always these huge, giant, data center-level cards going everywhere,” said Imagination’s Bubis. “But now we are implementing AI processing technology within our very smallest chips, because we see small chip edge AI customers who might have a tiny device in a television or a refrigerator for the home.”
While matrix multiplication tasks are important, edge AI GPUs are also needed for traditional graphics processing tasks. For example, a robot may have a display screen so a maintenance worker can see what’s going on. “We see the dual use case in edge AI,” said Bubis. “In automotive, that’s 100% the case, because you’ve got these ever-larger screens and displays demanding very complex graphics outputs whilst also demanding some AI workloads, either for ADAS or for the local LLMs that might be happening in the vehicle.”
In enterprise and client applications, various devices and widgets process data locally, with small language models and AI bots saving IT personnel time by fielding basic questions. “Extendable platforms can be connected to single-board computers to provide the ability to run heavy compute,” said Bubis.
Those processing choices also shape the surrounding data fabric, because edge AI systems must move information among sensors, accelerators, memory, and networks quickly enough to support real-time analytics.
Networking and memory for edge analytics
Compute, interfaces, and memory all play a key role in edge analytics.
“How to move data reliably and efficiently has become just as important as increasing compute capability in edge AI system design,” said Cadence’s Chen. “Long adopted in the mobile system, MIPI CSI-2 serves as a preferred vision ingress interface in embedded systems, along with other USB-based and proprietary links, efficiently feeding image data into the ISP pipeline and aligning well with edge device requirements. Beyond vision, many interface protocols foundational to modern cloud AI factory architectures, such as PCIe, Ethernet, LPDDR/DDR/GDDR, and UCIe, are increasingly deployed at the edge because of their proven topologies and mature ecosystems. Given the constraints typical of edge platforms, however, designs are strongly biased toward cost‑ and power‑efficient implementations.”
UCIe and PCIe are both utilized. “Although UCIe is commonly viewed as a premium interconnect for high‑end AI and chiplet-centric designs, heterogeneous execution at the edge is emerging and potentially relevant for future edge designs,” said Chen. “The modularity, flexibility, and reuse enabled by chiplet architectures are increasingly compelling for edge applications that demand tailored and heterogeneous I/O mixes. PCIe 3/4/5 plays a central role in attaching high‑throughput peripherals such as accelerators, NVMe storage, and NICs, while the long‑established Ethernet standards remain widely deployed and form the backbone of most edge networking environments, ranging from 1G to 10G for devices to 25G–100G for infrastructure.”
Memory can also be heterogeneous. “In memory subsystems, a practical mix of DDR5, GDDR6/7, and LPDDR5X/6 has been increasingly adopted in higher-performance edge systems, optimizing capacity, bandwidth, and energy efficiency across diverse edge use cases,” said Chen.
While HBM and DDR may be the right choice for high-performance systems, LPDDR is a common choice for edge and embedded AI, where energy efficiency and cost are important, according to Rambus. Applications include computer vision, robotics, industrial automation, medical devices, and battery-powered or thermally constrained systems. The memory controller must be optimized for low-power operation, work across challenging conditions, and integrate flexibly into diverse SoC architectures.
Also, an edge-optimized network architecture should deliver packet-level visibility, active monitoring, and application intelligence to ensure tools never miss a thing, according to Keysight.
 
Fig. 1: An edge-optimized network. Source: Keysight
Conclusion
Edge AI is a fast-growing space, particularly in the industrial sector, with new devices and use cases emerging all the time.
“The excitement I have is coming up with different designs and edge devices,” said Balasubramanian. “We are seeing a lot of momentum in putting intelligent devices at the edge — not just sensors, but real devices. That’s an entire system that can operate on its own, either air-gapped or connected to the internet, Wi-Fi, or the cloud. That’s the beauty of it. Essentially, you have everything connected to something, and it already has its own brain to operate.”
Edge AI systems need to take corrective action very quickly. “If it takes a lot of time to process and correct the mistake, then you might have a lot of defective parts already done in a car manufacturing factory, or in a GPU manufacturing fab, and everywhere else,” said Balasubramanian. “The goal is to have fewer humans involved in the factory, but to have more domain specialists monitoring it much more smartly, so that there is no downtime and the quality is always 100%. That’s the kind of metric that industrial teams look at.”
An end-to-end deployment flow is key. “As AI continues its journey into the physical world, sensors, intelligence, connectivity, and security must work together seamlessly,” said Infineon’s Zizala. “The real opportunity lies in creating systems that not only collect data but can understand their environment and act on it intelligently, reliably, and securely.”

articles.title: Injini to host 5th SA EdTech Week in Johannesburg, focus on teacher empowerment - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African ed-tech incubator and accelerator Injini will host the fifth edition of South African EdTech Week in partnership with the Mastercard Foundation, with the event moving to Gauteng for the first time.
Founded in 2017, Injini, which is a member of the UVU Africa Group, is a registered non-profit company that exists for the sole purpose of improving educational outcomes in Sub-Saharan Africa. Its programmes and research via the Injini Think Tank contribute towards its mission to increase the quality, accessibility, and relevance of education in the region. It announced its latest cohort earlier this year.
The two-day South African EdTech Week event takes place at Focus Rooms in Sandton, Johannesburg, on October 12-13, under the theme “Reclaiming the Classroom: EdTech as a Tool for Teacher Empowerment”.
Organisers say this year’s edition moves past familiar debates about devices and connectivity. Instead, it focuses on a persistent gap – digital tools are increasingly present in African schools but rarely part of daily teaching. When technology arrives as an administrative add-on or a top-down mandate, it can add to the workload of teachers who are already stretched.
“It’s not because teachers don’t want to learn,” said Nonku Nyathi, partnerships and ecosystem head at Injini. “It’s because few people have figured out how to demonstrate that these tools actually make teaching easier or save time.”
A highlight of the first day will be a showcase of the 10 startups in the fourth cohort of the Mastercard Foundation EdTech Fellowship, run by Injini. The ventures focus on accessibility and inclusion. Their solutions range from AI-powered tools that cut teacher marking time by up to 80 per cent to offline coding games and assistive platforms for learners with special educational needs.
“Technology can only transform learning when it is designed with educators, strengthens their agency, and responds to the realities of the classroom,” said Wariko Waita, director of the Centre for Innovative Teaching and Learning at the Mastercard Foundation.

articles.title: Test de Gears of War: E-Day, un pur plaisir en coopération
articles.text:
Pour moi, Gears of War rime avec franche camaraderie. J’ai terminé tous les épisodes en coopération, depuis le tout premier paru sur Xbox 360, une véritable claque à l’époque. Je ne conçois pas cette saga de jeux de tir autrement et je ne pense pas m’y épanouir en jouant seul. Avant de réaliser le test de Gears of War: E-Day, disponible le 6 octobre sur Xbox Series et PC, j’ai donc appelé mon meilleur partenaire. Il a dit oui sans aucune hésitation.
À bien des égards, Gears of War: E-Day est un jeu important pour Xbox, qui vit une année 2026 mouvementée alors que nous célébrons son 25e anniversaire. La marque vit un « reset » total, qui passe par 3 200 suppressions de postes annoncées en juillet (20 % des effectifs de Xbox) et par des revirements stratégiques forts. Gears of War: E-Day en est un. La précédente direction avait acté la fin des exclusivités Xbox, signifiant que ce nouvel opus aurait pu sortir sur PS5 — à l’instar de Gears of War: Reloaded. Asha Sharma, la nouvelle patronne, a rétropédalé. Gears of War: E-Day apparaît donc comme une lueur d’espoir pour Xbox. Un comble pour un jeu à l’univers si sombre.
Points forts
- Visuellement spectulaire
- Un gameplay aux petits oignons
- Le plaisir de la coopération
Points faibles
- Ces zones ouvertes infernales
- Un air de déjà joué tout de même
- Quelques bugs
Gears of War: E-Day est bien la vitrine de la Xbox Series X
Quid du multi ?
Ce test ne concerne que la campagne.
Les Gears of War ont toujours été des vitrines visuelles mettant en valeur les capacités des consoles Xbox. Gears of War: E-Day ne déroge pas à la règle. C’est du très, très grand spectacle, matérialisé par une immersion totale dans une ville assiégée et qui évolue de plus en plus dans le chaos au fur et à mesure des chapitres. Voir Kalona se transformer en un amoncellement de gravats et de cadavres est paradoxalement galvanisant. Les développeurs ont mis le paquet sur les décors, qui s’appuient sur des panoramas funestes saisissants.Gears of War: E-Day incarne à merveille une situation d’urgence, dans ce qu’elle a de pire.
Pour donner vie à la guerre, le studio The Coalition a réalisé un travail inouï sur les détails. Des reflets dans les flaques aux animations quand les soldats rechargent, en passant par les éclairages parfois aveuglants, chaque plan de Gears of War: E-Day est soigné. Alors qu’il y a des affrontements à mener, on a souvent envie de s’arrêter pour admirer les environnements et immortaliser ce que l’on voit. Une preuve que les développeurs étalent leur maîtrise de l’Unreal Engine 5. On soulignera quand même quelques bugs fâcheux (exemple : des pierres en lévitation), qui tranchent avec l’excellence affichée par ailleurs. Le moteur physique, lui, manque d’ambition et on aimerait des décors plus destructibles pour dynamiser l’action.
The Coalition avait pourtant fait de la destruction un argument. Il promettait des gouffres capables d’engloutir des véhicules et des immeubles entiers, et une « micro-destruction » qui grignote les couvertures sous les tirs. Manette en main, on aurait aimé en voir davantage et on reste sur notre faim.
Malgré ces limites, l’écrin graphique se met au service d’un véritable retour aux sources. Gears of War: E-Day est une préquelle, qui se déroule quatorze ans avant le premier épisode, lors de l’Émergence, le jour où les Locustes ont surgi des profondeurs de la planète Sera. On retrouve alors l’irrésistible duo formé par Dom Santiago et Marcus Fenix, qui rentrent à peine de la guerre et pleurent toujours la mort de Carlos, le frère de Dom. Dom pensait à la retraite, quand Marcus ne savait pas quoi faire de sa vie au moment où les Locustes sont apparus.
Le récit de Gears of War: E-Day, bourré de références cinématographiques (Predator, La Chute du faucon noir…) et lorgnant du côté de l’horreur pure, va un peu plus loin dans l’intime que ses prédécesseurs. Il y a même des relents politiques, quand on entend un PNJ nous traiter de fascistes. Il retranscrit en tout cas très bien le combat contre une force inconnue, avec des situations qui empirent au fil des minutes.
Ce n’est pas toujours mon Gears
Coopération
La campagne se joue à deux en écran partagé sur console, ou jusqu’à quatre en ligne.
En termes de gameplay, Gears of War: E-Day ne réinvente pas une formule qui marche. Il prend toujours la forme d’un jeu de tir à couvert (cover-shooter) d’une violence graphique extrême. Il ne cherche même pas à imaginer des séquences inédites, au point de donner l’impression d’y avoir déjà joué. Pour sa défense, le gameplay de la saga ô combien jouissif est toujours aussi excellent, avec de bonnes sensations de tir et un sentiment de puissance assez addictif quand on étrille les Locustes dans un torrent d’hémoglobine. Mention spéciale au découpage à la tronçonneuse (dont on découvre l’histoire d’origine).
Gears of War: E-Day apporte quand même un peu de souplesse aux déplacements et aux mouvements. Le rechargement éclair, régi par un mini-jeu à accomplir pour éviter que l’arme ne s’enraille, est plus technique (et la jauge a été déplacée dans l’interface). La possibilité de se mettre en couverture en étant allongé ajoute des options lors des escarmouches. Enfin, le corps-à-corps gagne lui aussi en fluidité. Gears of War: E-Day n’est pas une révolution et préfère s’en remettre à quelques évolutions par petites touches. On y joue comme on enfilerait des chaussons douillets, avec ce confort attendu.
On s’amuse beaucoup dans Gears of War: E-Day, surtout en coopération. Mais The Coalition a quand même commis une sacrée erreur de jugement au moment d’introduire une zone un peu trop ouverte au début de l’acte 2. Toute l’essence des Gears of War, notamment en matière de rythme et d’exaltation, se retrouve diluée dans une structure pénible. On comprend la volonté de bousculer les habitudes, mais c’est ici une fausse bonne idée.
On se retrouve alors à se balader dans des environnements remplis de choses à ramasser, au gré d’objectifs secondaires rébarbatifs qui s’apparentent à des tutoriels pour le mode multijoueur et mâtiné d’un semblant de système de personnalisation de l’arsenal. Cette portion étendue est beaucoup trop longue pour son propre bien, et on en vient vite à espérer un retour aux couloirs mieux maîtrisés. « Not my Gears », diront les fans. Heureusement que les choses reviennent à la normale dès l’acte 3, plongé dans une forêt touffue et inquiétante. « Voilà, ça c’est mon Gears », se réjouiront les fans. Ces phrases, on n’a cessé de les répéter avec mon partenaire, durant la dizaine d’heures nécessaires pour boucler l’aventure. Autant dire qu’on a vécu de véritables montagnes russes, frustrés devant certains choix, éblouis par d’autres.
Le verdict
Gears of War: E-Day
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Visuellement spectulaire
- Un gameplay aux petits oignons
- Le plaisir de la coopération
On a moins aimé
- Ces zones ouvertes infernales
- Un air de déjà joué tout de même
- Quelques bugs

articles.title: Peut-on vraiment se protéger des arnaques par e-mail ? Votre vigilance ne suffit plus
articles.text:
Faux colis en attente, paiement refusé, cadeau dont il faut payer les frais d’envoi : les tentatives d’escroquerie par e-mail n’ont jamais été aussi nombreuses… Et aussi crédibles ! S’il est impossible d’éliminer totalement le risque de se faire piéger, la combinaison de bonnes pratiques et d’outils adaptés peut tout de même le réduire de manière importante.
Si, durant de longues années, les visuels créés à la va-vite et les fautes d’orthographe présentes dans les e-mails permettaient de détecter les arnaques assez facilement, aujourd’hui, les choses ont changé. En effet,
entre les fuites massives de données personnelles et les intelligences artificielles génératives, les escrocs du Net ont accès à un véritable arsenal
afin de créer des arnaques ciblées et plus crédibles que jamais.
Cela peut passer par l’annonce d’un gain à un concours, la nécessité de payer le retrait ou l’envoi d’un colis, ou encore la nécessité de débloquer votre compte bancaire. Il s’agit, à chaque fois, de phishing, une technique aussi appelée hameçonnage : elle consiste à créer un sentiment d’urgence et à semer le doute chez la victime. Cette dernière est poussée à cliquer sur un lien, à communiquer ses identifiants ou ses coordonnées bancaires, voire, pour les tentatives les plus audacieuses, à effectuer un paiement en ligne. Et lorsque le piège se referme, il est trop tard.
Les bons réflexes à avoir face aux arnaques par e-mail
Il n’existe pas de solution capable d’intercepter toutes les arnaques par e-mail. Il est fort probable que la plupart d’entre elles arrivent directement dans les spams de votre messagerie, mais, paradoxalement, cela peut contribuer à rendre crédibles celles qui passent à travers les mailles du filet.
Face à un e-mail suspect, votre vigilance est votre première ligne de défense. Si la demande vous interpelle, par exemple, si elle concerne un colis que vous ne vous rappelez pas avoir commandé ou bien si vous ne reconnaissez pas l’adresse de votre conseiller bancaire, évitez de cliquer sur le premier lien venu. En cas de doute, vous pouvez passer par l’application officielle du service concerné, voire téléphoner directement à l’établissement.
Ces précautions permettent d’éviter de nombreux pièges, mais, face à une arnaque très bien ficelée, il reste possible de se faire berner. C’est pourquoi il peut être utile de compléter votre surveillance avec une solution de cybersécurité.
Surfshark One complète votre vigilance pour moins de 3 euros par mois
Vous connaissez peut-être Surfshark pour son VPN, mais ce que vous ne savez peut-être pas, c’est que le service met aussi à disposition une suite complète de cybersécurité au sein de son offre Surfshark One.
Cette formule vient justement d’accueillir de nouveaux outils destinés à lutter contre les arnaques en ligne. Parmi eux, on trouve un système basé sur l’IA qui analyse les e-mails reçus dans Gmail afin de détecter les tentatives d’hameçonnage, via l’extension Surfshark. Et comme le phishing ne se limite pas aux e-mails, la suite peut également repérer les SMS liés à des tentatives d’arnaque et les sites Web malveillants. Enfin, une protection contre les appels frauduleux est prévue dans les prochains mois.
Surfshark One comprend également le VPN du service utilisable sur un nombre illimité d’appareils, un antivirus, un générateur d’identités alternatives ainsi qu’un système de détection et d’alerte en cas de fuites de données personnelles.
En ce moment, vous pouvez souscrire à l’offre 24 mois de Surfshark One pour 2,79 euros par mois, avec trois mois d’abonnement supplémentaires offerts. Cette formule s’accompagne également d’une garantie satisfait ou remboursé de 30 jours : cela peut vous permettre de tester sereinement les multiples outils présents au sein de cette solution de cybersécurité, avant de vous engager pour deux ans.

articles.title: Hackers stole Pentagon personnel records of over 3 million people
articles.text:
The Pentagon's Defense Manpower Data Center (DMDC) is notifying millions of military service members that hackers stole their data after breaching the Pentagon's human resources management system in October 2025.
In data breach notification letters shared online by affected individuals, the DMDC told affected military personnel that "a small number of unauthorized users" had access to their sensitive data, including personally identifiable information (PII), between October 2025 and July 2026 after exploiting a vulnerability in its file-sharing systems.
The stolen data varies by person and includes Social Security numbers (SSNs), names, dates of birth, contact information, sex, race, and military personnel information.
Pentagon officials told Federal News Network that the data breach affects more than 3 million people, including nearly 2.8 million living individuals and 294,000 "deceased individuals."
"Upon discovery of the security vulnerability, DMDC immediately initiated privacy and cybersecurity incident response actions in accordance with Office of Management and Budget and Department guidelines and policies," the DMDC told affected individuals. "We are taking appropriate actions to assess and enhance the cybersecurity posture of the DMDC system."
The Pentagon is also offering 12 months of free credit monitoring services through the IDX data breach and recovery service provider and says affected individuals must enroll by August 19, 2027.
A Pentagon spokesperson was not immediately available to comment when BleepingComputer reached out for more information about the breach.
Founded in 1974, the DMDC is an operational support center that stores more than 60 million military, civilian, contractor, family member, retiree, and veteran records used to authorize benefits and entitlements, as well as training, financial, and other data for the U.S. Department of Defense (DoD). It also operates DoD personnel programs and conducts research and analysis as directed by the Office of the Secretary of Defense (OUSD).
"The services and access to data we provide support so many vital government entities, including the legislative branch, human services, national defense, labor, healthcare, finance, veterans affairs, research, and more," its DMDC says.
This incident follows another massive data breach claimed by the ShinyHunters extortion gang, who breached the FBI's FBIjobs.gov site using an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day.
ShinyHunters claimed to have stolen several terabytes of data (including names, Social Security numbers, home addresses, and assignments) belonging to "almost ALL FBI Agents," including employee records belonging to members of the FBI Remote Operations Unit, a team involved in hacking operations.
ShinyHunters told BleepingComputer that the FBI breach was not financially motivated and that the group doesn't intend to publish the stolen data or extort the bureau.
