articles.title: OpenAI dispara contra los creadores de Kimi por supuestamente copiar su IA
articles.text:
Moonshot, la empresa detrás de Kimi, una de las IA chinas más capaces y populares, ha quedado envuelta en una polémica por el desarrollo de su tecnología. OpenAI ha publicado un reporte sobre una campaña de destilación de sus modelos de lenguaje cuya autoría correspondería en parte a individuos vinculados con la firma del gigante asiático.
Según explica OpenAI, la destilación de modelos se inició el 1 de julio y alcanzó su pico entre los días 24 y 25 de ese mes. Pocos días más tarde, la compañía que lidera Sam Altman logró interrumpir el accionar de forma definitiva.
El reporte explica que los intentos de destilar los modelos que impulsan ChatGPT y otros productos de la compañía buscaban extraer razonamiento protegido. OpenAI menciona que para ello se utilizaron métodos bastante novedosos y que la propia firma considera que se volverán todavía más sofisticados con el correr del tiempo.
Tanto el cifrado como las bases de datos y otras infraestructuras de OpenAI no se vieron afectadas por el incidente, se menciona. Y si bien la empresa californiana no ha señalado al autor absoluto de esta campaña, sí ha apuntado contra individuos presuntamente relacionados con Moonshot, la startup china que desarrolla Kimi.
"No está claro si todos los operadores que observamos durante el periodo pertinente provenían de un mismo actor. Sin embargo, atribuimos un núcleo principal de la actividad a personas vinculadas a Moonshot AI, la empresa desarrolladora de Kimi", remarcan los estadounidenses.
Kimi, bajo la lupa por acusaciones de destilación de modelos de OpenAI
No es la primera vez que Moonshot recibe acusaciones de destilación de modelos occidentales. En julio pasado, la Oficina de Política de Ciencia y Tecnología de Estados Unidos acusó a la firma china de copiar sin autorización los datos de entrenamiento de Claude Fable, para usarlos en Kimi K3.
"La destilación legítima de IA, utilizada para crear modelos más pequeños y eficientes, desempeña un papel fundamental en este ecosistema de innovación abierta. Sin embargo, la destilación industrial encubierta a gran escala, cuyo objetivo es robar tecnología patentada estadounidense y socavar la investigación en Estados Unidos, es inaceptable", publicó por entonces el jefe del citado organismo.
Por lo pronto, Kimi no se ha pronunciado respecto de las acusaciones vertidas por OpenAI sobre la destilación de sus modelos. Esta práctica lleva tiempo generando polémica, pues permite el desarrollo de modelos de inteligencia artificial capaces, pero con una fracción del coste y del tiempo que se requiere al hacerlo desde cero.
Tanto empresas de inteligencia artificial estadounidenses como el gobierno de Donald Trump han catalogado la práctica como "robo". No obstante, NVIDIA parece ahora tener una mirada diferente. Días atrás, Jensen Huang, CEO de la compañía, lo definió como un tipo "competencia".

articles.title: Factory CEO just accused his VC board adviser of spying for Cognition | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Matan Grinberg, co-founder and CEO of the AI coding startup Factory, said in a post on X on Wednesday that he fired VC Chris Degnan from his role as a board adviser. Grinberg alleges that Degnan shared confidential information with Factory’s biggest competitor, Cognition.
Two hours after Grinberg’s post, Degnan announced on both X and LinkedIn that he had joined Cognition as its chief revenue officer. He also subsequently refuted Grinberg’s allegations, saying in a separate X post that he wasn’t fired but resigned when he told Grinberg he was taking the job.
Degnan was Snowflake’s first sales hire and later spent 11 years as the data company’s chief revenue officer. For the past five months, he has been a partner with RPT Partners, a Newport Beach, California, investor in Factory. Degnan is also a go-to-market adviser to startups at the much bigger venture firm Iconiq, a role that dates back to October of last year.
Three-year-old, San Francisco-based Factory is an agentic coding startup whose AI agents can carry out programming tasks largely on their own. The company raised $200 million at a $5 billion valuation this month from Khosla Ventures, Blackstone, Sequoia Capital, Insight Partners, and others. Its customers include Nvidia, Blackstone, Royal Bank of Canada, Palo Alto Networks, Adobe, and T-Mobile.
Grinberg said he sees Cognition, the maker of the Devin coding agent, as his biggest competitor. Cognition raised another $2 billion at a $48 billion valuation earlier this month, and counts Mercedes-Benz, NASA, Goldman Sachs, and Citi as customers.
Grinberg said on X that Degnan had earlier acknowledged having a “casual” conversation with a Cognition executive but had assured Grinberg that he had no interest in working for the competitor. According to Grinberg, Degnan said he had “made too much money” and was “too lazy to go work for Cognition,” which Grinberg said he “trusted and believed.”
On Monday, however, Degnan apparently disclosed that he had actually been in ongoing talks with Cognition.
This caused Grinberg to grow concerned about how much confidential information Degnan had about Factory, and how much he had shared and might share in the future with his new employer. He says he fired Degnan as a board adviser on Tuesday, writing:
For weeks, while he sat in our board meetings and advised our leadership team, he was also confiding with executives of our largest competitor. Chris was subject to confidentiality obligations in connection with his work with Factory. We do not know the extent of the information he shared, but it puts his timely questions about our product roadmap and what the parity gap involves into a new light.
But Degnan disputes that account as well. He says the last Factory board meeting he attended was weeks before he had “ever spoken” to Cognition and that he hasn’t shared confidential information. Degnan also says that when he told Grinberg that he was resigning to take the role at Cognition, Grinberg offered him a full-time job at Factory, which he declined.
Degnan’s post announcing his new job at Cognition doesn’t mention Factory. Very notably, it does say that RPT Partners and the firm’s managing partner, Chad Peets, will now be working with Cognition. “I am thrilled that Chad and the RPT team will be working closely with me in our pursuit of building a generational company,” Degnan wrote.
In the old, pre-AI world, a VC firm was especially cautious not to engage in conflict-of-interest business. In today’s world, many a VC has invested in direct AI competitors, such OpenAI and Anthropic.
In fact, Khosla Ventures is an investor in both Cognition (since at least early 2025) and Factory.
That didn’t stop the venture firm’s founder, Vinod Khosla, from jumping into the drama, seemingly in defense of his bigger portfolio company Cognition. Nor did it stop Khosla Ventures partner Keith Rabois from weighing in as well — in defense of Factory.
In a post on X, Khosla accused Grinberg of lying about firing Degnan. He called Factory a “struggling second tier competitor” and said Grinberg showed “no decency or sense of proper behavior,” which “shows your desperation.”
Grinberg replied that he has email receipts to verify his version of events but did not share them.
Meanwhile, Rabois opined on X, “It is unethical per se to even interview at a competitor while attending Board meetings and Board dinners.” He added that “to even sit for an interview while having access to board level information and without resigning is absolutely insane.”
Tracking the back-and-forth, Cognition co-founder and CEO Scott Wu also weighed in on the controversy on X. He politely expressed respect for the smaller competitor while insisting that his company has “no interest in Factory’s info.” Wu also contends that Degnan resigned on Monday but didn’t refute that Degnan was in talks with Cognition before that happened.
Either way, there could be consequences for perceived board-level conflicts of interest. VC giant Andreessen Horowitz is reportedly the subject of a Justice Department probe into its partners serving on competitors’ boards.
Grinberg argued that startup founders must be able to rely on their board members. “Chris’s conduct is unacceptable to me. Trust in Board Membership is one of the sacred bonds in the Silicon Valley, one that helps the startup ecosystem thrive. With it comes an enormous responsibility. That trust was violated.”
Degnan, Peets, Factory, and Khosla Ventures did not immediately respond to requests for further comment.
Note: This story was updated to include responses from Degnan, Khosla, Rabois, and Wu.

articles.title: The Chefman Coffee Station Pro replaces five countertop appliances in theory, but inconsistent performance keeps it from being a dream setup
articles.text:
TechRadar Verdict
The Chefman Coffee Station Pro makes coffee so many different ways, but some of them come out better than others. Use your own ground beans and make a carafe of drip coffee or an espresso drink. You can even use K-Cup pods and Nespresso capsules, but results with the latter were disappointing.
Reasons to buy
- +Extremely flexible with many coffee options
- +Use ground coffee, K-cups, or Nespresso capsules
- +Not overly large for how much it does
- +Includes milk frother
- +Can adjust brew strength and volume
- +Has a delay brew feature
- +Has a keep-warm feature
- +Fairly easy to use
- +Separate hot water spout
Reasons to avoid
- -Doesn't include a bean grinder
- -Some of the coffee brewing methods just aren't good
Why you can trust TechRadar
Chefman Coffee Station Pro: two-minute review
The Chefman Coffee Station Pro is a great idea. People like their coffee brewed in different ways, and it's easy to end up with two or even three coffee machines on the counter to accommodate households with multiple coffee drinkers. For example, my husband usually drinks drip coffee, but occasionally likes an espresso. I rotate between drip, espresso, and iced coffee, depending on my mood and the weather. I also like my Nespresso machine, since the capsules are available in some interesting flavors I occasionally enjoy. I also drink a lot of tea, so an instant hot feature is welcome. We don't often drink lattes or cappuccinos, but when our kids or guest come to visit, they often do. We could easily end up with three different coffee machines (plus a frother and a tea kettle) in our coffee nook, but the Chefman Coffee Station Pro can do all that and more.
Sounds like a dream, but unfortunately it doesn't do everything well, or even acceptably. For example, it doesn't brew Nespresso capsules fully or correctly, resulting in a weak and tiny brew. If you don't need every single feature, this machine might be a perfect fit for you because it does a lot of things well. I tested everything and found that it did some things far better than others.
Chefman Coffee Station Pro: price and availability
- Available on Chefman's website and other retailers
- Retails for $399.99 (about £300 / AU$570)
- Just one colorway, black and silver
You can buy the Chefman Coffee Station Pro on Chefman's website as well as brick-and-mortar and online retailers like Best Buy and Target. The retail price is $399.99, which is about £300 / AU$570, though it's not currently sold in the US and Australia.
Chefman Coffee Station Pro: specs
| Name | Chefman Coffee Station Pro | 
| Type | Semi-automatic | 
| Dimensions | 13 x 11.7 x 13.9 inches / 33.02 x 29.72 x 35.31 cm | 
| Pressure (for espresso brewing) | 20 bars | 
| Brew styles | Espresso, single serve, drip, cold press, cold brew | 
| Milk frother | Yes | 
| Connected device | No | 
Chefman Coffee Station Pro: design
- Smaller than you might expect
- Has storage for accessories
- Ten in one machine
The Chefman Coffee Station Pro is designed efficiently so it has a lot of features in its reasonably-sized footprint. The machine provides ten different brewing methods: espresso (with grounds or Nespresso capsules), cold press espresso, latte, cappuccino, milk frother, K-cup pods, carafe of drip coffee, drip over ice, cold brew, and instant hot water. You control everything with a touch-screen interface.
It comes with everything you need to make all of the beverages listed above. The big 100-ounce water tank fits onto the back of the machine. On the coffee side, you get a coffee filter holder and a reusable coffee filter basket. If you prefer, you can use paper filters instead. There is also a K-Cup adapter for brewing K-Cups. The glass carafe holds anywhere from four to twelve cups of coffee and it rests on a warming plate (which has a "hot" indicator light.) When you're brewing a single serve K-Cup rather than using the carafe, there is a fold-down cup platform with a removable rubber trivet for resting a mug.
On the espresso side, you get a portafilter with three different filters you can put inside. There's small filter for brewing single espresso, a larger one for double espresso, and an adapter for Nespresso capsules. You get a two-sided espresso tool, one side is a measuring scoop and the other side is a tamper. The included 16-ounce milk reservoir can be removed when not in use.
The Chefman Coffee Station Pro stores its own accessories cleverly. It has a hook on the side to store the portafilter and a compartment on top to store other accessories.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
When you first set up the Chefman Coffee Station Pro, you'll want to set the clock for the correct time. There is a Delay Brew feature so you can set the machine up when you go to bed and you'll have a hot carafe of drip coffee waiting for you in the morning. The Keep Warm feature will keep your carafe hot for up to two hours.
There is a hot water spout, which runs separately from the coffee so you don't have to worry about stale coffee taste mixing with your hot water. This is perfect for making hot chocolate, tea, and other hot beverages with ease. I suppose you could even use for making instant ramen or really anything you might need hot water for. It's worth noting that it's hot but not boiling.
As with any coffee machine, it does need to be cleaned regularly. Since this one has so many features, there's more cleaning that needs to be done. Every time you use it, you'll want to wash any accessories you use, run a clean cycle on the milk frother wand, and wipe down the exterior as needed. Of course you'll want to remove the milk reservoir and refrigerate any unused milk right after use.
On a weekly basis, empty and wash out the water tank, empty and wash the milk reservoir, run a clean cycle on the espresso side, and flush the frother system if you're using it daily. Every month or two, you'll want to do a deep clean of the frother's internal parts.
Roughly every 100 cycles (or 50 for hot water), you'll need to descale the coffee, espresso, and hot water systems. The owner's manual included detailed instruction on how to do all of that, plus you can find videos on Chefman's YouTube channel for guided instruction.
- Design score: 4/5
Chefman Coffee Station Pro: performance
- Fairly easy to use
- Most of the features work well
- Some features don't result in good coffee
In my testing, most of the drinks I made came out really well. Some came out ok, and some came out actually undrinkable.
Espresso
The espresso came out fine and it had a nice crema. It was pretty easy to do, just measure your grounds with the provided scoop, pour your grounds in the portafilter with the appropriate filter inside. Use one scoop in the smaller filter for a single espresso or two scoops in the larger filter for a double espresso. Tamp them down firmly with the included tamper, and then twist the portafilter into place. Select your drink from the touch-screen menu and you'll have espresso in just a minute or so. I used a carefully measured flat scoop, and found the espresso to be rather weak, but your tastes may vary.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Espresso with Nespresso capsule
Using the Nespresso capsule basket in the portafilter, you can brew any Nespresso or Nespresso-compatible capsule. Note that this is only for the small original line capsules, not the larger Vertuo line capsules.
This was a big fail, in my opinion. The capsule was only pierced partway, there was water left in the portafilter, and the resulting brew was sour and weak and had very little crema. It was not worth drinking.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
In the photo gallery below, I compare the results of brewing the same kind of Nespresso capsule in both the Chefman Coffee Station Pro and my actual Nespresso machine. In both machines, I brewed it as a small or single espresso. The Nespresso machine results are on the left and the Chefman on the right in both photos.
Latte and cappuccino
Technically, a latte and a cappuccino are pretty different. Though they are both espresso drinks with frothed milk added, the proportions are different. A cappuccino is one third espresso, one third steamed milk, and one third milk foam.
A latte is one-third espresso and two thirds steamed milk with a light layer of milk foam on top.
You can probably tell from my photos above, they don't look all that different. They didn't taste all that different, either, though they were both delicious.
I also tried just frothing some milk and then brewing an espresso separately and putting them together. Again, it just made a lovely foamy milky beverage.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Cold-pressed espresso
This was just a fail, in my opinion. It was so weak that I couldn't even drink it. Again, that's just my taste, yours may be different.
Note that pretty much every time you do a cold-pressed espresso brew, the machine will prompt you to run a cooling cycle on the carafe side first in order to prime the machine for cold press. It's not a big deal, but you'll have to factor in the extra time and place a container under it to catch the flushed water.
K-Cup
Using the included K-Cup adapater on the carafe side of the machine, you can make any K-Cup you like. I actually thought the Chefman Coffee Station Pro did a great job with this one. I'm not generally a fan of K-Cups but this machine brewed it as well as any Keurig machine I've tried. Note that unlike a Keurig machine, you are using a separate adapter part that you'll probably want to wash each time you use it before putting it away. So it is an extra step.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
There is also an option to brew the K-Cup pod as cold brew. But I can't recommend it, unless you like a super weak iced coffee. I used the same kind of pod, but look at the difference.
Drip coffee in carafe
The drip coffee came out great. It was easy to do, just like any traditional drip coffee machine. I used the metal and plastic reusable filter, but you could use a paper filter if you prefer. You have the option to set up a delayed brew, so you can get everything ready the night before and have a hot, fresh carafe of coffee when you wake up. The metal plate under the carafe can be set to keep your carafe warm for up to two hours, and an indicator light will let you know that it's hot.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Cold Brew
The Cold Brew feature brews your coffee slower, cooler, and with less water in order to extract the most flavor and give you less ice melt. This came out very well. It does take longer to brew, and it does usually require running a cool cycle first, but the results are tasty.
View Original
View Original
View Original
View Original
Over Ice (in carafe)
The Over Ice funtion is a little different from the Cold Brew. It's brewed into the carafe just like regular hot coffee but a bit stronger to compensate for ice melt. This worked fine, and it wasn't watered down too much. However, it was less smooth than the Cold Brew method and more bitter to my taste.
Hot Water
Hot water comes from a separate spout, not through the coffee system. It works fine and just tastes like pure water with no hint of coffee taste.
I selected maximum temperature setting, but water measured just 163°F/73°C. So, it's certainly hot enough to make hot cocoa, certain delicate teas, and perhaps your instant ramen. But it's not that all that close to boiling water, which would be 212°F/100°C.
- Performance score: 3/5
Should you buy the Chefman Coffee Station Pro?
| Chefman Coffee Station Pro score card |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Attribute | Notes | Score | 
|---|---|---|
| Value | The price is similar to other multi-functional semi-automatic machines | 4/5 | 
| Design | The clever design allows for many functions in a not-too-huge footprint | 4/5 | 
| Performance | This was very much a mixed bag; some types of brew came out great and some definitely not. | 3/5 | 
Buy it if
You have a multi-coffee-drinker household
The Chefman Coffee Station Pro does it all: espresso, latte, cappuccino, drip coffee, cold brew, iced coffee, K-cup, Nespresso capsule, and even hot water on demand.
You don't have space for many machines
While this isn't a small machine, it's certainly a lot smaller than separate machines for all of the different functions.
You want lots of options for guests
Even if your household doesn't need all of the features, it's nice to have just about any coffee option available for guests.
Don't buy it if
It's out of your price range
You can get a simple espresso machine plus a drip coffee machine and a basic frother for less than this all-in-one.
You want all of the features to be great
Though there are a lot of ways to brew coffee beverages with this machine, not all of them produce a great result.
You have extremely limited counter space
Considering how many features it has, the footprint isn't that huge. But it's still quite a bit bigger than most coffee machines.
Chefman Coffee Station Pro: also consider
Ninja AutoBarista Pro Fully Automatic Espresso Machine
This machine lacks the drip coffee carafe function and doesn't accept pods, but it has most of the other functions. Plus it has a built-in coffee grinder and comes with two different hoppers you can easily swap out.
Read my Ninja AutoBarista Pro Fully Automatic Espresso Machine review
Terra Kaffe TK-02
No pods here but you can make excellent drip coffee and espresso with just a tap. Use the built-in grinder or the ground coffee chute. The attached milk frother expands this machine's repertoire to six figures. Yes, you read that right. The Terra Kaffe TK-02 connects to an app (and Alexa!) so you can start your brew before you get out of bed.
Check out my Terra Kaffe TK-02 review.
How I tested the Chefman Coffee Station Pro
I brewed and drank every kind of coffee beverage the Chefman Coffee Station Pro makes. I brewed a Nespresso capsule and a K-cup. I brewed espresso from grounds, both hot and cold-pressed. I frothed milk (barista-style pistachio milk) and added a shot of espresso. I made latte and cappuccino. I brewed a carafe of drip coffee. I made cold brew and coffee over ice. I used the hot water feature, tasted it, and measured the temperature.
First reviewed September 2026

Karen is a world traveler, writer, teacher, family woman, and occasionally a movie extra. She has been writing about Apple, consumer tech, and lifestyle products since 2010 for various publications including TechRadar, CNET, Tom’s Guide, iMore, Macworld, AppAdvice, and WatchAware.

articles.title: The price of AI is crashing faster than the rate of Moore's Law, report suggests — intelligence costs are in freefall, outpacing comparative technologies like compute, DNA sequencing, and lithium batteries
articles.text:
The price of AI is crashing faster than the rate of Moore's Law, report suggests — intelligence costs are in freefall, outpacing comparative technologies like compute, DNA sequencing, and lithium batteries
Vendor loyalty and subscription schemes have limited appeal when prices can fall so fast.
A new report from AI research firm Epoch AI suggests the price of artificial intelligence has fallen by thousands of times in recent years — faster than any other transformational technology in the past century. The report suggests that the cost of artificial intelligence is just under 50% cheaper every quarter, and 13 times cheaper per year.
That's faster than lithium batteries, faster than DNA sequencing, and even faster than compute, which has been benefiting from the rapid advancements from Moore's Law for much of the past century
Although these falling costs are likely aiding adoption, it raises difficult questions about the necessity of remaining tied to frontier AI development, and could make it harder for third-party AI services to build customer loyalty and consistent revenue.
If you know that at any given time it's only a few weeks or months before the service you're interested in is going to be more capable and cheaper, what's the incentive to adopt it right now? If a competing service offers something better and cheaper, why stay with your current provider?
That poses a difficult conundrum for labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, which are racing towards ever greater AI capabilities. As the report suggests, finding large profits even with advanced models that outstrip the competition is difficult to imagine when it may only be a fleeting advantage.
Falling faster than DNA sequencing and 20th Century compute
Epoch's report paints a stark picture of the relative cost of what it terms "artificial thought." It shows the cost of AI falling by hundreds of thousands of times within just five years. Comparatively, it shows the price of Lithium Batteries between 1991 and 2024 as falling just 100 times over that near-25 year period. Compute fell the most over its lifetime, dropping 100s of billions of times over 60 years from 1940.
This is particularly relevant considering Moore's Law has remained a relevant constant throughout much of the past 60 years. With compute performance and efficiency improving by notable margins every year, the compound effect is modern computers that are both dramatically faster than their predecessors and vastly cheaper to run when measured against their compute capabilities.
AI performance and costs for that performance are falling even faster.
The metric that showcases the most similar fall in cost on the chart is DNA sequencing — an oft-cited example of the falling cost of technology. Its relative cost has fallen by an even greater extent than AI, but that took just over 20 years.
Epoch AI shows artificial intelligence doing the same in just half a decade. That works out to just under 50% cheaper every quarter, and 13 times cheaper per year. The fall is accelerating at a pace that's four times faster than DNA sequencing, and 18 times faster than lithium batteries.
There are several caveats to these results. Compute only covers the period up until 2001, with no numbers on the relative cost of it after that, and electricity is only tracked until 1973, which means it completely misses the explosion of solar energy in recent years. AI cost falling was also only tracked from 2023 onwards, too, with data prior to that date extrapolated from the existing shorter trend and outside research.
Epoch AI also didn't base these results on a particular model, but on models achieving an 81.25% or better result on the Graduate-Level Google-Proof Q&A (GPQA) Diamond benchmark, and tracked the cost of having the model answer one of the multiple-choice questions on the test.
That does measure AI capabilities across a range of knowledge disciplines, but it doesn't necessarily cover the entire range of AI capabilities. It can show how much easier these kinds of tasks are for newer models, though, because they're not just scoring higher on the test more readily; they're doing it for far less, too.
How much cheaper?
Epoch AI cites OpenAI's GPT o3 model, released in January 2025, as achieving a 75% score on the GPQA Diamond test with a price of $0.30 per question. Just a year and a half later, though, OpenAI released GPT-5.6 Luna, which can score just as well on the same test, but costs only $0.0004 per question.
But that kind of rapid cost reduction isn't uniform across different disciplines, or linear in its progression. Expanding its research to include additional benchmark results on chess puzzles and mathematics, Epoch AI discovered vastly different rates of cost efficiency improvements. Where its GPQA Diamond benchmark showed periods of rapid cost reduction followed by periods of stagnation and plateauing, the AIME OTIS Mock test showed much more regular progression at each data point. Chess puzzles, although not tracked to the same success percentage, showcased more regular and consistent improvement, too.
Frontier Math developments, however, barely improved between 2025 and 2026, and then the costs fell off a cliff midway through the year.
Epoch AI also highlights that the rate of cost reduction is in decline, and that appears to be the case for most measured metrics for any particular performance level. Across the five benchmarks, it tracked cost falls of 66% per quarter initially, but two years later, that's down to 32% per quarter.
That could suggest AI progression is slowing, or that it's becoming harder to cut AI use costs, particularly in 2026, as the price of energy and compute hardware has skyrocketed. It's hard to offer a cheaper service if the raw materials for AI intelligence are vastly more expensive than they used to be.
Benchmaxxing is still an issue
Arguably the biggest potential problem for this data is, as Epoch AI highlights, the potential for "Benchmaxxing." That involves AI developers specifically training their models to do well on benchmarks that are otherwise designed to test more generalized capabilities.
Fooling benchmarks is something software companies have always done — Nvidia and ATI got caught doing it with 3DMark in 2003, and thousands of Intel test results were invalidated in 2024 for doing much the same thing with another benchmark.
Epoch AI's benchmarking used randomized elements to try to avoid models from recognizing they're being tested or developers specifically training them to be effective at third-party tests. But that's not all tests, and the ones without it showed greater rates of decline, suggesting there is some measure of benchmark optimization going on in the data.
That doesn't invalidate the results, but it does warrant taking them with an ounce of skepticism.
Not everyone takes advantage of the savings
The major concern for AI developers, especially those developing frontier models while spending hundreds of billions of dollars on infrastructure, is that these results suggest there's little point in paying for any kind of privilege. Even though the likes of Fable, Mythos, and the latest OpenAI models are still expensive to run compared to their contemporaries, token costs are falling all the time as the flagship developers compete on the Pareto frontier — the point where efficient cost and high intelligence meet.
But if other models can achieve 90% of the same intelligence at a fraction of the cost, and that cost is only likely to fall in the weeks and months to come, then is there any need to pay for the latest features and capabilities? Especially if those other models end up being open-weight, meaning third parties can compete to offer the most efficient and affordable version of that model.
But like anything else people subscribe to, it's not just about price, and it's not just about intelligence or capabilities either. Familiarity is important: With UI, with workflows, with the rest of what your organization is running. Trust is huge with any kind of ongoing commitment, especially financial. Can you trust that new third-party service offering a cheaper model than the one you've used for the past year? Maybe, but is it worth the risk?
Switching to a new model means confirming the veracity of those new benchmarks, and trusting that prices won't change dramatically in the future (they probably will), potentially invalidating your savings. You have to trust that the system you were using won't just catch up a week from now, and that the new system doesn't have any bugs or privacy concerns.
Changing AI tools isn't as straightforward as just chasing cost or intelligence. While prices might be falling dramatically, that doesn't necessarily mean a subscription model for AI is impossible. Just harder to justify.
Jon Martindale is a contributing writer for Tom's Hardware. For the past 20 years, he's been writing about PC components, emerging technologies, and the latest software advances. His deep and broad journalistic experience gives him unique insights into the most exciting technology trends of today and tomorrow.

articles.title: Memory At The Edge: Non-Volatile Memory Challenges And Requirements For Humanoid Robots
articles.text:
Distributed NVM supports high-endurance telemetry logging, functional safety, and time-sensitive networking where resilience is critical.
Humanoid robots are rapidly transitioning from research demonstrations to commercial deployment in factories, warehouses, and service environments. As adoption scales, high-performant, reliable operation increasingly depends on the underlying electronic and memory architecture. Analyst reports from Goldman Sachs suggest annual humanoid robot shipments could reach more than 6 million units by 2035, up from fewer than 15,000 units in 2025. Similar to autonomous vehicles, these systems rely on high-density sensor arrays, power-efficient semiconductors, and AI-driven processing.
The operational demands of a humanoid robot require a distributed, multi-tier electronic architecture.
A centralized compute core performs vision processing, AI model execution, and real-time motion planning. A time-sensitive network then distributes commands to MCUs embedded in limbs, joint actuators, and battery management systems (BMS).
A humanoid robot platform typically employs multiple memory technologies – each selected to address and optimize design challenges related to performance, power consumption and reliability. AI inference and perception workloads require high-bandwidth memories to support large neural networks, while distributed motor control sub-systems powered by dedicated MCUs prioritize deterministic low-latency operation [1] and power-loss persistence to maintain control state at the edge. Different subsystems therefore place fundamentally different demands on memory, ranging from bandwidth-optimized storage for AI workloads to latency-optimized memory for real-time control functions. Within this broad spectrum, reliability-related characteristics become particularly important for distributed edge controllers to achieve real-time control.
Humanoid robots must continuously monitor actuator health, joint loads, and system stability to prevent failures that could affect safety, reliability, or availability. To support fault diagnostics, root-cause analysis, predictive maintenance, and regulatory traceability, these systems capture large volumes of operational telemetry. Logging motor torque, velocity, and limb position data at sampling rates above 10 kHz can quickly exceed the endurance limits of conventional non-volatile memories. As a result, reliable operation depends on selecting memory technologies optimized for the requirements of each subsystem.
Fig. 1: Zonal processing and networking architecture in humanoid platforms.
High-bandwidth DRAM supports AI inference and perception workloads, while NAND Flash stores operating systems, AI models, and application software. These centralized memories are optimized for bandwidth and storage density. In contrast, distributed non-volatile memories support boot management, networking infrastructure, telemetry logging, and functional safety, where endurance, deterministic latency, and power-loss resilience are often more critical than capacity. This article focuses on the unique requirements of that distributed memory layer.
This network layout shown in Figure 1 isolates computing workloads by subsystem. As a result, each domain has distinct memory requirements. In evolving humanoid architecture, high-capacity processing is centralized at the core, while high-frequency control loops are managed locally by individual zonal MCUs and edge motor controllers, as shown in Figure 1.
Standard Flash and EEPROM devices introduce a 5 to 10 ms page-write delay. During this process, data is staged in a volatile buffer while internal charge pumps program the memory cells. If a humanoid experiences a power failure or sudden emergency-stop during this window, the active position log fractures. Upon reboot, the joint controllers lose absolute coordinates, forcing a potentially disruptive and time-consuming mechanical homing sequence to re-calibrate.
Mechanical friction and electrical power dissipation within compact joint housings drive internal temperatures above +100°C. Elevated thermal stress degrades the oxide insulation layer in legacy charge-based NVMs, causing trapped electrical charges to leak from the cells, shortening data retention lifespans. In contrast, crystal-polarization memories store data through atomic alignment rather than trapped charge, eliminating this leakage mechanism.
High-torque BLDC motors generate significant EMI and stray magnetic fields near joint-control electronics. This noise can induce bit errors and voltage disturbances that corrupt telemetry data and affect system stability.
While there is no universally accepted humanoid memory architecture, most platforms combine centralized computing resources with distributed control and networking infrastructure. Table 1 illustrates representative volatile and non-volatile memory requirements across these three commonly found functional domains in a humanoid platform.
| Subsystem | Memory type | Performance Metrics | Structural Robotic Integration | 
| Distributed joint actuators & BMS | F-RAM | • Zero write-cycle programming delay • Near-infinite write endurance, (100 trillion cycles) • Native EMI / Magnetic field immunity | Direct integration adjacent to motor commutations and battery stacks | 
| Time-sensitive networking backbone | Standard High-Speed NOR Flash | • High-bandwidth SPI/QSPI interface execution • High-density firmware storage | Embedded within TSN Ethernet switches and communication hubs | 
| Centralized Computation platform, including AI inference, perception and sensing (multi-cam, IMU, tactile) [2] | Functional Safety compliant Hardware- NOR Flash with on-chip ECC | • On-chip automated hardware Error Correction Code • SafeBoot technology for crash-proof updates • SIL 3 / IEC 61508 compliance | Mounted on primary GPU / AI accelerator motherboards | 
|  | High-bandwidth DRAM and NVMe SSD | • High-bandwidth LPDDR5/5X memory access for inference • High-density memory • Low latency data retrieval | Mounted on primary GPU / AI accelerator motherboards | 
Table 1: Memory technology requirements by subsystem.
Memory selection ultimately depends on application-specific requirements including latency, endurance, density, functional safety, power consumption, and cost targets.
Fig. 2: Memory requirements across key humanoid robot functions.
To address these localized hardware constraints (see Figure 2), persistent memory requirements can be examined across the three representative functional domains in Table 1: F-RAM for joint-level data logging, functional-safety compliant NOR Flash for the compute platform, and standard NOR Flash for networking infrastructure.
To see how these requirements translate into physical silicon deployments, we look at the total memory distribution per robot frame. Figure 3 illustrates the allocation metrics and joint attachment counts required to sustain stable telemetry and boot functions.
Fig. 3: Typical memory distribution within a humanoid robot.
This physical distribution highlights the widespread use of distributed non-volatile memory throughout the humanoid platform, spanning edge-control subsystems (joint control, motor drives, and battery management), networking infrastructure (TSN switches and zone controllers), and centralized compute functions (AI processing, HMI, and system boot).
Fig. 4: Representative memory placement within humanoid control modules.
Motor control boards and battery management systems (BMS) rely on continuous data-logging for real-time edge processing. As shown in the module layouts in Figure 4, a standard platform deploys a dense network of serial F-RAM components to manage this streaming telemetry.
Table 2: Edge memory requirements and corresponding memory characteristics.
F-RAM offers write endurance of more than 100 trillion cycles, enabling continuous high-frequency logging without practical wear-out concerns. Under high-frequency logging workloads, memory endurance can become a key design consideration when selecting non-volatile storage technologies.
F-RAM data state transitions occur via atomic polarization alignment in less than 100 nanoseconds. This enables random access at bus speed with immediate non-volatility. Position data remains preserved during power loss, allowing operation to resume without a full re-homing sequence.
SPI NOR Flash and high-performance serial Flash devices, including Octal SPI memories, provide the read throughput needed for responsive HMI interaction. Functional safety NOR Flash devices can support ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 requirements through features such as hardware ECC and protected boot mechanisms. Beyond functional safety, modern humanoid robots also require cybersecurity safeguards. Secure boot mechanisms help verify firmware authenticity during startup, while cryptographic validation techniques protect firmware integrity throughout the system lifecycle. Authenticated update capabilities further reduce the risk of unauthorized software modifications, helping maintain reliable operation in connected industrial and commercial environments.
To connect these core systems to the limbs, dedicated SPI Flash components pair directly with TSN Ethernet switches, streaming network firmware via high-speed SPI/QSPI interfaces with minimal timing jitter to prevent communication lag down the chassis.
The central compute core communicates with the individual limbs via a high-bandwidth Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) Ethernet protocol backbone. To maintain deterministic packet routing across the chassis, dedicated high-speed SPI NOR Flash components pair directly with the system’s industrial Ethernet switches. These memories stream network configuration firmware via multi-I/O SPI interfaces with minimal timing jitter. This helps maintain deterministic communication between the central controller and individual joints, supporting synchronized motion across all axes.
While DRAM and NAND Flash provide the bandwidth and storage capacity required for AI workloads and operating systems, distributed control architectures introduce a separate class of memory requirements. Edge controllers, motor drives, and battery management systems prioritize deterministic latency, endurance, and power-loss resilience, making specialized non-volatile memory technologies an important complement to the central memory subsystem.
Humanoid robot architectures place diverse demands on non-volatile memory subsystems, ranging from high-endurance telemetry logging at the edge to functionally safe firmware storage in centralized compute platforms. Matching memory technologies to the specific requirements of each subsystem can improve system reliability, availability, and deterministic operation as humanoid deployments scale.

articles.title: Egypt's MoneyHash partners with Geidea to widen payment access in MENA - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian payment orchestration startup MoneyHash has partnered with Saudi fintech Geidea, giving businesses on its platform access to Geidea’s payment gateway across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt.
Founded in 2021 by Nader Abdelrazik and Mustafa Eid, MoneyHash has developed a proprietary payment orchestration platform and end-to-end payment operating system. After a successful beta launch in 2022, attracting key players in the region such as Foodics, Rain, and Tamatem, the startup launched its enterprise suite last October, targeting large enterprises.
The startup, which secured US$5.2 million in pre-Series A funding early last year, has been expanding its international operations recently, with key partnerships agreed in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Iraq, Bahrain and Oman.
Through this latest partnership, merchants using MoneyHash can tap Geidea’s online gateway and supported payment methods through their existing MoneyHash integration, without building or maintaining a separate connection. MoneyHash offers a single API that lets businesses connect to multiple payment gateways, with smart routing, multi-currency processing and a unified dashboard.
“Businesses should be spending their time building great products, serving customers, and growing into new markets, not repeatedly rebuilding and maintaining payment infrastructure,” said Nader Abdelrazik, co-founder and chief executive officer (CEO) of MoneyHash.
“Bringing Geidea’s strong regional payment capabilities into the MoneyHash ecosystem gives businesses a simpler way to access the infrastructure they need while we take care of the complexity behind the scenes.”

articles.title: Samsung unveils new Galaxy Tab S12 tablet series and smaller Galaxy SmartTag 3 trackers - Tech Guide
articles.text:
Samsung has unveiled its new Galaxy Tab S12 series – Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra and Tab S12+ – the most capable tablets it has ever created with outstanding performance, longer battery life, and the latest Galaxy AI onboard.
Samsung has also revealed its Galaxy Smart Tag 3 – it’s new tracker which is smaller and lighter with longer range finding.
SAMSUNG GALAXY TAB S12 SERIES – From $1,999
The Samsung Galaxy Tabs include their signature ultra-thin design and the power and performance to run complex workflows to satisfy all your productivity and creativity needs.
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra and the Tab S12+ feature bright immersive displays and come with the ergonomically designed S Pen for easy notetaking and precision editing.
The Tab S12 Ultra has a 14.6-inch Dynamic AMOLED 2X display while the Tab S12+ features a 12.6-inch screen.
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra is just 5.1 mm thick and supports your productivity for the entire day whether you’re working in an office, at a café or on your commute.
It has been engineered for durability with an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance.
Both models have ultra-long battery life with the Tab S12 Ultra lasting up to 23 hours and the Galaxy Tab S12+ up to 21 hours.
Under the hood is a new 3D vapour chamber to dissipate heat and promote more reliable performance during demanding tasks.
And on the audio side the new Samsung tablets have four-channel spatial audio, twice as many as the previous model, to deliver a more immersive experience while streaming content or playing games.
The Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 series is running Android 17 with One UI 9, as well as the latest Galaxy AI.
Users can turn the tablet into a professional workstation with the Pro keyboard, which has a premium aluminium finish and a dedicated Galaxy AI key for instant access to AI assistance.
The Book Cover Keyboard Slim is another accessory to offer flexibility with comfortable viewing and easy typing.
Customers will receive a 6-month trial of Google AI Pro when they purchase the Samsung tablet for expanded access to Google’s capable AI models.
The Samsung Galaxy Tab S12 series will go on sale on October 22.
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra will be priced from $2,299 while the Galaxy Tab S12 Plus will start at $1,999.
SAMSUNG GALAXY SMARTTAG 3
The Samsung Galaxy Smart Tag 3 is 35 per cent smaller by volume and 33 per cent lighter than the previous model, which makes it even easier to attach to keys, bags and luggage and even a pet’s collar.
It now has a more rounded form factor and finish with an aluminium button for a more durable look and feel.
And for the first time the Galaxy Smart Tag 3 offers cross-OS compatibility for Galaxy and iOS devices to make it even easier for families and groups to access finding and sharing features across platforms.
And when Galaxy SmartTag 3 moves outside of direct connection range, the Galaxy Find network helps keep the search going thanks to more than 900 million participating Galaxy devices around the world, which act as finding nodes to help detect the Galaxy Smart Tag 3 and update its location.
The Samsung Galaxy Smart Tab 3 will be available in Australia in early 2027 in black and white.

articles.title: Android dit non à l'Union européenne : Google refuse d'ouvrir l'OS à ChatGPT et Claude
articles.text:
Depuis le 16 juillet, deux décisions de la Commission européenne imposent à Google d’ouvrir Android aux assistants IA concurrents et de partager ses données de recherche, au titre du DMA, le règlement européen sur les marchés numériques. Ce mardi 29 septembre, l’entreprise a annoncé contester les deux textes devant le Tribunal de l’Union européenne, à Luxembourg. Le recours décidera de votre liberté de remplacer Gemini par l’assistant de votre choix.
ChatGPT au bouton, Claude à la voix : l’Android que Bruxelles exige
La décision Android, adoptée après six mois d’instruction, contraint Google à ouvrir onze fonctions du système aux assistants concurrents. Un appui long sur le bouton d’accueil pourra réveiller un autre service que Gemini, et chaque éditeur pourra définir son propre mot d’activation, l’équivalent du « Hey Google » maison. Les assistants tiers obtiendront aussi l’accès au contexte de vos applications, à l’automatisation d’actions à l’écran, aux modèles embarqués comme Gemini Nano et à l’exécution en arrière-plan. L’essentiel doit arriver avec Android 18, au plus tard le 1er août 2027 ; l’écoute simultanée de plusieurs mots d’activation attendra Android 19, à l’été 2028. Les accès les plus sensibles passeront par un programme de certification, dont les conditions définitives sont attendues pour le 1er mai 2027.
Google refuse d’ouvrir ces portes et met la sécurité en avant. Confier à des applications tierces un micro toujours actif, la lecture de l’écran et des automatisations système reviendrait, d’après ses équipes, à « saper le modèle de sécurité fondamental d’Android ». La firme brandit aussi le risque d’injection de commandes : des instructions cachées dans une page ou un document, qui détournent un agent IA sans que son propriétaire ne s’aperçoive de rien.
Vos recherches, l’autre trésor que Google ne veut pas céder
La seconde décision touche à plus intime encore : vos requêtes. À partir de janvier 2027, Google devra fournir aux moteurs concurrents, chatbots IA compris, ses données de recherche anonymisées (requêtes, clics, classements), à prix encadré, dès lors que le demandeur dépasse 50 000 utilisateurs européens par mois. L’entreprise plaide que ces données racontent nos vies, « des préoccupations de santé à l’intimité », et qu’un partage mal protégé causerait un « préjudice irréparable » à la vie privée des utilisateurs.
Bruxelles oppose ses garde-fous : anonymisation des données, consentement explicite de l’utilisateur pour les accès sensibles, conservation limitée à treize mois et audits indépendants imposés aux bénéficiaires. Le 23 juillet, la Commission a déjà infligé 890 millions d’euros d’amende à Google pour deux manquements distincts au même règlement. Ignorer les décisions de juillet exposerait cette fois l’entreprise à des sanctions pouvant atteindre 10 % de son chiffre d’affaires mondial.
En attendant les juges, rien ne bouge sur votre écran : Gemini reste seul à décrocher quand vous pressez le bouton, et le calendrier fixé par Bruxelles n’a pas varié à ce stade. Si la Commission tient bon, votre Android devra faire de la place aux assistants rivaux d’ici à l’été 2027. Si Google l’emporte, l’assistant de votre fidèle téléphone restera ce qu’il est aujourd’hui : préinstallé, exclusif et non négociable.

Source : Reuters

articles.title: IA, batteries, grande vitesse… Alstom et ses rivaux dessinent votre prochain train
articles.text:
Le futur du rail se joue autant dans le confort du voyageur que dans la consommation électrique des rames. À Berlin, les principaux acteurs du ferroviaire ont montré comment les batteries, les satellites et l’intelligence artificielle pourraient changer nos trajets sur les rails.
Le train de demain ne se résumera pas à une nouvelle motrice ou à quelques kilomètres par heure gagnés. À InnoTrans 2026, organisé à Berlin du 22 au 25 septembre, les constructeurs ont surtout montré comment le logiciel, l’intelligence artificielle, les batteries et la connectivité sont en train de transformer le rail. Alstom, Siemens, CAF, Stadler ou encore le chinois CRRC ont chacun avancé leurs solutions, certaines devant équiper des trains déjà commandés, d’autres étant encore au stade de la démonstration technique.
La grande vitesse soigne sa consommation et sa connexion
Chez Alstom, la recherche d’économies d’énergie passe notamment par l’Avelia Horizon, la plateforme dont est issu le TGV M. Le constructeur annonce une consommation réduite de 20% par rapport aux TGV existants, grâce à une aérodynamique retravaillée et à une traction plus efficace. Ses motrices raccourcies dégagent aussi davantage de place pour les voyageurs.
Un autre chantier se prépare en Italie, où douze Avelia Stream sont en construction pour Italo avec une mise en service prévue à partir de fin 2027. L’opérateur travaille par ailleurs avec Nomad Digital, filiale d’Alstom, au déploiement d’une connexion combinant réseaux 5G et satellites Starlink. L’ambition est de maintenir un accès Internet plus fiable sur les parcours difficiles à couvrir. Pouvoir terminer un document ou regarder une vidéo sans surveiller les barres de réseau serait déjà un progrès appréciable.
Le confort se travaille jusque sous le plancher
Pour les trajets de moyenne et longue distance, Trenitalia a dévoilé l’Intercity 200, également conçu par le constructeur français sur sa plateforme Coradia Stream. Cette rame capable d’atteindre les 200 km/h a été conçue pour consommer jusqu’à 30% d’énergie en moins que les modèles précédents, selon le fabricant. Ses 403 places assises s’accompagnent d’espaces familiaux, de trois emplacements pour les personnes à mobilité réduite et de huit places pour vélos, avec des possibilités de recharge pour les modèles électriques.
Le travail porte aussi sur les composants que les passagers ne verront jamais. Alstom exposait ainsi un bogie sans châssis classique, cet ensemble placé sous la caisse qui porte les roues. L’architecture vise à réduire le poids et les vibrations tout en améliorant l’accessibilité.
L’allègement occupe également CRRC, le numéro un mondial du matériel ferroviaire. Avec son métro Vellink, le groupe chinois revendique un poids réduit d’environ 18% et une consommation abaissée de plus de 10% par rapport à des véhicules conventionnels. À bord, CRRC mise sur de grandes baies panoramiques et des sièges pivotants. Les capteurs et l’IA embarqués doivent, eux, surveiller les voies et repérer les défaillances en temps réel.
Des rames qui évoluent et des pannes plus vite comprises
Un train doit pouvoir profiter des progrès techniques bien après sa livraison. C’est l’idée défendue par Alstom avec son approche Software Defined Train. En partageant davantage leurs données et leurs ressources informatiques, les équipements de traction, de climatisation, d’information voyageurs ou de maintenance pourraient évoluer plus facilement par mises à jour logicielles.
Siemens pousse cette logique jusqu’au magasin d’applications. Sa locomotive Vectron X réunit sur un écran central les données de fonctionnement, les informations sur le parcours et des applications de l’opérateur ou d’éditeurs tiers. De nouvelles fonctions peuvent ainsi être ajoutées au fil de sa carrière. L’allemand présentait aussi TPS.live, qui utilise l’intelligence artificielle pour aider à résoudre les conflits de circulation et mieux exploiter le réseau.
Dans les ateliers, l’intérêt se mesure surtout au temps gagné pour remettre une rame en service. Avec Talk to My Train, un technicien peut interroger un assistant qui recoupe les données du train, son historique de maintenance et la documentation technique. L’outil aide à remonter à l’origine possible d’une anomalie et présente les éléments sur lesquels repose sa réponse. Dans cette approche, le technicien reste responsable de la décision.
Depuis son stand berlinois, Alstom a également téléconduit une rame du S-Bahn de Munich qui circulait sur son site d’Hennigsdorf, à une vingtaine de kilomètres. Cette démonstration, menée avec la Deutsche Bahn et le S-Bahn München, relevait bien de la conduite à distance : un opérateur humain restait aux commandes.
Les batteries ouvrent une nouvelle voie aux lignes encore au diesel
L'innovation ferroviaire pourrait être particulièrement visible à l'avenir sur les dessertes régionales. Ainsi, le Flirt Akku du suisse Stadler, présenté dans sa version destinée aux chemins de fer autrichiens ÖBB, sait recharger ses batteries sous caténaire, puis utiliser cette réserve pour parcourir les sections non électrifiées. Le diesel peut ainsi être remplacé sans devoir installer une caténaire sur l’ensemble de la ligne. Le déploiement commercial de ces rames est prévu à partir de 2028 sur la ligne autrichienne du Kamptal.
L'espagnol CAF exposait pour sa part le Civity BEMU, destiné notamment aux réseaux allemands VRR et NWL. Avant le salon, une rame équipée de ses batteries de série avait parcouru 273 kilomètres en mode 100% batterie lors d’un essai à Wildenrath. Le résultat ne constitue pas une autonomie garantie en service commercial, mais donne un aperçu des distances que cette technologie peut permettre de franchir.
Enfin, l’hydrogène conserve ses partisans. Stadler présentait ainsi un train pour les voies étroites de Sardaigne, de Calabre et de Sicile. Le chinois CRRC associait quant à lui piles à combustible et batteries électriques dans sa locomotive Velforce de 2 MW, destinée au fret sur des lignes partiellement électrifiées. Décidément, le vénérable chemin de fer reprend des couleurs d'année en année.
Sources : Alstom, Siemens, CAF, Stadler et CRRC.

articles.title: Pourquoi tout le monde ne parle que du spécial LEGO One Piece débarqué sur Netflix ?
articles.text:
Après le succès critique et commercial surprise de sa série en prises de vues réelles One Piece, la plateforme au N rouge a décidé de pousser le curseur encore plus loin dans l’expérimentation.
Sorti ce mardi 29 septembre, ce programme spécial en deux parties réinvente l’arc légendaire d’East Blue et l’entrée sur Grand Line sous forme de briques emboîtables.
Netflix n’a pas encore publié d’audience pour le programme. Son Top 10 officiel couvre des semaines du lundi au dimanche et paraît le mardi suivant, donc le mardi 6 octobre pour cette semaine. Le démarrage semble pourtant solide.
Ce mercredi 30 septembre, au lendemain de sa sortie, le programme était deuxième au classement mondial des séries Netflix, juste derrière Monster, selon FlixPatrol. Ce site additionne les classements que Netflix affiche dans chaque pays. Il mesure donc une popularité relative, pas un nombre de spectateurs.
Usopp, le menteur de l’équipage, raconte l’histoire de One Piece sauce Lego
Plutôt que d’offrir un simple condensé plan par plan de la série originale, le showrunner Tom Hyndman a confié la narration à Usopp, le menteur invétéré de l’équipage du Chapeau de paille. Assis aux côtés de Tony Tony Chopper, le canonnier retrace les exploits passés de ses camarades avec toute l’exagération et la mauvaise foi qu’on lui connaît. Le tout avec, évidemment, l’humour Lego.
Le programme compte deux épisodes d’une trentaine de minutes chacun, intitulés Tall Tales From the East Blue et Grand Line, Grand Time. Il reprend les grands événements des deux premières saisons de la série live-action, et les acteurs de cette série prêtent leur voix à leur double en briques : Iñaki Godoy pour Luffy, Emily Rudd pour Nami, Mackenyu pour Zoro, Jacob Romero Gibson pour Usopp et Taz Skylar pour Sanji. Mikaela Hoover, qui prête sa voix à Chopper dans la saison 2, reprend aussi son rôle.
Le format Lego se prête bien à ce parti pris. Le ton est volontairement absurde, et les scènes de combat cultes tournent aux gags visuels, avec des personnages qui se démontent littéralement brique par brique.
Usopp se donne le beau rôle dans des événements où il n’était même pas présent, offrant une réécriture parodique et assumée. Enfin, le programme vise clairement un public plus jeune et Tom Hyndman le présente comme une porte d’entrée pour les plus petits. Il garde assez de second degré pour amuser les fans de la première heure.
Qui se cache derrière les briques ?
Le spécial réunit plusieurs partenaires de poids : le studio canadien Atomic Cartoons à l’animation, Tomorrow Studios (déjà à la barre du live-action), l’éditeur historique Shueisha, et bien sûr le géant Lego.
Atomic Cartoons connaît déjà les briques : le studio de Vancouver a animé la série Lego Star Wars : Rebuild the Galaxy. Chelsea Ker réalise les deux épisodes, écrits par Tom Hyndman.
Surtout, Eiichiro Oda figure parmi les producteurs exécutifs, comme sur la série live-action. L’auteur de One Piece, d’ordinaire très protecteur avec sa création, a donc validé cette version parodique.

articles.title: Xgimi Aura 3 Max et Pro : précommandes jusqu’à -56 % sur les deux vidéoprojecteurs 4K 120 Hz — Frandroid
articles.text:
Présentée fin août, la série Aura 3 comprend l’Aura 3 Max et l’Aura 3 Pro. Ces appareils sont des modèles à ultra-courte focale, donc destinés à être installés à seulement quelques centimètres du mur ou d’un écran.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Quels sont les meilleurs vidéoprojecteurs à ultra courte focale en 2026 ? Notre sélection
            
Le rapport de projection de 0,163:1 permet, selon Xgimi, d’afficher une image de 120 pouces, soit 305 cm de diagonale, avec un recul d’environ 20 cm par rapport à l’écran. Cette configuration vise les salons où l’installation d’un projecteur classique reste difficile.
Ils utilisent la technologie DLP avec une matrice native Full HD, pour une définition 4K UHD simulée. La source lumineuse est un triple laser RVB.
La principale nouveauté de ces modèles est l’intégration d’un double iris mécanique, grâce auquel Xgimi annonce un contraste natif de 8 000:1 pour l’Aura 3 Max et de 7 000:1 pour l’Aura 3 Pro.
Luminosité, fréquence et concurrence
La luminosité varie selon le modèle : l’Aura 3 Max revendique 5700 lumens ISO, contre 4100 lumens ISO pour la version Pro.
En outre, notez que les deux modèles acceptent la 4K à 120 Hz sur deux de leurs trois entrées HDMI. Xgimi revendique la première gamme de vidéoprojecteurs à ultra-courte focale capable de cette fréquence de rafraîchissement et vise les joueurs sur console ou sur PC. Les Aura 3 ne sont toutefois pas seuls sur ce créneau. Présenté lui aussi à l’IFA de Berlin, le LuxVision d’AWOL Vision est également un modèle à ultra-courte focale compatible 4K à 120 Hz, annoncé à 5999 euros. En focale classique, JMGO propose aussi la 4K à 120 Hz avec ses Iris Ultra et Iris Ultra Max.
Financement participatif : des économies substantielles à la clé
Xgimi a déjà vendu sa série Titan Noir via Kickstarter au printemps. Ces vidéoprojecteurs à focale classique, pensés pour une installation en fond de salle, ont levé plus de 18,8 millions de dollars (environ 16,5 millions d’euros) auprès de plus de 5900 contributeurs, selon la marque. Xgimi reprend la même formule avec les Aura 3 Pro et Aura 3 Max.
Un acompte de 50 € sur le site français de Xgimi, versé avant le 20 octobre, donne droit à 200 dollars (environ 175 euros) de réduction supplémentaire sur le tarif Kickstarter. Xgimi verse cette réduction sous forme de remboursement, avec l’acompte de 50 euros, dans les dix jours ouvrés qui suivent la fin de la campagne. Il faut utiliser la même adresse e-mail sur le site de la marque et sur Kickstarter.
La campagne se déroule du 20 octobre au 4 décembre. Aux États-Unis, Xgimi annonce des prix publics de 4999 dollars (environ 4380 euros, hors taxes) pour l’Aura 3 Max et de 3999 dollars (environ 3500 euros, hors taxes) pour l’Aura 3 Pro. Les tarifs français n’ont pas encore été communiqués.
Aura 3 Max :
- Offre Early Bird (avec les 200 $ de réduction) : 2199 $ (environ 1927 €)
- Offre Kickstarter standard : 2399 $ (environ 2102 €)
- Estimation avec la TVA française de 20 %, à régler à la livraison : environ 2312 €
Aura 3 Pro :
- Offre Early Bird (avec les 200 $ de réduction) : 1999 $ (environ 1752 €)
- Offre Kickstarter standard : 2199 $ (environ 1927 €)
- Estimation avec la TVA française de 20 %, à régler à la livraison : environ 2102 €
Xgimi prévoit les premières expéditions en décembre, dans l’ordre des contributions sur Kickstarter, en précisant que ces dates restent indicatives. Notez aussi que les tarifs Kickstarter sont libellés en dollars et n’incluent pas la TVA. Selon la FAQ de la marque, celle-ci est calculée après la campagne en fonction de l’adresse de livraison et reste à la charge de l’acheteur.
Enfin, si la campagne n’atteint pas son objectif de financement, Kickstarter ne débite pas la contribution et l’acompte est remboursé.

articles.title: Google investiga un fallo de Android Auto que afecta las llamadas cuando el celular plegable está cerrado
articles.text:
Un fallo de Android Auto impide realizar llamadas salientes desde algunos teléfonos plegables de Motorola cuando están cerrados y conectados al sistema del automóvil. El problema afecta a modelos de la familia Razr y obliga a los usuarios a desplegar el dispositivo para poder comunicarse. Tanto Google como Motorola ya están al tanto del error, aunque todavía no se ha anunciado una solución generalizada.
El inconveniente resulta especialmente llamativo porque una de las ventajas de los celulares plegables es que permiten realizar determinadas acciones desde la pantalla exterior, sin necesidad de abrir el dispositivo. Sin embargo, al conectarlos a Android Auto, esa posibilidad queda limitada por un error que afecta a las llamadas telefónicas.
PUBLICIDAD
Según los reportes publicados en los foros de soporte de Motorola y Google, el problema aparece cuando el usuario intenta realizar una llamada con el teléfono cerrado. En ese momento, Android Auto muestra un mensaje de error que solicita abrir el dispositivo. Una vez desplegado, la llamada se puede efectuar con normalidad.
Qué teléfonos plegables están afectados por el error de Android Auto
Los informes de los usuarios mencionan principalmente los teléfonos de la familia Motorola Razr, desde el Razr Ultra de 2025 hasta el modelo de 2026. Los testimonios indican que el fallo se presenta cuando estos dispositivos están conectados a Android Auto, tanto en determinadas configuraciones como durante el uso cotidiano del sistema.
PUBLICIDAD
El inconveniente afecta específicamente a las llamadas salientes. De acuerdo con las experiencias compartidas, el sistema impide iniciar la comunicación mientras el teléfono permanece cerrado, pero permite hacerlo cuando se despliega la pantalla principal.
La situación también plantea un problema de seguridad y comodidad durante la conducción. Los teléfonos plegables están diseñados para ofrecer funciones desde su pantalla exterior, lo que permite consultar información o realizar determinadas operaciones sin abrirlos. Tener que desplegarlos para efectuar una llamada puede resultar poco práctico, especialmente cuando el dispositivo está conectado al sistema multimedia del vehículo.
Además, mantener el teléfono abierto dentro del automóvil no siempre es una alternativa conveniente. Los fabricantes recomiendan tomar precauciones para evitar daños en las pantallas plegables, que requieren determinados cuidados durante su utilización y transporte.
PUBLICIDAD
Gemini podría estar relacionado con una solución temporal
Algunos usuarios encontraron una manera de evitar el error mediante el uso del Asistente de Google en lugar de Gemini. Según los reportes, volver a utilizar el antiguo asistente permite realizar llamadas desde el teléfono plegable cerrado y conectado a Android Auto.
Sin embargo, esta alternativa tiene una limitación importante: Google retiró el Asistente de Google de Android el 28 de septiembre de 2026, como parte de la transición hacia Gemini. Por ello, la solución temporal podría dejar de estar disponible para quienes ya utilizan el nuevo asistente.
La sustitución del antiguo asistente por Gemini también plantea interrogantes sobre la compatibilidad de las funciones de Android Auto con los teléfonos plegables. Aunque ambos servicios permiten interactuar con el dispositivo mediante comandos de voz, el error demuestra que todavía existen problemas que pueden afectar a determinadas configuraciones.
PUBLICIDAD
Google y Motorola ya conocen el problema
Tanto Google como Motorola confirmaron que están al tanto de los inconvenientes. En el foro oficial de Motorola aparece una respuesta de la compañía publicada menos de dos semanas antes de los últimos reportes, lo que indica que el problema ya llegó a los equipos de soporte.
Por el momento, no se ha comunicado una fecha concreta para la distribución de una actualización que corrija el fallo. Tampoco se ha precisado si la solución llegará mediante una actualización de Android Auto, una modificación de Gemini o un parche específico para los teléfonos de Motorola.
Mientras las compañías trabajan en el inconveniente, los usuarios afectados deben desplegar el teléfono para realizar llamadas salientes desde Android Auto. La falta de una solución definitiva podría ampliar el alcance del problema, especialmente ahora que Gemini está sustituyendo al Asistente de Google en los dispositivos Android.

articles.title: 5 Lessons from The Psychology of Money about wealth
articles.text:
5 Lessons from The Psychology of Money about wealth
Discover five powerful lessons from The Psychology of Money by Morgan Housel about building wealth, making smarter decisions, and thinking long term.
When people think about wealth, they often focus on investment strategies, stock market predictions, or complex financial formulas.
Yet, according to Morgan Housel's bestselling book The Psychology of Money, financial success is often less about knowledge and more about behaviour. Through engaging stories and timeless insights,
Housel explores how emotions, habits, and personal experiences shape the way people think about money. The book argues that wealth is not simply a result of earning more; it's often the result of making better decisions consistently over time.
Here are five valuable lessons from The Psychology of Money about building and preserving wealth.
1. Wealth is what you don't see
Many people associate wealth with expensive cars, luxury homes, or designer products. Housel challenges this idea by explaining that true wealth is often invisible. Real wealth consists of assets that have not yet been spent. It is the money saved, invested, and allowed to grow over time.
People who appear wealthy may not necessarily be financially secure, while those living modestly may be building substantial wealth behind the scenes.
The lesson is simple: focus less on looking rich and more on becoming financially secure.
2. Saving matters more than income
A high salary does not automatically lead to wealth. What matters is how much of that income is saved and invested. Housel emphasises that building wealth often depends on creating a gap between what you earn and what you spend. Even people with average incomes can accumulate significant wealth if they consistently save over long periods.
This lesson highlights the importance of financial discipline rather than relying solely on earning more money.
3. Time is the most powerful wealth-building tool
One of the book's central themes is the power of compounding. Small amounts of money invested consistently can grow dramatically when given enough time. Housel points to the success of long-term investors who benefited not only from good decisions but also from allowing those decisions to compound over decades.
The lesson encourages patience. Wealth is often built gradually rather than through quick wins or sudden breakthroughs.
4. Financial freedom is the ultimate luxury
Many people chase money to buy things, but Housel argues that the greatest benefit of wealth is control over your time.
Financial freedom provides the ability to make choices without being entirely dependent on a paycheck or external pressures. It allows people to spend time on meaningful work, relationships, hobbies, and personal goals.
According to the book, having the freedom to decide how you spend your days is one of the most valuable forms of wealth.
5. Avoid comparing your finances to others
Comparison can be one of the biggest obstacles to building wealth. It often encourages unnecessary spending and pushes people to pursue lifestyles they cannot comfortably afford. Housel explains that there will always be someone with more money, a larger house, or a more impressive lifestyle. Constant comparison creates a cycle where satisfaction becomes difficult to achieve.
Instead, the book encourages readers to define their own financial goals and make decisions based on their personal values rather than external expectations.
Final thoughts
The Psychology of Money offers a refreshing perspective on wealth. Rather than focusing on complicated financial strategies, it highlights the behaviours and mindsets that often determine long-term success.
The book reminds readers that wealth is not about impressing others or chasing endless growth. It is about making thoughtful decisions, saving consistently, thinking long term, and creating the freedom to live life on your own terms.
For anyone interested in building a healthier relationship with money, these lessons provide a valuable foundation that extends far beyond finance.

articles.title: Metamask discloses security incident affecting its infrastructure
articles.text:
On Thursday, cryptocurrency wallet provider MetaMask has disclosed an ongoing infrastructure security incident affecting some of its infrastructure.
The company is working to address the issue internally, with help from external partners and security advisors, and says there is "no immediate threat to MetaMask wallets."
"As a precautionary measure, we are proactively exiting affected validators within our non-custodial staking operations, in coordination with clients and partners," MetaMask noted. "As a reminder, our staking operations are non-custodial in nature and we do not manage withdrawal keys for stake on behalf of our clients."
Validators are nodes on the Ethereum network that run software responsible for proposing blocks, verifying crypto transactions, and maintaining the security of the Ethereum blockchain.
A MetaMask spokesperson redirected BleepingComputer to the company's public statement when asked what part of its infrastructure was affected and whether any systems or data were accessed or compromised.
While MetaMask hasn't shared further details about the incident, the decentralized liquid staking platform Lido Finance said earlier today that MetaMask Staking (ex Consensys Staking) has taken precautionary measures to protect client assets related to Ethereum validators.
"These steps include exiting its Ethereum (ETH) validators in the Lido protocol, and will likely incur foregone rewards as well as possible downtime penalties should validators be taken offline in the near future to reduce risks related to potential network penalties," Lido Finance said.
"Relevant validators have begun the exit process, with the final validators expected to be exited (but not fully withdrawn) by the end of October 7th, 2026."
The MetaMask non-custodial crypto wallet, developed by blockchain software company Consensys, lets users store and manage assets on the Ethereum network and other compatible blockchains.
