articles.title: Personne n'est à l'abri ! L'ANSSI et la Dinum victimes d'une fuite de données
articles.text:
Même les services de l'État censés se battre contre la cybercriminalité sont vulnérables. La preuve avec l'ANSSI et la Dinum.
Quand un problème de piratage d'importance est repéré, c'est l'ANSSI (Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d'Information) qui est en général appelée à la rescousse. C'est ainsi elle qui s'est penchée sur le cas très grave du piratage des impôts, et qui vient de publier son rapport d'incident sur ce dossier. Et pourtant, même cette institution doit semble-t-il passer par la case piratage !
La DINUM et l'ANSSI piratées à cause d'une vulnérabilité Metabase
La plateforme open-source Business Intelligence et de visualisation de données Metabase annonçait le 6 août dernier avoir détecté une faille zero-day critique, qui avait reçu le score CVS 10.0 - soit la note maximale pour la sévérité d'une vulnérabilité informatique.
Une faille qui a été utilisée par des pirates pour dérober des accès à des comptes utilisateurs du côté de l'ANSSI, mais aussi pour en créer de nouveaux malveillants à la DINUM (direction interministérielle du numérique), comme nous l'apprend FrenchBreaches.
118 comptes utilisateurs du laboratoire de l'innovation de l'ANSSI compromis
Au total, la DINUM a subi la compromission de deux de ses instances Metabase (l'une dédiée à ProConnect et l'autre à Nuage-Public), alors que le laboratoire d'innovation de l'ANSSI a lui vu 118 comptes utilisateurs être compromis.
Pour ce qui est du cas DINUM, des informations administratives d'organismes publics, des métadonnées de projets logiciels et des historiques de connexion ont été dérobés. Un problème qui serait ici limité, la majorité des données volées étant publiques, quand les historiques sont eux anonymisés. Pour ce qui est de la fuite de données chez l'ANSSI, des identifiants, des adresses emails et des mots de passe hachés ont été dérobés.
La DINUM a indiqué que les vulnérabilités ont été corrigées, que les comptes utilisateurs malveillants créés ont été détruits et que des accès ont été réinitialisés. L'ANSSI a elle aussi pris des mesures de correction des vulnérabilités, et a réinitialisé les mots de passe de l'ensemble des comptes (tout en désactivant au passage les comptes inactifs depuis au moins trois mois).

articles.title: Warum Compliance-Anfragen dreifach geprüft werden
articles.text:
Wie aus einer Anfrage dreifacher Aufwand wird und wie er sich vermeiden lässt
Warum werden regulatorische Prozesse für Unternehmen immer aufwendiger?
Die regulatorischen Anforderungen wachsen schneller als die verfügbaren Compliance-Ressourcen. DSGVO, KI-VO, NIS2: Neue Anforderungen betreffen dieselben Fachbereiche, dieselben Compliance-Rollen und die Informationssicherheit.
Dabei fällt die Menge an regulatorischen Vorgaben weniger ins Gewicht als die Menge an internen Abstimmungen. Eine einzige Anfrage (z. B. für ein neues Tool, einen neuen Dienstleister oder eine neue KI-Anwendung) betrifft heute gleichermaßen Datenschutz, Informationssicherheit und KI-Governance.
Für die Geschäftsführung zeigt sich das nicht als rechtliches Problem, sondern als Effizienzproblem: längere Durchlaufzeiten, steigende Kosten, mehr organisatorische Reibung.
Warum prüfen Datenschutz, Informationssicherheit und KI-Governance dieselbe Anfrage?
Weil die Zuständigkeit erst geklärt wird, nachdem die Anfrage längst an diese drei Abteilungen verteilt wurde. Der Fachbereich weiß bei einem Vorgang nicht, wen genau er einbeziehen muss, und schreibt im Zweifel alle oder nur einen Bereich an. Die Anfrage landet in mehreren Postfächern. Drei Teams starten drei eigene Prüfungen, ohne Kenntnis darüber zu haben, dass sie unabhängig voneinander am selben Sachverhalt arbeiten. Nicht die fachliche Prüfung wird dabei mehrfach durchgeführt, sondern vor allem die Organisation rund um dieselbe Anfrage.
Das Ergebnis ist redundante Arbeit an einer einzigen Anfrage: Ressourcen werden durch dreifache Kommunikation, Rückfragen und Dokumentation gebunden. Und Unternehmen bezahlen damit für drei Prozesse statt nur einen.
Wer prüft neue Tools in einem Unternehmen?
Das erklärt sich anhand eines Fallbeispiels: Der Vertrieb will ein Sales-Tool mit KI-Funktion einführen. Es entstehen daraus Aufgaben für drei Teams: Datenschutz (u. a. Verarbeitungstätigkeit, AVV-Prüfung), Informationssicherheit (z. B. Dienstleisterprüfung) und KI-Governance (u. a. Risikoklassifizierung nach KI-VO, Eintrag ins KI-Verzeichnis).
Das Warten auf die Freigabe ist nicht nur ein organisatorisches Ärgernis. Denn jeder Tag, an dem der Vorgang zwischen drei Postfächern hängt, ist ein Tag, an dem der Vertrieb ohne das Tool auskommen muss: entgangene potenzielle Kunden, entgangener Umsatz. Die Alternative kann dabei noch teurer werden: Das Tool ist längst als Schatten-KI im Einsatz, ohne dass die Compliance-Prüfung vorab erfolgt ist. Eine gefährliche Compliance-Black-Box entsteht.
Wie lassen sich Compliance-Anfragen ohne doppelte Abstimmungen organisieren?
caralegal ist die Software für Datenschutz und KI-Governance in Unternehmen mit komplexen Strukturen. Als Data Responsibility Platform bündelt caralegal Verarbeitungstätigkeiten, Risikoanalysen, Audits und KI-Compliance an einem Ort, ISO 27001-zertifiziert und in Deutschland gehostet. Tel: +49 (0) 30 311 938 97
Die Lösung des Problems liegt in einem gemeinsamen Eingang. Genau dort setzt caralegal Lightway an:
- ein Eingang für jede Compliance-relevante Anfrage, vom Tool-Request bis zum Vorfall
- ein Vorgang mit eindeutiger Zuständigkeit, Status und ID
- Kommunikation, Dateien und Fristen an einem Ort
- Jeder Bereich sieht seinen Teil, die Verantwortlichen den gesamten Vorgang
Der Fachbereich stellt eine Anfrage, ohne wissen zu müssen, welche regulatorische Vorgabe betroffen ist. Lightway bezieht die zuständigen Bereiche gezielt ein, Status und Verlauf bleiben für alle Beteiligten sichtbar. KI-Agenten übernehmen hier weitere Schritte: das Erkennen von KI-Funktionen in Dienstleisterverträgen und von Zusammenhängen zwischen Meldungen aus unterschiedlichen Fachbereichen.
Der Vorteil für die Geschäftsführung: Sie muss nicht zwingend mehr Personal einstellen und profitiert von weniger Doppelarbeit in der bestehenden Organisation.
Lightway steht dabei nicht allein: Es ist mit Privacy Flow und AI Flow von caralegal verbunden. Die Prüfung eines Tools landet nicht isoliert in einem Ticketsystem, sondern dort, wo Verarbeitungstätigkeiten, DSFA und KI-Verzeichnis bereits gepflegt werden. So entsteht eine Orchestrierung über alle Compliance-relevanten Anfragen hinweg. Ein zentraler Ort, an dem konzernweit sichtbar ist, was angefragt, geprüft und entschieden wird.
Warum ist organisatorische Effizienz heute ein Wettbewerbsvorteil?
Weniger Rückfragen sorgen für weniger Abstimmungsschleifen. Das Ergebnis ist der schnellere Erhalt einer belastbaren Dokumentation. Verzeichnis von Verarbeitungstätigkeiten (VVT), Datenschutz-Folgenabschätzung (DSFA) und Risikoeinschätzung sind in einem Workflow gepflegt und liegen anschließend nicht verstreut. Das wirkt sich auch auf Audits aus: Wenn Nachweise im Prozess entstehen und nicht erst nachträglich rekonstruiert werden, sinkt die Wahrscheinlichkeit lückenhafter Dokumentation bei einer Behördenprüfung.
Effizienz entsteht nicht durch weniger Compliance-Arbeit. Sie entsteht vielmehr durch die Reduzierung der organisatorischen Reibung.
Wer regulatorische Zusammenarbeit zentral organisiert, entscheidet schneller, weist Compliance besser nach und kann Prozesse skalieren, statt bei jeder neuen Verordnung Ressourcen aufstocken zu müssen.
Eine Anfrage statt drei: Ein Vorgang, eine Zuständigkeit, ein Nachweis. Erfahre, wie Freigaben vereinfacht und beschleunigt werden.

articles.title: CISA warns of critical pre-auth RCE flaw in MikroTik RouterOS
articles.text:
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) is warning of a new critical vulnerability in MikroTik RouterOS that could lead to remote code execution or cause a denial-of-service condition.
Tracked as CVE-2026-84411, the security issue is a pre-authentication integer underflow in RouterOS’s web-management HTTP request handling.
CISA says that a single crafted request can produce code execution with root privileges or denial of service.
“The web management service in affected RouterOS versions contains an integer underflow in its HTTP request body handling that is reachable before authentication,” reads the alert.
“This can be leveraged by an unauthenticated network attacker to achieve arbitrary code execution as root, or to cause a denial of service, using a single crafted request.”
Although the agency has no knowledge of the vulnerability being actively exploited, it released the advisory to alert organizations of the risk and to provide defensive measures.
CISA notes that MikroTik RouterOS versions below 7.24 are currently affected. However, the agency also says that the vendor recommends that users update to version 7.23 or later to mitigate the risk.
It should be noted that the latest stable version of MikroTik RouterOS is 7.24.4, while the most recent long-term release is 7.23.7, both available since September 16.
BleepingComputer has emailed both MikroTik and CISA for clarification about the RouterOS versions affected by CVE-2026-84411, but we have not received a response as of publication. The vendor has yet to publish a security advisory about the issue.
CISA's recommendations to MikroTik router owners include the following defensive actions:
- Keep control systems inaccessible from the internet.
- Place control networks and remote devices behind firewalls, isolated from business networks.
- Use updated VPNs for remote access and secure all connected devices.
Although no active exploitation of CVE-2026-84411 has been publicly disclosed, hackers and botnet malware often target MikroTik flaws.
Recently, Poland’s CERT agency warned that attackers used an exploit chain of two MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-67276 and CVE-2026-86060, to take full control of devices with SSH services exposed to the internet.

articles.title: Google Pixel 11a : vous ne devinerez jamais à quoi il ressemble
articles.text:
C’est sous le nom de code « Formosan » que le Google Pixel 11a fait parler de lui à travers des premières images partagées par Android Headlines. Le Pixel 10a ressemblait déjà beaucoup au Pixel 9a, et cela devrait également être le cas du Pixel 11a si l’on en croit ces images. Mais les changements seraient à aller chercher à l’intérieur.
Le Pixel 11a, un Pixel 10a avec une moustache ?
Impossible d’être surpris en découvrant les lignes de ce Pixel 11a, puisque Google conserverait le même design que sur les deux générations précédentes. Le smartphone garde un bloc photo arrière totalement plat et un format minimaliste, même si la forme du module photo évolue légèrement vers un ovale un peu plus court. Côté mensurations, les leaks annoncent un boîtier d’environ 153,46 x 72,35 x 9 mm pour un écran de 6,3 pouces, ce qui le rend un tout petit peu plus court que les Pixel 9a et 10a.
Source : Android Headlines / OnLeaks
Quatre coloris seraient disponibles au lancement : noir (Obsidian), argent (Fog), vert (Olive) et une option violette. À l’avant, les bordures restent en revanche assez épaisses, un choix qui donne un petit coup de vieux à l’appareil avant même sa sortie. Côté affichage, la dalle de 6,3 pouces profiterait toujours d’un taux de rafraîchissement allant de 60 à 120 Hz et d’une luminosité maximale en plein soleil jusqu’à 3 350 nits.
La bascule vers la puce Tensor G6 et un nouveau modem
Contrairement au Pixel 10a qui avait la même puce que le Pixel 9a (un Tensor G4), le Pixel 11a passerait directement au processeur Tensor G6, c’est-à-dire celui qui équipe les Pixel 11 et Pixel 11 Pro. Le SoC serait accompagné d’un modem MediaTek censé régler les petits soucis de réseau des générations précédentes, tout en grappillant de précieuses heures d’autonomie grâce à une meilleure gestion du signal.
Pour épauler ce nouveau processeur, Google intégrerait le co-processeur de sécurité Titan M3 afin d’assurer la protection des mots de passe et des paiements. L’appareil embarquera également une batterie avoisinant les 5 000 mAh et tournera sous Android 17. Côté photo, le duo de capteurs arrière de 48 et 13 mégapixels reste en place, mais la caméra selfie profiterait d’un tout nouveau capteur. Quant au tarif, si la marque est restée bloquée à 499 dollars pendant quatre ans, la hausse générale des composants liée à l’intelligence artificielle pourrait bien faire grimper la facture à 599 dollars. Reste maintenant à voir comment cela se traduira en euros chez nous. Pour rappel, les Pixel 9a et Pixel 10a ont été lancés à 549 €.

articles.title: MuleSoft founder’s DIG Ventures closes €106 million Fund III to back Europe’s AI and cloud infrastructure startups | EU-Startups
articles.text:
DIG Ventures, the London-based venture capital firm backing the enterprise and cloud infrastructure companies underpinning the future of AI, has announced the close of its third fund at €106 million ($120 million).
Fund III is backed by institutional LPs including Horsley Bridge, Sofina, Granite, and a leading US university endowment. The company also announced a number of entrepreneurial LPs backing the fund, including the founders of Slack, Datadog, Nord Security, Cast AI, Supercell and Dash0. In April 2025, DIG Ventures closed a €90 million Fund for early-stage startups.
“I don’t think there is another VC in Europe that offers true partnership the way that DIG does. They think like founders, are deeply connected in the enterprise fabric globally, and never waver from their conviction,” Mirko Novakovic, CEO, Dash0.
Founded in 2018 by Ross Mason, founder of the enterprise integration company MuleSoft, which Salesforce acquired for €5.3 billion ($6.5 billion), the firm has transitioned from serving as Mason’s family office to backing technical founders at the earliest stages of company formation across enterprise AI and cloud infrastructure.
The Fund III follows Fund II, DIG’s first institutional fund, and ranks in the top decile globally for its vintage and size, according to Carta benchmarking data. The Fund II portfolio includes Dash0, an AI-native observability platform that became a unicorn after its €94 million ($110 million) Series B in March 2026, and Taktile, an AI decisioning platform that raised a $110 million Series C led by Goldman Sachs.
Other Fund II portfolio companies include CUBE, a regulatory technology company used by more than 30 global financial institutions; AI HR platform Jack & Jill, which raised €34.68 million in a Series A round earlier this month; and AI orchestration platform Nexos.ai, founded by the founders of Nord Security.
The venture firm has also seen several exits, including the insurance infrastructure company Flock, acquired by Admiral; the data infrastructure platform Tower, acquired by MotherDuck; and the workload identity company Cofide, acquired by Keyfactor.
According to DIG’s internal data, 80% of Fund II companies went on to raise additional institutional capital within two years of DIG’s investment, and more than 90% of those companies entered the US market commercially within a year.
“Our conviction as a fund is clear: as development accelerates and differentiation erodes, the truly scalable, defensible companies will be the ones building the foundations on which wider enterprise software depends. These are the companies whose advantages compound as the cost of building software falls,” said Mason, founding partner at DIG Ventures.
He added, “In Europe, we are seeing huge waves of innovation on this frontier – the continent is not short of technical talent. But the challenge is turning technical advantage into global distribution. Having built and sold enterprise software globally, our operator-led team knows what it takes to cross that gap. We built DIG to help founders do exactly that. We guide our startups from day zero through to their first US customers, and beyond. With Fund III, we’ll steer a further generation of founders towards global growth.”
With an operator-led partner team including Mason, Melissa Klinger, former UK sales lead of MuleSoft, and Rytis Vitkauskas, founder of YPlan and a former partner at Lightspeed Venture Partners, DIG Ventures says Fund III will back 30 European pre-Seed and Seed-stage companies working across the critical AI control points: data, identity, compliance and orchestration layers.
The firm intends to lead most of the rounds it enters and has already begun deploying capital from the new fund. It also plans to continue helping founders from their earliest days through to their first US customers and beyond.

articles.title: What even is a ‘microdrama’?
articles.text:
On Monday, Variety reported that RoseBerry Media is recutting episodes of the Australian soap opera Neighbours “into microdramas.” These clips will be available on Epis, a short-form vertical video streaming platform. Though Neighbours ran for 41 seasons from 1985 to 2025, at launch, RoseBerry is only recutting two storylines from the late aughts focused on a character played by the now-internationally famous Margot Robbie.
What even is a ‘microdrama’?
Most microdramas are vertical content, but not all vertical content feels like a real microdrama.
In a statement about the project, RoseBerry cofounder / CEO Guy Hameiri described Neighbours as “an iconic piece of television history” that’s well suited to be adapted for vertical viewing with the company’s proprietary, AI-powered production workflow. Hameiri also said that he believes the project will demonstrate how “premium vertical television will become a significant new entertainment category” — one that can help introduce new audiences to a classic series.
Variety’s framing of RoseBerry’s new vertical cut of Neighbours as a kind of microdrama is curious. Microdramas are short-form vertical videos often featuring characters who get caught up in convoluted romance plots, which makes them somewhat similar to Neighbours in terms of their shared subject matter. But unlike network television shows with sizable budgets, microdramas are produced on the cheap and crafted specifically to be consumed on mobile. And when you factor in how microdramas tend to adhere to a narrative formula that opens with intrigue and closes on melodramatic cliffhangers, it’s easy to see the format as a storytelling genre unto itself.
Over the past year, entertainment trades’ reporting has made it seem like Hollywood is ready to go all in on microdramas, and that these kinds of projects could help the industry bring much-needed production work back to Los Angeles. It’s unclear whether Variety’s phrasing is reflective of the industry’s definition of microdramas changing, or if studios are just trying to use buzzwords to drum up hype. But if microdramas really are going to be a key part of Hollywood’s future, we should probably all have a general understanding of what they actually are.
Both the amount of money that went into Neighbours and the quality of the cast’s acting make it a very different kind of entertainment compared to the microdramas that have become hits for companies like ReelShort and DramaBox. What RoseBerry is doing with Neighbours is much more akin to what Tattle TV did with Alfred Hitchcock’s silent film The Lodger: A Story of the London Fog earlier this year, and what startup Snips is doing with series like Big Brother and MasterChef. While there might be an audience for these things, it feels somewhat disingenuous to lump them in with the campy, bite-sized series like Forbidden Fling With My Bestie’s Dad that defined and popularized microdramas as a format in the West.
Microdramas originated in China, where they first began gaining traction around 2018 on platforms like Douyin and Kuaishou (both TikTok analogs). Kuaishou’s Unexpectedness — a satirical comedy about a man struggling to achieve his goals — was one of the first Chinese microseries to make a splash, and as the social video platforms embraced e-commerce, brands began to see microdramas as a viable way to market their products to viewers. As the audiences for microdramas grew, more Chinese film / TV production studios began producing microdramas, and by 2021, revenue from short-form video was projected to hit $500 million. That figure was expected to hit $7 billion by 2024 and $16.2 billion by 2030.
Though microdramas in all languages tend to be seen as lower-quality entertainment, their core appeal is fairly easy to grasp. The series lean heavily into well-established narrative tropes, and their stories are usually designed to leave viewers guessing about what kind of outlandish twists they’re about to see next. Microdramas’ verticality and the way they’re served up in short minuteslong segments makes them the sort of content that’s meant to be consumed through a phone screen. Microdramas’ relatively small production budgets also positioned them to become a viable way for up-and-coming actors and filmmakers to book consistent work. But in recent months, that promise has been waylaid by the spread of generative artificial intelligence.
In China especially, gen AI has had a devastating impact on the microdrama economy for human actors. Ninety-five percent of the Chinese microdramas produced in the first three months of this year were created with AI, which has led to fewer jobs and lower pay. A similar story is now playing out in Hollywood, where actors have reported being pressured by studios to sign over the rights to their digital likenesses. Though the details are somewhat different, presenting repurposed films and TV series as “microdramas” poses a similar threat to the people working in the business because of the way it cuts them out of opportunities like RoseBerry’s partnership with Epis. It’s also unclear how and whether this new vertical presentation of Neighbours might result in royalty payments to the show’s original cast and crew.
Streamers and studios’ interest in vertical content of all kinds has been driven by a desire to recapture some of the attention lost to rival platforms like TikTok and YouTube where microdramas have been able to thrive. For the most part, studios have been leading with repurposed, verticalized clips of preexisting content, which are presented in scrollable feeds that are meant to give you a preview of things that can be watched horizontally. These feeds’ content might be useful for discovery, but very much like microserialized (read: chopped-up) films and TV shows, they aren’t exactly a new entertainment format that seems worth making much noise about.
Traditional microdramas haven’t even really had a chance to live up to all the industry hype, but it feels like companies are already rushing to redefine the format as anything that happens to be short, dramatic, and vertically oriented. Platforms might be more interested in turning old shows and films into clip content because it’s less expensive than producing and building an audience for a wholly original microdrama. That doesn’t lend credence to the idea that this format can actually “save” Hollywood, though — if anything, it makes the industry seem like it’s trying to cannibalize itself.

articles.title: Deploying an HSTU Generative Recommender with NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
Generative recommender (GR) systems are emerging as a powerful new approach for large-scale personalization. Instead of treating recommendation as a set of isolated retrieval, ranking, and prediction stages, GRs reformulate recommendation as sequence modeling over user behavior. A user’s interactions, context, candidate items, and actions become tokens in a high-cardinality event stream, and the model learns to generate or score the next relevant items from that sequence.
This approach is especially attractive for modern recommendation workloads, where user histories can be long, item catalogs are constantly changing, and personalization quality depends on modeling rich sequential behavior. But it also introduces a serving challenge: GR models need low-latency inference despite long histories, large embedding tables, and sequence-heavy model architectures.
NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton (formerly NVIDIA Triton Inference Server) now supports an end-to-end Hierarchical Sequential Transduction Unit (HSTU) GR inference workflow through the NVIDIA recsys-examples repository. The workflow combines HTSUs, PyTorch Ahead-of-Time Inductor compilation, FlexKV-backed KV caching, native C++ validation, NV embedding cache, and Dynamo-Triton deployment.
The result is a practical path for serving HSTU ranking models with strong latency performance. At dynamic batch size 8 on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU, Dynamo-Triton with PyTorch AOTI achieved best-case speedups of up to 4.47x for the three-layer HSTU model and 5.93x for the eight-layer model under a 100% GPU KV-cache hit rate, relative to the same AOTI configuration without KV caching.
This post shows you how to move an HSTU generative recommender from PyTorch development to production inference with NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton, PyTorch AOTI, and FlexKV. You will learn how to export and ahead-of-time compile the model, validate the resulting deployment artifact in Python and native C++, and serve it through Dynamo-Triton without rewriting the model for a separate runtime.
It also examines how GPU-backed KV caching reduces repeated computation and presents benchmarks demonstrating up to 5.93x lower latency, highlighting the practical performance benefits of this deployment workflow.
Why use HSTUs for generative recommendation?
HSTUs were introduced for GR workloads that operate over high-cardinality, nonstationary event streams. In a traditional recommender system, retrieval and ranking are often built from a collection of specialized models and feature pipelines. GRs instead model recommendation as a sequential prediction problem, allowing the model to reason over user context, item history, action history, and candidate items in one sequence-aware architecture.
In the NVIDIA HSTU ranking example, the model input is built from categorical tokens. Contextual tokens represent user-side information, item tokens represent items, and optional action tokens represent user interactions with those items.
The HSTU preprocessing path retrieves embeddings, interleaves item and action embeddings when action tokens are present, appends contextual information, and applies positional encoding. HSTU blocks then process the sequence, and a prediction head produces multitask ranking outputs.
This structure is well-suited for recommendation systems where recency, order, and repeated interaction patterns matter. However, it also means inference can become expensive when each request repeatedly processes long historical sequences. Production systems need to preserve HSTU modeling benefits while reducing redundant computation during serving.
Why is serving large sequential recommenders challenging?
Serving large sequential recommenders is different from serving a small dense ranking model. The serving stack must handle jagged sequence inputs, large categorical embedding state, long histories, and request patterns where the same user may return repeatedly with only a small amount of new information. Recomputing the full key-value state for a user history on every request wastes work and increases latency.
This is where KV caching becomes important. A KV cache stores reusable key-value data from prior sequence computation, allowing the model to avoid recomputing cached portions of the user history. For recommender inference, this is particularly useful when a user’s long-term history remains mostly stable while new candidate items or recent actions arrive.
The NVIDIA HSTU inference workflow includes a KVCacheManager that uses GPU memory and host storage for KV data caches. The GPU cache is organized as a paged KV data table and supports lookup, allocation, append, and eviction. When GPU cache space is constrained, older users can be evicted according to an LRU-style policy. Host-side storage provides another tier for cached KV data, and the workflow includes a FlexKV-backed backend for the KV-cache runtime.
The HSTU attention kernel can consume KV data from the paged cache, and the exported inference path includes cache-aware custom operations for lookup, allocation, onboarding, appending, and offloading. This allows the serving path to preserve the model’s sequence semantics while reducing redundant computation.
PyTorch AOTI for native inference
The Pytorch AOTI (Ahead-of-Time Inductor) workflow starts from a PyTorch model and exports it using torch.export and PyTorch AOTI. AOTI compiles the model ahead of time into a package that can be loaded by a native C++ runtime. This reduces Python runtime overhead and provides a deployment-friendly artifact for the Dynamo-Triton PyTorch AOTI backend.
The exported model package contains the AOTI model archive plus metadata and embedding table files. In the NVIDIA example, the embedding implementation combines DynamicEmb inference embedding tables and NV Embedding Cache that reduces GPU memory usage by storing only the popular embeddings in GPU memory while keeping the entire table in CPU memory. The export path writes layer metadata and embedding table data alongside the compiled .pt2 archive so the model can be loaded without unnecessary duplicate embedding table copies.
The workflow validates the same exported artifacts in multiple ways. Python export scripts generate the package and replay tensors. Native C++ executables load and replay the exported model for correctness and performance validation. The Dynamo-Triton deployment then uses the same AOTI package and replay path, which helps keep development validation and production serving aligned.
Dynamo-Triton deployment path
Dynamo-Triton provides the production serving layer for the exported HSTU model. The AOTI deployment uses the Dynamo-Triton PyTorch backend with platform: "torch_aoti". This allows Dynamo-Triton to load and serve the ahead-of-time compiled PyTorch model package.
The full workflow includes the following five stages:
- Build the required custom operators and runtime libraries
- Export the HSTU ranking model with PyTorch AOTI
- Start the FlexKV-backed KV-cache service
- Validate the exported artifacts with native C++ replay
- Serve the exported KV-cache AOTI model with Dynamo-Triton
This approach is important because recommender serving requires more than just a fast model kernel. Dynamo-Triton brings model repository management, request handling, backend integration, metrics, and deployment structure. AOTI brings a lower-overhead compiled model artifact. NV Embedding Cache lowers GPU memory requirements by keeping only the hot parts of embedding tables in GPU memory. FlexKV reduces recomputation for long user histories by caching attention blocks. Together these form a serving stack aimed at realistic generative recommender inference.
Benchmarking HSTU serving latency
This benchmark compares HSTU serving latency across Dynamo-Triton backends, model sizes, batch sizes, and KV-cache states.
The goal is to quantify the performance benefits of the production HSTU serving stack. It compares the Dynamo-Triton PyTorch AOTI backend with the Python backend, measures the additional latency reduction from GPU KV caching, and evaluates how those benefits scale across model depths and batch sizes. Ultimately, it shows developers the performance they can expect when moving from uncached Python-based inference to compiled, cache-aware HSTU deployment with Dynamo-Triton.
The benchmark results in recsys-examples use the KuaiRand-1K ranking configuration on a single GPU. The model structure includes three-layer and eight-layer HSTU variants, hidden size 512, four attention heads, BF16 model weights, BF16 KV cache, maximum history sequence length of 8,192 in total (4,096 item plus action pairs) history stream, maximum candidate sequence length of 100, and six contextual features. The effective sequence length before alignment is 8,298 tokens, exported with a maximum aligned sequence length of 8,320.
The benchmark protocol reports latency per logical request. For the Dynamo-Triton AOTI benchmark, each Dynamo-Triton call contains one logical batch, and latency per logical request is calculated by dividing end-to-end pass time by the number of Dynamo-Triton calls times the logical batch size. Dataset loading, validation, rebatching, user-ID generation, server startup, warmup, and post-warmup sleep are excluded from the measured time.
The hardware used for the Dynamo-Triton backend comparison and batch-size results is an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition GPU.
Dynamo-Triton backend comparison
At Dynamo-Triton batch size 2, PyTorch AOTI improves latency over the Dynamo-Triton Python backend even without KV-cache hits. With hits from the GPU KV cache of 20 GB, the latency improvement is significantly larger.
These results show two different gains. First, AOTI reduces serving overhead compared with the Python backend. Second, KV cache hits reduce model work by reusing cached sequence state. The cache benefit is especially visible on the deeper eight-layer model, where avoiding recomputation has more impact.
Batch-size scaling with AOTI and KV cache
The PyTorch AOTI backend results by batch size show that KV caching becomes increasingly effective as logical batch size grows.
At batch size 8, the three-layer HSTU model reaches 0.423 ms latency per logical request with GPU KV-cache hits. The eight-layer HSTU model reaches 0.678 ms. These are strong results for long-sequence ranking inference and demonstrate the value of combining compiled model execution with cache-aware serving.
What are the benefits of accelerating HSTU GR inference?
Recommendation systems operate under tight latency budgets. Additional ranking latency can affect page-load times, feed responsiveness, and ad-serving deadlines. Meanwhile, increasingly sequence-aware and personalized models can require more inference compute, particularly as user histories grow.
The HSTU serving workflow combines complementary technologies to address this challenge. HSTU provides the generative recommendation architecture, PyTorch AOTInductor produces an ahead-of-time compiled deployment artifact, FlexKV-backed KV caching enables reuse of previously computed attention state, and NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton provides the production serving environment.
This approach is especially valuable when successive requests share an unchanged prefix of a user’s interaction history. Rather than recomputing attention over that portion of the sequence, the model can reuse its cached key-value state and compute only what is required for newly appended tokens. The potential savings increase with longer sequences and deeper models, where repeated computation across multiple HSTU layers would otherwise add significant latency.
Get started accelerating HSTU GR inference
You can reproduce and extend this workflow from the NVIDIA/recsys-examples GitHub repo. The HSTU overview introduces the GR model structure, including contextual tokens, item tokens, action tokens, embedding tables, HSTU blocks, and prediction heads.
The AOTI inference guide walks through building the required images and libraries, preparing KuaiRand-1K data, training a checkpoint, exporting the KV-cache AOTI model, validating it with C++ replay, packaging the Dynamo-Triton runtime image, and replaying requests through the Dynamo-Triton server.
To learn more, check out these related resources:
Acknowledgments
This post is a cross-functional effort across several NVIDIA teams. We would like to thank J, Runchu Zhao, Yulu Liu, Lin Hu, Zhuofan Li, Jacob Subag, and Tomer Bar-On for their contributions.

articles.title: Mitigating Threats With Pre-Silicon Security Verification
articles.text:
The types of threats that must be mitigated and a process to verify that designs are secure in real-world deployment.
The safety and security of the silicon chips ubiquitous in modern life have become prime considerations in semiconductor development. Functional safety is well understood, with numerous industry standards and a variety of established mechanisms embedded in silicon to ensure that systems do not misbehave due to environmental conditions or aging. Security is an equally important concern, but techniques to design secure chips have emerged relatively recently. This post discusses the types of threats that must be mitigated and a process to verify that designs are secure in real-world deployment.
Advocates for functional safety often cite the example of a chip failure causing an autonomous vehicle to crash. Just as this motivates designers to consider safety mechanisms, the specter of a malicious agent taking control of a vehicle and intentionally crashing it is equally terrifying. There have already been demonstrations that such actions are possible in certain cases. System-level security is often thought of as a software problem, such as preventing denial of service (DOS) and buffer overflow attacks. However, hardware-level threats must also be considered.
Silicon security is a complex topic. Preventing an agent from accessing a chip and altering its behavior is the goal, but there are at least two types of scenarios to consider. The first is making a system misbehave, such as the car crash example. Not all scenarios are this dramatic, but they still must be avoided. These include a burglar electronically unlocking a door, a competitor disabling the cooling system in a company’s warehouse, and a voyeur hacking into a webcam or smart speaker to spy on someone. Secure silicon means preventing all these bad situations.
The other type of security failure scenario is compromising private information. Data breaches can be due to unauthorized hardware access as well as software attacks. Personal identifiers, financial information, medical records, and other sensitive data can be compromised if the chips allow illegal access. Semiconductor designers must ensure that their devices remain secure in the presence of real-world threats, preventing both external control of systems and release of private information to the outside.
Humans have been hacking electronic systems for as long as they have existed, but the rise of the Internet meant that physical access was no longer required. The risk is now increasing even more with the rise of agentic AI. Several examples of agents under test breaking into other systems over the Internet have been in the news lately. There is every reason to believe that malicious actors will increasingly use AI agents for their attacks. This makes it more critical than ever to design secure chips.
Another challenge of silicon security is the wide range of ways that malicious agents can try to gain access. Sometimes called threat vectors, these methods vary over the silicon lifecycle and affect many parts of the semiconductor supply chain. At the architectural and RTL design stages, “Trojans” might be inserted into the design by a rogue designer or inadvertently incorporated via a third-party IP block. Someone who knows how to access and trigger a hardware Trojan can potentially make the chip do undesirable things.
Trojans can also potentially be inserted during design implementation, for example during logic synthesis or the place and route process. During the manufacturing process, wafer probing might reveal unintended data to aid in reverse engineering or cloning the design. Once the chip is included in an end product and deployed in the field, the scariest scenarios emerge. Trojans can be activated, side-channel leakage such as power and voltage variations can reveal private data, and faults can be injected via lasers, electromagnetic pulses, or power supply glitching.
Developing a secure chip that can mitigate all the threat vectors and scenarios outlined above is far from a simple proposition. It requires the support of many EDA tools in the development flow. The process starts with assessing possible threats, deciding how to model them, and developing a set of security requirements. The design phase includes using a set of reusable security IP components, each pre-verified, pre-certified, and silicon-proven. The designers certainly don’t want to introduce Trojans via IP that claims to improve silicon security.
The chip assembly process must ensure that these components are connected properly to provide their intended benefits. As the design evolves, it must be analyzed by advanced checks that look for security weaknesses. The verification phase employs a combination of static, formal, and simulation techniques to identify vulnerabilities to possible threats. Finally, implementation (layout, equivalence checking, static timing analysis, and power computation) must preserve security and ensure final hardware is tamper-proof. The result is end-to-end design, verification, and implementation for secure chip development with tamper-proof assurance.
Both the designers and the verification team play key roles in developing a secure chip design. Together, they develop a security verification plan in addition to a functional verification plan. They identify the parts of the design where security is critical, including registers holding private data and access points for secure blocks. The designers choose appropriate security IP and employ a variety of techniques to protect the critical portions of the design. They also run RTL-level linting and other static checks for potential design vulnerabilities.
Going beyond static checks requires the analytic power of formal verification and the scaling of simulation and emulation. The designers may assist in this effort, but it is mainly driven by the dedicated verification team. Formal methods can perform deeper analysis on the design to check for security issues. Formal verification can be applied early in the development process since no testbench is required, but it works best at the block level. For full SoC verification, simulation using constrained-random testbenches and functional coverage metrics is the primary solution.
Pre-silicon security verification has several goals:
Synopsys provides a complete solution for implementing secure silicon by design and for verifying that it can mitigate real-world threats in the field. The process starts with the Synopsys IP portfolio, which includes functionality such as root of trust, secure boot, secure keying, secure processing, secure interfaces, encryption, decryption, and authentication. These IP blocks are all inherently secure and validated by use in many previous chips. Of course, they must be connected properly into the overall design to provide the desired protection.
The designers write a lot of RTL code and integrate other types of IP blocks, and it is essential to know that all of this has been coded in a way that does not make them vulnerable to security threats. This is accomplished by checking for such vulnerabilities during the early RTL phase using the security checks in the Synopsys VC SpyGlass RTL static signoff platform. These checks do not require special verification knowledge and can be run easily by the designers every time they make RTL modifications.
The second phase of verification addresses the security of data at rest and in motion. For sign-off, the verification team must have evidence that security-critical data cannot be read illegally and leaked to unsecured destinations (confidentiality) or written from an unsecured source (integrity). The Formal Security Verification (FSV) app for Synopsys VC Formal verifies data security and prevents data leaks or integrity violations for sensitive data such as encryption keys, passwords, and biometric information inside secure modules.
The Synopsys VCS simulator has taint propagation (T-Prop) functionality that enables users to set, trace, and monitor “taints” that act as proxies for malicious attacks. This allows RTL simulation to verify how taints travel through the design (permeability) and how long they remain in the system (permanence). Simulation with taints detects design bugs that lead to security issues. The Synopsys Verdi debug and verification management solution displays taint simulation results in a way that is easy to understand.
The final step in verification security entails checking the design’s resiliency to tampering, such as high-precision bit-flips using laser fault injection. Modeling faults due to such attacks leverages the well-established methods for modeling manufacturing faults. The Synopsys VC Z01X fault injection and simulation solution shows the effects of these faults and verifies that they cannot compromise security at the silicon level.
Security is no longer a distant relative of functional safety: it is now a primary concern for semiconductors in many end applications. The complete development flow must ensure that the result is hardware that can do its job in the field without being vulnerable to attacks or leakage of private data. Verification using static, formal, and simulation methods is a key part of this process. The Synopsys pre-silicon security verification solution is a proven way to produce secure chips. A white paper is available with more details.

articles.title: Cisco warns of new SD-WAN zero-day exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Cisco released security updates to address a critical zero-day in the Catalyst SD-WAN Manager (tracked as CVE-2026-76504) that attackers are actively exploiting to escalate to admin privileges.
Formerly known as SD-WAN vManage, Catalyst SD-WAN Manager is network management software that lets admins monitor and manage up to 6,000 SD-WAN devices from a single dashboard.
"In September 2026, the Cisco PSIRT became aware of active exploitation of this vulnerability," the company warned on Wednesday. "Cisco strongly recommends that customers upgrade to a fixed software release to remediate this vulnerability."
The CVE-2026-76504 vulnerability affects all deployments regardless of system configuration, was found in API session-based authentication management, and allows unauthenticated attackers to access vulnerable systems remotely with admin privileges.
"This vulnerability is due to improper handling of URI encoding in an HTTP request, which allows the request to bypass an authentication rule that is intended to restrict access to a specific API endpoint," Cisco added.
"An attacker could exploit this vulnerability by sending a crafted HTTP request to the API of the affected system."
While the company didn't share further details regarding attacks exploiting CVE-2026-76504, it shared indicators of compromise (IOCs) warning admins that threat actors are using %6a as the URI-encoded character "j" in malicious requests.
It also advised security teams investigating potentially compromised SD-WAN systems to check the serviceproxy-access.log file located under /var/log/nms/containers/service-proxy and the vmanage-server.log file under /var/log/nms/for entries related to j_security_check from unknown or unauthorized IP addresses.
"For help determining if a Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager has been compromised, customers may open a case with the Cisco TAC," it added, advising admins first to collect admin-tech files to support the review.
| Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Release | First Fixed Release | 
|---|---|
| Earlier than 20.9 | Migrate to a fixed release. | 
| 20.9 | 20.9.10.1 | 
| 20.12 | 20.12.8.2 | 
| 20.15 | 20.15.6.1 | 
| 20.18 | 20.18.4.1 | 
| 26.1 | 26.1.2.1 | 
| 26.2 | 26.2.1 | 
Fifth actively exploited SD-WAN zero-day in 2026
CVE-2026-76504 is the fifth SD-WAN zero-day vulnerability actively exploited in the wild since the start of the year.
Cisco patched an SD-WAN Manager information disclosure security flaw (CVE-2026-20127) in February, exploited since at least 2023, and tagged a maximum-severity Catalyst SD-WAN Controller auth bypass flaw (CVE-2026-20182) as actively exploited in zero-day attacks to gain admin privileges on unpatched devices in May.
More recently, in early June, Cisco warned of two more SD-WAN zero-days (CVE-2026-20245 and CVE-2026-20262) that attackers exploited to gain root privileges on vulnerable systems.
Today, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) also added CVE-2026-76504 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog and ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure their systems against attacks by Saturday, October 3.
Since November 2021, CISA has tagged 90 Cisco vulnerabilities as exploited in the wild, including four in Cisco Catalyst SD-WAN Manager and seven abused by ransomware operations.
Build your security blueprint for AI-powered attacks
Join Mikko Hyppönen and security leaders from the NFL, CHANEL, and Atlassian for a two-hour digital summit on what AI-speed attacks change, what defenders should stop doing, and how to validate, decide, fix, and re-validate at machine speed.

articles.title: From Idea to Final Cut: A Practical Workflow for AI-Assisted Video Projects - Tech Guide
articles.text:
AI-assisted video tools are changing how small teams turn early ideas into finished visual stories. The most useful change is not simply faster rendering. It is the ability to explore several directions before committing expensive time to production.
A creator can compare framing, pacing, colour, camera movement and scene transitions while the project is still flexible. That makes planning more important, not less. When the workflow has clear stages, generated footage becomes a practical part of production rather than a collection of disconnected experiments.
A reliable process begins with the communication goal. Before writing prompts or choosing a visual style, the team should define what the viewer needs to understand, feel or do after watching. A product demonstration may need clarity and continuity. A short brand film may prioritise atmosphere. A social clip may need an immediate visual hook and a compact ending. This goal becomes the standard for judging every later choice, which prevents the project from drifting toward images that look impressive but do not serve the story.
Turn the brief into a visual outline
The next step is to convert the brief into a sequence of beats. Each beat should describe one clear unit of meaning: an establishing view, a character action, a product detail, a transition or a closing message. Keeping these units separate makes it easier to revise one part without rebuilding the whole video. It also helps the team identify which shots require precise continuity and which can be treated as flexible visual texture.
A simple shot table is often enough. Useful columns include purpose, subject, setting, action, camera behaviour, duration and continuity notes. The table does not need cinematic jargon. Plain descriptions such as “wide view of the workspace,” “slow push toward the device,” or “hands arrange the components” are easier to review. If a shot cannot be explained clearly in one or two sentences, its purpose may still be uncertain.
Design prompts as production instructions
Effective prompts work best when they describe observable details instead of broad praise. Words such as beautiful, premium or dynamic can mean different things to different people. More concrete guidance names the subject, environment, time of day, lighting direction, movement and intended mood. A team might specify soft window light, a fixed eye-level camera, restrained motion and a calm documentary tone. Those details give reviewers something specific to approve or change.
Prompt structure should stay consistent across related shots. Using the same order for subject, action, setting, camera and lighting makes variations easier to compare. It also reduces accidental changes. When testing a generation platform such as Wan 3.0, creators can keep most of the instruction stable and adjust one variable at a time. One pass might test camera motion, while another tests the time of day. Controlled comparisons reveal which instruction caused the visible difference.
Build continuity deliberately
Continuity is one of the hardest parts of assembling generated clips. Small shifts in wardrobe, props, screen layouts or background geometry become obvious when shots appear back to back. A continuity sheet can reduce these surprises. It should record recurring colours, materials, character details, object positions and environmental features. Reference frames can be labelled with the same shot names used in the outline so that everyone reviews the same visual target.
Camera logic also matters. If one shot shows a person looking toward the right side of the frame, the next shot should usually respect that direction unless the edit intentionally resets the viewer. Changes in lens feeling, horizon height or movement speed can make a sequence feel uneven even when each clip looks strong on its own. Reviewing low-resolution drafts in sequence is therefore more informative than judging isolated outputs.
Use short tests before long renders
Early tests should answer specific questions. Does the subject remain readable during motion? Is there enough negative space for captions? Does the action begin quickly enough for the intended platform? Short drafts are useful because they expose structural problems without consuming the full production budget. Once timing and composition are approved, the team can create longer or higher-quality versions with greater confidence.
It is helpful to name each iteration consistently. A filename can include the scene number, shot number, version and the variable being tested. For example, a label might identify a second camera-motion test for shot three. This small habit prevents confusion when many similar clips are exported. A shared review note should record why one version was selected, not merely that it was selected.
Edit for rhythm and clarity
Generated footage still benefits from conventional editing discipline. A strong edit removes repeated information, enters each shot as late as practical and leaves as soon as the idea is clear. Music should support the pace instead of forcing every cut onto a beat. Natural pauses can help viewers process a product feature or a change in location. When a transition attracts more attention than the message, a simpler cut is often more effective.
Sound design can also create unity between clips made at different times. A consistent room tone, subtle environmental effects and carefully balanced music help separate images feel as though they belong to one world. Dialogue and voice-over should remain understandable on ordinary speakers, not only on headphones. Captions are worth preparing early because their placement may affect framing and the amount of safe space required around important subjects.
Review technical and editorial risks
Before publication, the team should check more than resolution. Faces, hands, logos, written text and reflections deserve close inspection. Background details can change unexpectedly, and fast motion may hide defects that become visible when paused. Any claim shown or spoken in the video should be verified. If a sequence represents a real product, location or person, the final edit should avoid implying features or events that were not confirmed.
Rights and permissions are equally important. Teams should understand the terms for the tools, source images, music, fonts and voice assets they use. Internal records should identify where key materials came from and who approved the final version. This documentation is especially useful when a campaign is adapted later for another market or channel.
Prepare versions for real viewing conditions
One master edit rarely fits every destination. A horizontal version may work for a website, while vertical and square crops may be needed for social feeds. Reframing should be planned rather than left to automatic cropping. Important subjects, captions and interface details must remain visible in each aspect ratio. Testing on a phone can reveal text that looked readable on a large monitor but feels too small in normal use.
Compression deserves a final check as well. Fine textures, gradients and rapid motion can break down after a platform processes the upload. A short test export helps identify these problems before the full release. Teams should keep a high-quality master, a clean version without captions and the project notes so future updates do not require starting from zero.
A repeatable process creates better experiments
AI-assisted video production works best when experimentation sits inside a clear decision process. Define the communication goal, outline the visual beats, write concrete prompts, test one variable at a time and review clips in sequence. Then apply familiar editing, sound, rights and delivery checks. The result is not only a stronger video. It is a workflow the team can explain, repeat and improve with every project.

articles.title: Lefant se adelanta a la Fiesta de Ofertas Prime Amazon con descuentazos de hasta el 77 % en sus robots aspiradores
articles.text:
En apenas unos días, tendremos una nueva Fiesta de Ofertas Prime de Amazon. Ya tenemos varios dispositivos que cuentan con oferta anticipada, por lo que no tenemos que esperar hasta la semana que viene para lanzarnos a por ellos. Si estás buscando un nuevo robot aspirador, entonces puede que te encaje en casa uno de los que tiene Lefant con descuento ahora mismo.
Lefant M210 Omni
Ahora mismo tenemos muy buenas opciones dentro del catálogo de esta marca, independientemente de cuáles sean nuestras necesidades. Justo a continuación, os dejamos cinco de sus robots aspiradores en oferta más destacados que estarán disponibles únicamente hasta el 7 de octubre:

Empezamos por el M5 Pro, un robot aspirador con 23.000 Pa de potencia de succión y un sistema que hace que el rodillo mopa se vaya limpiando continuamente mientras friega para no arrastrar la suciedad de una habitación a otra. También cuenta con un sistema de guiado con 9 sensores con rango de 190 grados pensado para que el robot no vaya dándose cabezazos por toda la casa.
El PVP del mismo es 599,99 euros, pero está rebajado hasta los 249,99 euros. Usando el código '5SOVIQKV', se queda en 229,99 euros.
Lefant M210 Omni

articles.title: Pagaille sur l'iPhone : des milliers d’applications iOS plantent à cause… de Google
articles.text:
Des milliers d’applications iOS ont soudainement planté dès que les utilisateurs tentaient de les ouvrir. Du côté des développeurs, la situation a semé la panique. Certains d’entre eux ont pensé qu’il s’agissait d’un problème au niveau du logiciel ou d’une attaque. En réalité, ce problème qui a touché des applications iOS trouve son origine… chez Google. Un correctif a depuis été déployé, mais certaines applications peuvent encore planter.
Des milliers d’applications iOS ont commencé à planter
Des milliers d’applications iOS ont commencé à planter, et la cause se situe du côté de Google. Pour être plus précis, ce plantage massif a pour origine un problème affectant le kit de développement logiciel Firebase de Google. Bon nombre d’applications iOS dépendent de Firebase iOS et de Google Analytics pour fonctionner et bénéficier de statistiques d’utilisation.
Mais les développeurs n’étaient pas au courant de cette explication lorsque les plantages ont commencé. Certains d’entre eux ont cru qu’ils avaient commis une erreur et ont ainsi remué ciel et terre pour tenter de régler le problème au plus vite, notamment en dépensant de l’argent dans des jetons d’IA. En réalité, ils ne pouvaient rien faire. Seul Google pouvait résoudre la situation.
Google a déployé un correctif, sans préciser l’origine du problème
Google s’est montré très réactif en déployant un correctif quelques heures après le début du problème. Cependant, des plantages ont continué après le déploiement du correctif en raison des anciennes données encore présentes dans le cache. Les plantages d’application iOS ont donc considérablement diminué, mais peuvent encore tout de même survenir.
Et si l’entreprise de Mountain View s’est montrée très réactive dans cette affaire, elle n’a pas expliqué avec précision l’origine du problème. Le tableau de bord d’état de Firebase n’a d’ailleurs indiqué aucune anomalie. Nous savons seulement que l’incident est en lien avec un kit de développement logiciel Firebase. Quoi qu’il en soit, le problème a été résolu, ou devrait l’être complètement très prochainement.

articles.title: Apple lanzaría más dispositivos durante el año y este sería el plan de John Ternus para lograrlo
articles.text:
John Ternus, el nuevo director ejecutivo de Apple, prepara una reorganización que busca terminar con la dependencia de la compañía a sus tradicionales eventos de primavera y otoño. Según un reporte de Bloomberg, el sucesor de Tim Cook quiere que la empresa lance dispositivos con mayor frecuencia a lo largo del año, en lugar de concentrar casi todas las novedades en septiembre.
El cambio de estrategia responde a la necesidad de competir en la era de la inteligencia artificial, un terreno en el que Apple llegó tarde.
PUBLICIDAD
Cómo sería el nuevo calendario de lanzamientos de Apple
El plan contempla romper con la coreografía que Apple siguió durante años: septiembre para el iPhone y el Apple Watch, la primavera para renovaciones de iPad y Mac, y octubre para completar la temporada con nuevas computadoras.
La idea de Ternus es que, si un producto está terminado, la compañía lo presente sin esperar a la siguiente ventana comercial. Eso permitiría distribuir la atención mediática durante todo el año y evitar que demasiadas novedades compitan entre sí en pocas semanas.
Los primeros indicios de este cambio llegarían a comienzos de 2027, cuando se esperan los anuncios de los iPhone 18, 18e y el modelo Air 2. En septiembre, Apple ya había presentado únicamente los modelos Pro y Pro Max de la serie 18, junto al iPhone Duo, el primer teléfono plegable de la marca. Ese desdoblamiento funciona como indicio de la estrategia que impulsa el nuevo CEO.
PUBLICIDAD
El plegable llegó además en el primer evento encabezado por Ternus, de cara al vigésimo aniversario del iPhone que se cumplirá el año próximo. Para esa fecha, la compañía también planea lanzar sus primeras gafas inteligentes y unos AirPods con cámara, con lanzamientos escalonados durante el año que impulsarían los ingresos de sus divisiones de hardware y servicios.
Cómo sería el esquema de trabajo para lograr este ritmo de lanzamiento
Para lograr esa velocidad, Ternus no solo busca mover fechas de presentación. También pretende reducir los puestos de mando intermedio y acercar a los ingenieros directamente a los altos ejecutivos, con menos capas de gestión y decisiones más rápidas.
En su primer memo interno como máximo responsable de Apple, recogido por MacRumors, Ternus prometió a los empleados una semana “fenomenal” de lanzamientos. El mensaje llegó el 1 de septiembre de 2026, día en el que asumió oficialmente el mando tras Tim Cook.
PUBLICIDAD
En una presentación interna, el CEO defendió la idea de que Apple debe conseguir más resultados con menos empleados, según una diapositiva sobre el crecimiento de la plantilla mostrada a sus equipos. Esa filosofía ya se tradujo en recortes: directores y gestores de programas de ingeniería recibieron varias semanas para encontrar otra posición dentro de la compañía o abandonarla.
Los ajustes alcanzaron también áreas como Siri, Vision Pro, el software de inteligencia artificial y Fitness+, divisiones que ya habían sufrido bajas desde que comenzó la reestructuración a inicios de 2025.
Cómo afectaría este plan a los gastos y la calidad de Apple
La aceleración de los lanzamientos tiene una segunda lectura vinculada al dinero. Con el crecimiento del negocio de servicios en desaceleración, la dirección pidió reducir el gasto en marketing y limitar los incrementos presupuestarios previstos para 2027.
PUBLICIDAD
La consecuencia es una compañía que intenta aumentar el ritmo de entrega de productos mientras mantiene presupuestos más contenidos y reorganiza su estructura interna, algo que contrasta con la lógica habitual de invertir más recursos para producir más.
Empleados consultados advirtieron que modificar prácticas de desarrollo tan arraigadas podría tomar años, según Bloomberg. Reducir la burocracia puede permitir que los equipos de ingeniería trabajen con mayor agilidad, pero aumentar el número de lanzamientos mientras se limitan las contrataciones también abre una duda sobre hasta dónde puede acelerar Apple sin afectar la calidad de sus productos.
Esa tensión entre velocidad y nivel de acabado, uno de los rasgos que históricamente distinguió a los productos de la compañía, quedará expuesta con mayor claridad cuando avance el cronograma de lanzamientos previsto para 2027.

articles.title: Home interiors startup Gravity raises $15M led by 3one4 Capital and Info Edge Ventures
articles.text:
Home interiors startup Gravity raises $15M led by 3one4 Capital and Info Edge Ventures
Gravity will use this funding round to strengthen its technology, distribution and key-account infrastructure, and support category expansion.
Home interiors startup Gravity has raised $15 million in funding led by 3one4 Capital and Info Edge Ventures, with participation from Alteria Capital, Genesia Ventures and angel investors. This funding round was a combination of equity and debt.
Gravity will use this funding round to strengthen its technology, distribution and key-account infrastructure, support category expansion, build brand capabilities and provide the working capital needed to scale the platform over time.
Founded by former Livspace executives, Saurabh Jain and Lalit Mittal, Gravity is building common infrastructure for India's interior materials ecosystem by bringing together specialist businesses across the kitchen and wardrobe segment with a shared technology, distribution, key-account management and operating backbone.
Gravity Co-founder Saurabh Jain said, “Over the last decade, organised design and execution have transformed the home interiors market. However, the materials layer behind every project remains fragmented and complex. Designers, studios and suppliers continue to navigate multiple stakeholders, systems and processes to get projects delivered. We are building Gravity to make sourcing simpler, more dependable and more efficient through a platform designed around the needs of the industry. Our focus is to combine product depth with strong service, availability and execution at scale.”
According to Gravity, there is a structural shift underway in India's home interiors market. While designers, architects, modular showrooms and design-and-build studios increasingly influence material decisions, the supply landscape remains fragmented across dealers, distributors and single-category suppliers.
Gravity aims to simplify sourcing for these customers while improving availability, service levels, fulfilment and pricing visibility across categories.
Gravity co-founder Lalit Mittal said, “Designers and studios today influence a significant share of material decisions, yet managing sourcing across categories remains time-consuming and operationally challenging. Gravity brings together common capabilities across technology, distribution, procurement and customer service, enabling a better experience for both category businesses and specifiers.”
As part of its future plans, Gravity plans to expand beyond kitchens and wardrobes into adjacent interior systems, leveraging its shared operating infrastructure to serve a wider set of material categories.

articles.title: "Ce n'est pas l'IA, c'est vous" : OpenAI visé par la première plainte au monde pour piratage commis par une IA
articles.text:
"Ce n'est pas l'IA, c'est vous" : OpenAI visé par la première plainte au monde pour piratage commis par une IA
700 agents d'intelligence artificielle se coordonnent seuls, piratent une plateforme majeure, et personne chez OpenAI n'appuie sur le bouton d'arrêt. Une ONG de quatre salariés vient de déposer plainte à San Francisco, armée d'une loi californienne entrée en vigueur en janvier 2026 : désormais, une entreprise ne peut plus se défendre en disant que son IA a agi toute seule.
Quatre employés, zéro financement de l'industrie de l'IA, et l'ambition de créer un précédent mondial. LASST, fondée à Washington par Tyler Whitmer, a choisi de frapper là où le droit californien offre ses armes les plus tranchantes : le Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act (CDAFA, article 502 du code pénal de Californie) et l'Unfair Competition Law (UCL), qui qualifie de déloyale toute pratique commerciale dont la gravité du préjudice dépasse l'utilité.
La plainte, déposée avec le cabinet Gerstein Harrow LLP, vise OpenAI Group PBC et la Fondation OpenAI. Elle ne réclame aucune indemnité. L'objectif est une injonction judiciaire : interdire aux agents d'OpenAI d'accéder à des systèmes tiers sans autorisation et prohiber les pratiques de développement jugées dangereuses pour le public, dans un secteur où les propres créateurs de ces technologies alertent sur des "risques existentiels pour l'humanité".
	
Les entreprises d'IA construisent des agents qui agissent de manière autonome. Le droit californien est limpide : les entreprises ne peuvent pas échapper à leur responsabilité pour ce que font leurs agents.
La loi AB 316, arme fatale contre la défense "ce n'est pas nous, c'est l'IA"
L'argument juridique le plus redoutable de la plainte repose sur l'article 1714.46 du code civil californien, issu de la loi AB 316 entrée en vigueur le 1er janvier 2026. Ce texte interdit formellement à un défendeur d'invoquer l'autonomie de son intelligence artificielle pour se dédouaner. Développeurs de modèles fondateurs, intégrateurs, entreprises qui déploient la technologie : toute la chaîne de valeur est concernée.
LASST affirme que des employés d'OpenAI avaient connaissance des communications entre agents et ont poursuivi les évaluations malgré les signaux d'alerte.
La plainte parle d'un accès "en connaissance de cause ou par aveuglement volontaire". Environ 1 200 agents auraient utilisé un forum de discussion non autorisé au sein de l'infrastructure d'OpenAI, et quelque 700 d'entre eux auraient coordonné l'attaque contre Hugging Face, volant des identifiants, téléchargeant des fichiers malveillants et compromettant le contrôle de systèmes critiques, comme le détaille la chronologie technique publiée par Hugging Face.
Les raisonnements des agents, rédigés en anglais lisible, documentaient explicitement leur intention de pirater la plateforme.
Au-delà de Hugging Face, une série d'incidents invoqués par la plainte
LASST ne se limite pas au piratage de juillet. La plainte cite également l'attaque contre le gestionnaire de paquets RubyGems, survenue deux mois avant l'incident Hugging Face, ainsi que l'accès non autorisé au portail statistique du système de santé australien Medicare en juin, qu'OpenAI n'avait signalé à Canberra que trois mois plus tard. Des agents ChatGPT déployés ont aussi ciblé plusieurs sites du gouvernement américain, dont le Census Bureau et le département de l'Éducation.
	
Quand ces agents causent des dommages, quelqu'un doit en être responsable. Nous sommes devant le tribunal pour nous assurer que ce soit l'entreprise qui les a construits.
L'avocat Charlie Gerstein, du cabinet Gerstein Harrow, résume la logique de la plainte : "Tout le monde s'accorde à dire que le piratage de Hugging Face était illégal. OpenAI va découvrir à ses dépens que c'est vrai."
OpenAI n'a pas répondu aux sollicitations de la presse.
