articles.title: AI companies want to embed safety evaluators, but countries need their own
articles.text:
The growing number of instances of artificial intelligence agents hacking the websites of governments and other institutions is a warning to countries using American models to do their own safety evaluations, experts said at a Rest of World event in New York last week.
An OpenAI agent hacked into an Australian national healthcare database and accessed “public and non-public files,” Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said last week. It was the first such reported case. Days later, OpenAI said it had alerted “dozens” of global institutions that its AI agents had acted improperly to get information from their websites, sometimes circumventing security measures.
The disclosures came on the heels of other incidents reported by OpenAI, Anthropic, and Meta in recent months, prompting Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to call for an industrywide slowdown in AI development. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and xAI CEO Elon Musk backed his call, even as President Donald Trump rejected it.
Leaving AI safety in the hands of a few companies is a threat to the sovereignty of nations, in particular smaller countries that lack the resources to assess the models or demand greater accountability, Amba Kak, co-executive director at AI Now Institute, an independent research organization, said at the Rest of World event.
The Australia hack is “another example of the most shoddy, irresponsible cybersecurity hygiene on the part of some of the most powerful, wealthy source companies in the world,” she said. “The concentration of power is itself a safety risk.”
OpenAI said the Australia incident occurred in June, and that the company became aware of it in August, and informed the Australian government in September via an email to a generic inbox. It took OpenAI “way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable,” Albanese told reporters.
OpenAI was not “as fast as we would have liked, but we are trying to balance our desire for transparency with gaining a clear understanding from petabytes of agent activity logs, and working with impacted organizations,” Altman wrote on X.
Hours after it disclosed the incidents, OpenAI said it had decided to pause training of its most powerful models, and will resume training “only when we are confident that we have additional safeguards.” This week, the company said it would not release its newest AI model because of security concerns.
Equitable access, equitable outcomes
As AI adoption grows worldwide, every country needs to take safety into its own hands without relying on the U.S. or the AI companies for action, Rumman Chowdhury, chief executive of Humane Intelligence Public Benefit Corp., an independent testing and evaluation firm, said at the Rest of World event.
“I don’t think any of us think we live in a world in which AI models are adequately secure,” Chowdhury said. “Every minister and ambassador is saying, we’re putting AI in education, we’re using AI for healthcare. What I would love is for every single one of those ministers to be equally thinking about how they secure and ensure equitable access and equitable outcomes from AI implementation, rather than seeing this loss of control as ‘That is for the big, powerful countries [to sort].’”
OpenAI has said it is working with Anthropic and Google to establish a standards body, an idea initially proposed by Google DeepMind’s Demis Hassabis as a self-regulatory agency that would test the most powerful AI systems before they are released to the public. On Tuesday, President Trump said that top AI executives had agreed to voluntary standards aimed at reviewing AI systems and increasing industry oversight.
These measures do not account for the environments in which AI is deployed in low- and middle-income countries, which are very different from sandboxes in the U.S., said Kak.
“Even if these companies poured billions of dollars into making their models secure, we’re not dealing with the other side of the problem, which is how resilient are the environments in which these systems are being integrated,” she said. “Those costs are never going to be borne by these trillion-dollar companies. They’re going to be borne by hospitals, by schools, by banks in countries which are extremely unprepared.”
Many countries also lack the resources and expertise to do their own evaluations, Wafa Ben-Hassine, chief of the digital tech and human rights section at the Office of the U.N. High Commissioner for Human Rights, said at the Rest of World event.
“There is a dire lack of technical expertise, both in advanced economies as well as everywhere else,” Ben-Hassine said. Poorer nations can use the U.N. human rights impact assessments to ensure AI is deployed safely and securely.
“Human rights due diligence, human rights impact assessments … are quantifiable and proven ways of being able to have better products that reach people in a way that honors them and their human dignity,” she said.
Massive underinvestment
The debate over AI safety has divided the industry. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, whose chips power American AI models, said on a recent podcast that companies should not release products they cannot control, and that if they cannot contain models during testing, “we have to shut the labs down.”
The heads of Anthropic and OpenAI told the U.N. Security Council last week that nations must cooperate to develop international standards to manage AI risks.
Anthropic had earlier called for independent evaluations of AI models, and said that consulting firm Accenture will embed evaluators at Anthropic to “verify that it is keeping its safety commitments, and identify blind spots.” The companies will each invest at least $1 billion in building capacity for evaluations over the next five years, it said.
Separately, more than 25 countries recently endorsed a call for frontier AI companies to develop “mandatory pre-deployment testing and independent evaluation, with qualified evaluators granted sufficient access to assess risks.”
Still, AI safety evaluations are designed largely by the companies being evaluated, and the infrastructure is linguistically and geographically concentrated in the West. Without “standardized, rigorous, independent third-party assessment, similar to what exists for the pharmaceutical and aeronautical industries, assurance of safety largely depends on developer goodwill,” the U.N. Independent International Scientific Panel on AI noted in its report earlier this year.
Even in the U.S., there has been a “massive underinvestment in safety and security,” said Chowdhury, noting that Anthropic earmarks only about one-tenth of its training budget for securing its models. Yet AI companies describe their agents “going rogue” as though that outcome were unexpected, she said.
Chowdhury last week launched the Independent AI Evaluation Foundation to build independent, third-party checks of AI systems. For smaller countries and small and medium-sized businesses, “doing an evaluation seems like an insurmountable task because it has been framed as such, that they don’t know what questions they have to ask, they don’t have the tools to do the testing, they don’t have the people to do the work,” she said.
IAEF’s goal is to “build the infrastructure and the tooling to drive the costs down, and then upskilling the right people to be evaluators” in their own countries, Chowdhury said.
Ultimately, for nations that have been sidelined by the U.S.-China AI race, it is important to determine how safety is defined, Kak said.
“Let’s talk about all of the ways in which what safety means, or can mean, for the ordinary person, and where those interests are,” she said. “Similarly with sovereignty. We do need to resist industry capture in many forms.”

articles.title: Bezahlt und trotzdem Werbung? Was in den Abos von Netflix, Disney Plus und Prime Video läuft
articles.text:
Streaming ohne Werbung: Wo ist das eigentlich noch möglich?
Draußen ist es schon dunkel, der Herbstwind weht, es regnet. Drinnen läuft der Filmabend bei Snacks und gedimmtem Licht. Der Detektiv ist gerade dabei, den Mörder zu entlarven. „Der Täter ist …“ Schnitt. „Ralf Schumacher?!“ Das ist natürlich überspitzt dargestellt, dürfte aber für viele deutsche Streaming-Nutzer ein Stück weit zur Realität gehören. Denn laut einer Statista-Umfrage unter 4.781 Personen zwischen 18 und 64 Jahren nutzten 51 Prozent der Befragten zwischen Juni 2025 und Juni 2026 kostenlose und werbefinanzierte Streaming-Dienste, 46 Prozent zahlen für Angebote mit Werbung wie etwa Netflix.
Zwar waren mehrfache Angaben möglich und die Daten deuten laut dem Statistikdienst darauf hin, dass viele Streaming-Fans „mehrere Streamingabos abgeschlossen haben und dabei werbefinanzierte und werbefreie Angebote mischen“. (Schließlich gaben 41 Prozent an, für Angebote ohne Reklame zu zahlen.) Die Umfrage zeigt aber deutlich, dass Werbung mittlerweile für viele zum Erlebnis dazugehört.
Günstiger Einstieg ins Streaming nur mit Werbung
Bei der Strategie einzelner Anbieter verwundert das nicht. So kostet das Netflix-Standardabo mittlerweile 15,99 Euro im Monat. Zum Start in Deutschland 2014 waren es noch 8,99 Euro. Da wirkt der Abschluss des Werbeangebots wie der logische Schluss. Auf dem Papier gleichen sich die Leistungen schließlich. Streaming in Full-HD auf zwei Geräten gleichzeitig, Downloads sind möglich. Nur kostet das Werbeabo eben nur 6,99 Euro im Monat.
Andersherum läuft es bei Amazon Prime Video. Dort läuft seit Februar 2024 Werbung vor und zwischen Filmen und Serien – grundsätzlich für alle. Wer die Anzeigen nicht sehen will, kann sie für drei Euro monatlich abschalten. Auf die eine oder andere Weise haben fast alle großen Anbieter mittlerweile Werbeabos eingeführt. Sie sehen darin offenbar lukrative Wege, um mehr Einnahmen zu generieren. Doch dabei bleibt es nicht. Bei manchen Diensten gibt es auch in teureren Abo-Varianten Anzeigen zu sehen.
Netflix
Netflix gilt als einer der Pioniere für werbefinanziertes Streaming. Zum Start des sogenannten „Standard-Abos mit Werbung“ war die Rede davon, dass es pro Stunde Streaming vier bis fünf Minuten Reklame zu sehen geben soll. Allerdings hat das Unternehmen bei der Abo-Option in den vergangenen Jahren nachgedreht. Anders als in der Ankündigung beschrieben, sind Downloads mittlerweile (eingeschränkt) möglich, die Auflösung liegt jetzt bei Full-HD, nicht mehr bei HD.
Wie viel Werbung es heute zu sehen gibt, lässt sich pauschal nicht sagen. Das Unternehmen spricht nur noch von wenigen kurzen Unterbrechungen. Diese sollen immerhin nach Möglichkeit so gelegt werden, dass sie wichtige Szenen nicht unterbrechen. Bei manchen kürzlich veröffentlichten Filmen soll die Reklame nur vor Beginn der eigentlichen Wiedergabe gezeigt werden. Komplett ausgenommen davon sind Videospiele und Titel im Kinderprofil.
Disney Plus
Auch Disney Plus bietet ein reines Werbeabo an, bei dem Anzeigen vor und während des Streamings von Inhalten laufen. Allerdings weist der Streaming-Anbieter darauf hin, dass die Optionen Standard und Premium ebenfalls „Werbeinhalte, Werbung vor oder nach der Wiedergabe von Inhalten, Clips und Trailer für Disney-Inhalte, -Produkte und -Dienste sowie Inhalte mit Branding oder Sponsoring beinhalten“ können. Die Regelung ist neu und dürfte Kunden der teureren Optionen für 10,99 und 15,99 Euro nicht zwingend erfreuen.
Amazon Prime Video
Amazon macht für seinen Dienst Prime Video deutlich weniger Angaben. „Prime-Filme und -Serien enthalten begrenzte Werbung“, schreibt das Unternehmen als einzige echte Information. Anfangs soll es bis zu drei Minuten Reklame zu sehen gegeben haben. Mittlerweile habe sich der Wert verdoppelt, schrieb Adweek mit Verweis auf interne Dokumente bereits Mitte 2025. Eine offizielle Ankündigung gab es dazu nicht. Ohne Prime-Abo kostet der Dienst 8,99 Euro im Monat oder 89,90 Euro pro Jahr. Um die Werbung abzuschalten, werden drei Euro extra monatlich fällig.
HBO Max
Seit einigen Monaten ist HBO Max in Deutschland verfügbar. Der Dienst ist direkt mit einem Werbe-Abo gestartet. Wie viel Werbung es zu sehen gibt, verrät der Anbieter allerdings nicht. „Wenn du das Basis-Abo mit Werbung hast, wird vor und während On-Demand-Serien und -Filmen Werbung abgespielt“, ist die einzige Info, die HBO Max mitgibt. Wie bei anderen Diensten lässt sich die Werbung nicht vorspulen oder ganz überspringen. Wer keine Werbung sehen will, muss mindestens 11,99 Euro im Monat für das Standard-Abo zahlen.
Paramount Plus
Bei Paramount Plus enthalten laut einer Support-Seite alle Abo-Optionen Werbung. Abonnenten sehen dann vor und nach einzelnen Titeln Trailer für die Inhalte der Streaming-Plattform. Es gibt zusätzlich ein dediziertes Basic-Abo mit Werbeunterbrechungen in laufenden Filmen und Serien. Auch Paramount Plus nennt keine genaue Minutenanzahl für Reklame pro Streaming-Stunde. Auf Plattformen wie Reddit beschweren sich Nutzer aber schon jahrelang über zu viel Werbung. Eine Auswertung von Ampere Analysis, über die Business Insider berichtet, kommt zum Schluss, dass der Dienst in den USA neun Minuten Werbung pro Stunde zeigt. Mit dem deutschen Angebot ist das jedoch nicht vergleichbar.
RTL Plus
Bei RTL Plus gibt es in zwei von drei Abo-Optionen Werbung zu sehen. Wie viele Minuten genau pro Stunde verrät das Unternehmen nicht. Die Anzeigen laufen jeweils vor und während der abgespielten Inhalte. Beim Premium-Abo sollen sie jedoch „deutlich weniger“ zu sehen sein als beim günstigeren RTL Plus Basic, informiert der Sender auf einer Übersichtsseite. Auf der Auswahlseite für die Abos gibt der Anbieter zudem noch an, im Basic-Plan werde die Reklame „regelmäßig“ eingespielt. Wie der Name schon sagt, könnt ihr den Anzeigen mit der Option „Premium Werbefrei“ aus dem Weg gehen. Der Zugang kostet 12,99 Euro im Monat.
Apple TV Plus
Als einziger großer Streaming-Dienst verzichtet Apple TV Plus auf ein eigenes Werbe-Abo. Ein wenig Reklame gibt es trotzdem zu sehen. Vor Wiedergabe der Inhalte zeigt Apple Trailer, die auf Filme und Serien im eigenen Angebot hinweisen. Diese lassen sich aber auch überspringen. Auf der eigenen Webseite beschreibt das iPhone-Unternehmen seinen Dienst als werbefrei – abgesehen von den Werbeblöcken bei der Übertragung von Live-Sport-Events.
Als Kunde von Werbe-Abos Werbung umgehen
In vielen Fällen lassen sich Anzeigen trotz eines gebuchten Werbe-Abos auf zwei Wegen umgehen. Dafür muss man allerdings Einschnitte in Kauf nehmen. So wird in Kinderprofilen in der Regel keine Werbung ausgespielt. Diese bieten aber natürlich keinen Zugriff auf Blockbuster. Möglichkeit zwei ist der Download der Inhalte aufs Smartphone oder Tablet. Das ist oft aber nur eingeschränkt möglich. Im Werbe-Abo von Netflix darf man pro Monat nur 15 Titel herunterladen. Disney Plus bietet in der günstigen Option gar keine Möglichkeit zum Download an. Auf Smart-TVs fehlt die Funktion logischerweise.

articles.title: From Training to Production, NVIDIA and CoreWeave Close the Loop on Agentic AI
articles.text:
Building on nearly a decade of co-engineering, CoreWeave has built NVIDIA compute, networking and software into a cloud purpose-built for AI that’s still returning on investment across multiple generations of deployment. Now, CoreWeave is bringing the next generation of NVIDIA infrastructure to production.
At CoreWeave Fully Connected, running this week in San Francisco, CoreWeave announced availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems with Spectrum-X 102.4T Ethernet networking. Cognition, the applied AI lab behind the Devin AI software engineer, is the first customer running production workloads on Vera Rubin.
CoreWeave will also offer NVIDIA Vera, the first CPU built for AI agents. In addition, CoreWeave launched CoreWeave Forge, a connected environment for training, evaluating and improving models and agents on NVIDIA accelerated computing.
“NVIDIA accelerated computing delivers value across generations,” said Ian Buck, vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “CoreWeave’s NVIDIA V100 GPUs are still running customer workloads nearly a decade after Volta launched, even as CoreWeave brings Vera Rubin NVL72 into production. That’s the strength of the NVIDIA platform: infrastructure that keeps earning for years, and the flexibility to put the right GPU on the right workload.”
Cognition Runs on Vera Rubin NVL72 With 4.8x Higher Token Throughput
Cognition runs training, reinforcement learning and production inference for Devin on CoreWeave. The company scaled to thousands of GPUs on CoreWeave in nine months, powering Cognition inference workloads.
Earlier this month, CoreWeave received its first Vera Rubin NVL72 production racks. Shortly after, Cognition benchmarked Vera Rubin’s inference performance against a GB200 NVL72 baseline using a real-world software engineering workload. To generate this workload, it sampled a subset of tasks from FrontierCode and deployed AI agents to solve them.
In its early tests, Cognition saw Vera Rubin NVL72 deliver up to a 4.8x increase in total token throughput for SWE-2 inference workloads over GB200 NVL72. For Devin, those gains mean faster real-time code generation and more responsive multistep reasoning.
“Agentic coding is a complex workload: long contexts, high concurrency and token volumes where cost per token decides what we can ship,” said Silas Alberti, founding team at Cognition. “Having all of it on one platform, with NVIDIA and CoreWeave engineers who work the hard problems alongside ours, matters more to us than any single spec.”
CoreWeave Announces NVIDIA Vera Rubin Availability on CoreWeave Cloud
CoreWeave announced availability of NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 on CoreWeave Cloud, making it one of the first cloud providers to deliver the platform in customers’ hands.
Early-access customers can put the performance of NVIDIA’s full-stack AI factory platform to work quickly on CoreWeave Cloud. In days, CoreWeave stood up a production Vera Rubin cluster for Cognition, achieved as a result of the codesign and collaboration between NVIDIA and CoreWeave up and down the stack, from infrastructure to tokens served.
Capacity can be operated through CoreWeave Kubernetes Service, SUNK, CoreWeave Mission Control, CoreWeave Sandboxes and CoreWeave Inference.
NVIDIA Vera CPU to Come to CoreWeave Cloud, Tests Show More Than 3x Faster Agentic Sandbox Startups
Agentic AI puts pressure on infrastructure from two directions: serving agents demands low-latency compute at scale, while improving them through post-training requires thousands of isolated environments running at once.
NVIDIA Vera CPU is purpose-built for agentic workloads. For agentic AI, a key performance measure is how many isolated agent environments can run at once and how consistent and performant each one stays as that number grows.
CoreWeave’s deployment of Vera puts 128 CPUs and 11,264 cores in a single rack, enough for more than 11,000 concurrent environments at one core each. With CoreWeave Sandboxes, these environments are hardware-isolated and run alongside the training jobs they support, with Spectrum-X Ethernet switches and BlueField-4 DPUs ensuring secure, high-performance, secure agent communication at low latency.
In testing, CoreWeave achieved more than 3x faster agent sandbox startup times on NVIDIA Vera CPUs, accelerating and scaling its sandboxes, an execution layer for reinforcement learning (RL), agent tool use and model evaluation that let AI teams run code in isolated environments on CoreWeave. On Terminal-Bench, CoreWeave saw a 1.7x performance gain on Vera CPU across all passing tasks.
CoreWeave Forge: Closing the AI Loop From Production Back to Training
Models and agents improve by running a loop: production behavior informs the next training run, and each evaluation sharpens the next version. This loop has historically been split across tools from different vendors, with signal lost at every handoff.
CoreWeave Forge unifies Weights & Biases, post-training expertise from OpenPipe and the open source marimo notebook project in one connected environment built for continuous model and agent improvement. It stays open across models, frameworks and clouds.
New and expanded capabilities available include:
- CoreWeave ARIA — now generally available — helps users learn, research, code and iterate across the AI loop, analyzing runs, proposing experiments, recommending code changes and storing them in GitHub, and bringing back actionable evidence that analyzes experiment data, surfaces what drove a change and proposes the next experiments to run.

articles.title: Workplace AI adoption accelerates among Indigenous peoples | BetaKit
articles.text:
Indigenous people are using AI at nearly twice the rate of their non-Indigenous colleagues in some areas of the workplace, a new report from Toronto Metropolitan University (TMU) shows.
The news: The report, which examined the broad experiences of Indigenous people in the workplace, found that AI adoption has grown faster among Indigenous people across a variety of education levels and employment types.
From the source: Conducted between March and April of 2025, the report is part of the Survey on Employment and Skills—a project designed to explore Canadians’ experiences with the changing nature of work. Over the survey period, researchers engaged 281 First Nations, Métis, and Inuit people. Individuals between ages 15 and 54 represented the largest cohort.
The context: Led by TMU’s Diversity Institute, with research carried out by Environics Institute for Survey Research, the federally funded report found that both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people are using AI at work to improve productivity. However, Indigenous respondents were far more likely to report higher rates of familiarity with using AI in the workplace, with 32 percent of Indigenous respondents saying they were “very familiar” with AI programs versus 17 percent of non-Indigenous respondents. Likewise, Indigenous workers showed a higher degree of productivity gains, reporting a 46 percent increase versus 30 percent in other groups. They also reported a higher instance of accessing AI-related training programs.
The report found that AI use among both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people varied considerably across education levels. For those with a high-school-level education, Indigenous AI use dwarfs its counterpart at 25 percent to five percent. That dichotomy repeats among those involved in apprenticeship programs. At the university level, the numbers flip, with higher AI use by non-Indigenous workers.
Final thought: TMU’s report doesn’t provide concrete evidence on what is driving these differences in AI adoption levels, admitting that more research is needed to determine whether patterns reflect the types of roles Indigenous workers more commonly hold, or where they work. It does reference some potential variables, including higher public-sector representation and younger workforce demographics.
Workplace AI adoption is on the rise in Canada more broadly, with Statistics Canada reporting that 30 percent of Canadian workers had used AI at work within the past 12 months. That number grew from 18 percent in 2024.
Feature image courtesy Unsplash. Photo by Daniil Komov.

articles.title: This very fancy e-bike is one of the first to go semi-solid state
articles.text:
The Lemmo 3 is the first cargo bike from the respected German e-bike maker. This premium, step-through longtail is a slightly less insane take on Rivian’s Also TM-B, with one major advantage: It’s one of the first electric bikes to feature a semi-solid state battery.
This very fancy e-bike is one of the first to go semi-solid state
The Lemmo 3 has more range, fewer explosions.
The Lemmo 3 has more range, fewer explosions.
Semi-solid state batteries are far safer than traditional lithium-ion batteries. Their gel-like composition offers improved energy density, with far less risk of thermal runaway. That translates to improved range and longevity from a more compact battery that’s unlikely to catch fire when left charging overnight in your house or business. The semi-solid state electrolyte even remains stable when punctured in a crash.
The Lemmo 3 is fitted with a massive 960Wh battery promising up to 180km (110 miles) of range. And by going with a semi-solid state chemistry, the company claims the battery is 20 percent smaller and lighter while still offering 30 percent longer lifespan. The removable battery can also power your AC appliances (up to 1000W) and USB-C devices (up to 66W) once you arrive at your destination, similar to Cake’s now-defunct Ösa.
The Lemmo 3 is being marketed as an eSUV just like the Amflow TL Carbon I reviewed. But this very heavy full suspension cargo bike will feel more comfortable on daily commutes to daycare, work, and stores than weekend single tracks. The bike weighs 39kg (86 pounds) with the 5kg (11 pound) battery installed.
Instead of doing something proprietary, Lemmo made its longtail compatible with MIK HD accessories. These include a wide variety of child seats, bags, and boxes that can be mounted on the rear rack. It can handle a 200kg (441lb) total load, with 80kg (176lbs) supported in the rear and 20kg (44lbs) on the front rack.
A quick-adjust saddle and handlebar makes the Lemmo 3 easily shareable, supporting riders from 155cm (5 feet 1 inch) to 195cm (6 feet 5 inches). The bike is fitted with wide tires on a 24-inch front wheel paired with a smaller 20-inch wheel in the back.
Powering this beast is a rear-hub motor (750W in the US, 500W Canada, 250W for Europe). It can deliver up to 90Nm of torque to get heavy loads rolling or to help surmount hills. Naturally, there’s AI baked in as well. The motor and e-derailleur combine data from a variety of sensors to “feed an adaptive Al model that selects the optimal gear in real time, creating a natural, responsive, and effortless ride.” That sounds expensive to fix when the drivetrain eventually needs servicing. The motor can also be paired with a 3-speed auto-shifting gearbox and belt drive for flatter environments.
Other features include fully integrated lighting (with turn signals and brake lights), a 3.5-inch touchscreen, a USB-C port to charge your phone, OTA updates, rear-facing radar to alert you of approaching vehicles, and hydraulic brakes that apply stopping power to both wheels simultaneously when pulling just one brake lever. Security features include embedded frame and battery locks and GPS / LTE tracking.
The Lemmo 3 already has a teaser page up on Kickstarter that says “launching soon” for the EU, UK, US, and Canada. You can reserve it now for a refundable deposit of €39.90, which locks you into tax-exclusive pricing of €1,890 (or about $2,155). The company says retail pricing will climb well beyond €3,390 (over $3,800). Lemmo is targeting first deliveries for April 2027.
